The working expenses have correspondingly increased and last year the working expenses were $G,196,653.19 against gross earnings of $6,324,323.72. It will be seen, therefore, that in asking for an appropriation of six and one-half million dollars for the present year we are allowing for a very moderate increase in the business as compared with those of the year recently closed. If we may judge from the increase of business of recent years this sum will be required for the expenses and will be fully met by increased earnings.
You did not give the net earnings.
Last year, 1902-3, the net earnings were $127,-[DOT]670.53.

I see no objection to this item being charged against revenue ; my objection lias been rather the other way, that the government have year after year, asked for too small an amount to be charged to revenue and have managed to g,et on by charging to capital what ought to have been included in this item. I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman will require the money for which he is asking provided he charges to revenue everything that ought to be charged to revenue. I observe that he is charging to capital in the estimates at page 42, $320,000 for rolling stock. Looking at the stock account in the last report, June, 1902. I think it is highly probable that every dollar of that $700,000 should be included in the item now under consideration. However, that may be, I think the hon. gentleman is doing right in increasing the amount of this vote for working expenses for the reason I have mentioned, that in the past the government have asked for too little, charging too little to this particular item in order that they may show a fictitious net earning.

I would ask the hon. minister if in this increased item for working expenses for next year he has included anything for the trackmen in case he decides to give them an increase. I understand that the trackmen on the Intercolonial have made an application for an increase, and in case he decides to grant their request is there sufficient in this vote to provide for that increase ?

No, these estimates were prepared rather on the basis of the present rates of pay, as respects the officials generally. But it is in a general estimate that if it is determined to increase the pay of any class of servants we would have ample authority under this vote to pay the men but it might necessitate our coming to parliament for a supplementary estimate at a later stage.
There is an increase of $1,000,000 over last year.
Not over the working expenses of last year. The actual working expenses last year were $6,196,653 ; we had to take a supplementary estimate.
The object then is to include in this estimate the total amount, including what was in the supplementary estimates last year.
Yes, if possible.
Has. business on the road developed to such an extent as to justify this ?
Yes, the earnings have increased very considerably. For the year 1902 they were $5,671,000 and for 1903, $0,324,000. The increase for that year was very considerable.

May I he allowed to divert the discussion from this point to an item which was passed last night in my absence in reference to the vote of $83,000 for increased accommodation at Halifax ? I have already pointed out, both in previous sessions and during this session, the desirability of acquiring certain property at Halifax, immediately south of the present passenger station. I do not wish to repeat what I have already said two or three times in the House, but I believe that if the Intercolonial is going to have the increased business which we expect, it will be necessary to acquire the properties from North

street to Cornwallis street, fronting on Water street and extending westward to the rear of the lots on Lockman street. The property has deteriorated to some extent owing to the fact that a portion of Water street has already keen taken up by the Intercolonial Railway. Claims for compensation on that account have been made by the property owners. These claims they attempted to enforce in the Exchequer Court, but unsuccessfully. I have always thought that although there was a legal defence to their claim under the statute of limitations, nevertheless they were claims that might very properly be taken into consideration by the Crown, notwithstanding that they are barred by the statute of limitations. ' Although I myself, acting as solicitor, had to raise that point I have felt that it was a point whch the Crown might very well waive. I do not know that there would be any legal claim ; the solicitors of these parties think there would be, and it is certainly an arguable question, outside the statute of limitations. These claims, which are regarded as a grievance by the people interested, could no doubt be adjusted on very easy terms if these properties were acquired by the Crown at a fair valuation ; in fact that would result in a settlement of that kind being made with these parties. It seems to me that unless the advice of the experienced officials of the department is absolutely against the view I entertain, it will be in the interest of this country to acquire these properties. If that is likely to be the case 1 think that measure should be taken to acquire them as early as possible. It will not be very expensive to acquire them, and their acquisition may lead to decreased expenditure elsewhere. I am not familiar with the details of the work at Halifax, but now and then we have items for blasting and: filling in, and it seems to me that that work could be decreased if we acquired this property.

The estimates now before the House do not contemplate the acquisition of that property. The damage said to have been done to it by the extension of the railway down to deep water was done a long while ago, and the government of that day were not able to recognize any of the claims set up. I do not think that we can view the matter from the standpoint of any claim these people may have, but it might possibly bq wise to acquire the land for railway purposes. We need some land at present, but for immediate necessity that property would not be suitable; and, even in its present depreciated condition, it would cost a very considerable sum. For these reasons we have not undertaken to acquire it. Still there is much force in the contention that as the property is close to the railway, it might be well to acquire it if we can do so at a fair and reasonable cost. But the difficulty is the moment the government try to Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
buy a piece of ground, its value becomes very much enhanced. This property is not likely to be valuable for other purposes, and probably at no distant day it might be advisable for the railway authorities to purchase it, but it would only be purchased at a fair value, and not at the extravagant prices which property owners attach to their land as soon as they hear the government may require it. It is not wise therefore that we should bring down an appropriation, but if, as the result of negotiation, we find that tiie property can be obtained at anything like a fair and reasonable price, we might another session consider the advisability of buying it.

I would not ask anything more at this stage. I quite understand that high values are sometimes put on property under certain conditions, but of course the Crown always has a certain control by exercising the power of expropriation. I know what that leads to sometimes. We often find great differences in opinion among experts regarding values. In the case of one property, which was expropriated in Halifax some years ago, the value put upon it varied from $15,000 to $90,000, and there were about fifteen or twenty witnesses on each side. With regard to the claims for damages by the owners of this property, I have not very much to say. The Exchequer Court held that under the statute of limitations, the parties had no claim, and apart from that, there was a question whether the Crown had not a defence under certain legislation passed by the province of Nova Scotia. But while these people may not have a legal claim, their property was very much damaged in value by the fact of a railway running along the opposite side of the street. And in matters of that kind, where damages have resulted to the individuals, the Crown does not usually stand on its legal rights. Take, for instance, the sum paid Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann. They had certainly no legal right to compensation. They made a claim against the Crown on account of the failure of parliament to ratify a certain agreement. They had incurred certain expenses and took the risk of that agreement not being ratified, but nevertheless parliament thought it right that they should be recouped their expenses. Therefore, while these parties may or may not have a legal claim, still they have a moral claim, and I would be inclined to think that the Crown should take into consideration the question of giving them some reasonable compensation.

Why is there such an increase in this item ? I understand that this vote is not for the purpose of giving to the department the expenditure of anything for expropriations, where land may be needed, or for rolling stock, but only to make available for book-keeping purposes

tlie amount of revenue likely to be received from the Intercolonial.

The two items of revenue and expenditure very nearly balance, and in that sense perhaps the bon. gentleman is correct, but as a matter of fact the one does not necessarily relate to the other. This is an expropriation for the expense of working the Intercolonial, and whether the revenue equals that or not, we still need it.
It is limited entirely to that ?
Entirely to working expenses.
Anything out of ordinary expenses, such as harbour improvements, cannot be paid out of this fund ? But the amount seems an abnormal one. Do you expect an increased business ?
Yes.
I see that there are resolutions brought down for the stores account, I should judge that that is merely a book-keeping vote also.
Quite correct.
Which is not intended to give to the stores management on the Intercolonial the right of purchasing locomotives or anything else but the intention is simply to balance the stores account.

Inasmuch as the stores on hand and the amount of the vote in the Bill are substantially the same, it may be treated as a mere book-keeping account ; but it fixes a limit within which the department may hold stores. On the other question, the hon. gentleman is right.

With regard to many items there is a difference of opinion as to whether they should be charged to capital account or to income. Has the ministfjr directed his attention to the revision of the book-keeping in order to decide which items should be charged to one or to the other ? For, so long as there is no definite understanding. it is impossible to tell whether the road is growing better or worse. It seems to me it should be understood what items are to be charged to capital and what to running expenses. And, if that cannot be done under the present system, we should have a new system of book-keeping altogether.

I have tried to look into the matter a little, not with a view to these estimates, which were prepared by my predecessor, but because of my own interest in the matter. I am inclined to think that in many of these charges there is room for differences of opinion as to the account in which it should appear. A good many years ago, I had occasion to
seek the advice of an eminent railway man as to what a certain railway would earn, and he asked me how much I wanted it to earn. I admit that, in the accounts of any large undertaking there is always room for differences of opinion as to what should be charged to capital. There have been such differences of opinion between the late Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) and hon. gentlemen opposite. But I think that, after all, the amounts involved are not so great as to materially affect the result. I can only say that, so far as I am concerned, I desire to see sound methods of book-keeping. But I may say frankly, that I am not so anxious as some parties to make a profit or showing a surplus. I do not see why we should insist on having a surplus out of the Intercolonial any more than out of any other public work. We should see that the money is wisely and fairly expended, and if we can make ends meet, and show a balance, that is satisfactory. But if there is not a balance on the right side, I do not admit that that necessarily shows that there is anything wrong. In the case of another class of great works we do not even raise the question whether there is to be a profit or a loss. I speak of the canals. We do not attempt to make the canals pay even working expenses-and never did. We are content to lose, if it can be called a loss, the interest on the investment. Of course, it is not a loss, because it helps on the business of the country. But, so far as immediate return is concerned, the canals not only do not pay a profit, but do not even pay working expenses ; and, this year, without a moment's hesitation, we have thrown off the canal tolls altogether, and so have cut off our revenue from canals. So, I would ask the hon. gentlemen on both sides not to be too anxious about making a profit out of the Intercolonial, or even showing a surplus over working expenses. If we can make it, we will do it; but, if we expend the money wisely and faithfully and give the public the accommodation they require, the public gets the benefit just as in the case of a canal. I would not say this was a reason why we should be indifferent as to the balance. We should have a balance if we can. But, if. as a result of the operation of the road there is a balance on the wrong side, it is not reasonable to assume that the country is the loser.

There is only one way by which we can be enabled to judge fairly of the work of the Intercolonial, and that is by following the course recommended by the late Alexander Mackenzie when Minister of Public Works, and often discussed since. Here is a road finished a number of years ago. Unless there is an addition to the road in the shape of a building or purchase of some other railway, or something of that kind the capital ac-

count should be closed entirely. An expenditure at Halifax or St. John for terminal facilities or any similar expenditure should not be charged to capital, but to ordinary expenditure. The reason why it is desirable to have the same system of bookkeeping by one Minister of Railways as by another is that only in this way can we make comparisons. The making of a comparison does not necessarily mean that fault is to lie found with the expenditure. We are not finding fault with the expenditure. But there may be on that road a number of employees that are not necessary, there may lie lavish expenditure upon the road itself which is not justifiable. The only way by which we can judge of that is to compare one management with the other; and, if this is to be done the capital account should be closed entirely, so that all expenditures will be charged to current account. If one Minister of Railways, anxious to balance his accounts or make a favourable showing, charges to capital items which his predecessor charged to current expenses, comparison of the two administrations is quite impossible. This adds to the temptation to make unjustifiable expenditure, for the minister who makes it knows that his account can be so doctored that he cannot be compared with his predecessor. A minister may run the road in an economical way, while affording the public every accommodation, and his predecessor may be lavish in his expenditure, yet, by having recourse to charging his expenditure to capital, he can make as favourable a showing on revenue account as the other. This temptation to lavish expenditure would be removed if the capital account were closed.

So far as concerns my hon. friend's (Hon. Mr. (Haggart) remark that the purpose of a uniform system is that comparisons may be made, I think that is quite reasonable. But I think he goes too far when he advocates the closing of the capital account. He himself qualifies that by saying that in case of the building or acquiring of new railway there could be a charge to capital account. There have been considerable additions made to the Intercolonial since the construction of what may be called the original road. For instance, there was the St. Charles branch-that, the hon. gentleman will admit might properly be charged to capital. Then there was the short line- the so-called short line, for it did not prove to be very short. There was the Cape Breton extension. That is an addition to capital account. There was the Drummond County road, built to extend the Intercolonial to Montreal ; aud there are various other small branches and lines, additional sidings

No, additional sidings should not be charged to capital.
Hon. Mr. HAGGART

Well, the items I have given, together with others that do not occur to me at the moment, are fairly chargeable to capital account of the Intercolonial, and fairly increase that capital account, though the road is sometimes referred to in the course of discussion as being the same property as was brought into existence by the original construction. Let me show my hon. friend that we could not possibly justify the closing of the capital account even without constructing a new road. It is known to all men of experience in railway matters that during the last ten years there has been a revolution in regard to railway construction. Railways which were equipped in a very light manner are now putting on heavy equipments. A road with 56-pound rails fifteen years ago is today putting on 90-pound rails, some are putting on even heavier rails. A locomotive a few years ago cost only a small sum, but to-day you are paying practically double the price for it, and you are getting double value. Without the addition of a single mile to the length of that road, you might find it necessary in the case of a road like the Intercolonial Railway to expend several millions in the way of betterments, something which any railway manager would consider as betterments, in the shape of heavier rails, in the shape of improved grades, in the shape of better rolling stock. In all these things railroad construction and operation have been revolutionized in the last ten years, and you would find it necessary to have a capital account from which to purchase these things, because no railroad could purchase them out of its revenue. If the capital account were to be closed, it would mean that there could be no advance with the times at all. My hon. friend presses the matter too far when he says that the capital account should be closed.

It is for the very purposes that the hon. gentleman has mentioned that I wish the capital account to be closed. This is not my own idea alone, but it is the idea of the friends of the government when they were in opposition. I have heard Mr. Mackenzie state again and again in this House that the only remedy for the unsatisfactory state of affairs on the Intercolonial Railway, and the charges to capital account, was to close that account altogether. I differ with the Minister of Finance in that respect. On an ordinary road, if you take up a 56-pound rail and put on a 90-pound rail, the difference is charged to capital account. My opinion is that if it is necessary for a road to put on a 90-pound rail, it should be charged1 to the ordinary revenue of the road-it will earn more afterwards ; but do not charge it to capital account. I know that railroads ordinarily proceed as the hon. Minister of Finance has stated, and I tried to adopt that

system, which I thought was the correct one. I think now that when you change a locomotive from a lighter type to a heavier type, the difference should not be charged to capital account, and the same with rails. The only true remedy, and the Finance Minister ought to insist upon it, is to give no latitude of that kind to the department. If they want to improve the road let the bald statement be made to the public that there is a certain expenditure in excess of revenue, and let the company judge whether that is justifiable or not; but keep them strictly to this principle, that everything that is expended on the road, either for terminals, or for improvements in the way of better locomotives, better track and so forth, shall be charged to the ordinary revenue of the road. Then you will have a management better than any devices that you can imagine in arranging the accouuts.

My hon. friend is asking us to go a great deal further than, I am sure, his friends generally would ask us to go. The most that anybody could claim is that we should keep the capital account confined strictly to betterments of the road. Now, I think that the principle the hon. gentleman has laid down is one that practical railway men do not agree with. There are differences of opinion as to whether a given expenditure is a mere renewal or a betterment. I think it can be safely laid down as a principle that if you add something which increases the value of your road, and if you make two blades of grass to grow where only one grew before, if I may use that illustration, you have a betterment for your road, and you have value for it. and that is a proper addition to your capital account. My hon. friend says: Charge these larger locomotives and everything of that kind to the revenue account. But there is no revenue account to bear it. and there will be no such revenue account. Any railroad that has to provide all these things out of revenue would not get them at all. It would simply mean coming here and asking, on revenue account, for large sums of money which would not be fairly chargeable to revenue.
What is the difference, so far as the country is concerned, since the country has to pay it ?

Yes, I can answer that. That is a rough-and-ready way of looking at it, and if that is the correct way. then you might as well say, What difference does it make anyhow whether you charge an item to capital or revenue since the country has to pay for it ?

The country would know how to compare the management of the road under one minister with its management under another. Notv we do not know what one minister charges to capital account and what another minister charges
to revenue. I would like to ask the Finance Minister how an ordinary railway corporation would furnish the money, if they kept the account as he proposes. I may be wrong, but I am asking for information. For instance, if the hon. gentleman was managing the Grand Trunk Railway and he required betterments in the cars, in the weight of rails, &c., how would the Grand Trunk raise the money if they did not pay it out of revenue ? Would you have to issue new stock all the time ?

Most certainly, that is exactly what any railway company would do. If it requires anything in the way of betterment, it must issue new stock. If the road is very prosperous and has the revenue to pay all its dividends and leave a handsome balance, it might use some portion of that for improvements. There is many a corporation which is making a good deal of money, but is only paying moderate dividends, because it applies its profits to improvements all the time. But no ordinary railway company can do that. Railway companies generally provide for betterments by the issue of capital stock. I think I can show my hon. friend that what would be done in the case of a great railway company is what we are willing to do in the case of the Intercolonial Railway.

I was not complaining that we could not understand whether the road was paying or not, nor was I complaining because the road is not paying. But it seems to me we ought to have some barometer to tell us whether the road is running behind, or whether it is managed in such a way as to make it a paying road. We ought to know whether there is business enough in that part of the country to make the road pay expenses. The minister says : Suppose you wanted betterments on that road, out of what account are you going to pay them, if you do not charge them to capital account How do we pay them now ? We vote the money here, and could we not do that with regard to betterments in the same way as we do with deficits ? It makes no difference. I agree with the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. I have always thought, though not knowing much about the methods of keeping railway accounts, that that was the only solution of the situation, namely, to close your capital account. Then the country will know, whether it is wise to run such a railway. I never imagined that the railway ought to be run so as to bring in a big revenue, I always understood it was constructed for the benefit of the country. The earnings of the railway, however, ought to be somewhere near enough to pay the running exn penses. otherwise there is evidently no need for that railway. Now, if it does not pay running expenses, certain things are lacking, either the freight rates and the passenger rates are too low. or else the railway

must be running through a portion of country where there is not sufficient trade, or it must be managed in such a way that other railways are taking trade away from it. On the other hand, the government ought to be able to make a comparison as between its management by different administrations. When you have the road badly managed it does not pay, when you have it well managed it does pay. The country requires to be able to make some comparison, and the object of keeping the books should be that a fair comparison may be made, that there may be some barometer to show how the road is running. I suggest that, but if any other means can be devised that would be better, it is most desirable that they should be adopted.

It certainly would not be a fair means of comparison if we were to undertake to charge all these things to revenue account, because they have not been charged to revenue account in the past. The points of difference between the classes of items charged to capital now and in former days are not very wide. The same classes of items were charged to capital account in former days as are charged now. It may be that in late years, owing to the increased - business, the items have been larger, but that items of the same class have been charged to capital account in past years is beyond all question. Keeping accounts in the way suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) would not be fair for the purposes of comparison, not fair as a means of keeping railway accounts. He perhaps knows that last session the Grand Trunk Railway Company received authority from us to issue a- large amount of new stock, and that the Canadian Pacific Railway increased its stock by $20,000,000, although I do not think they added a mile of road ,to their system. They used that money in providing betterments and improvements upon the road. Certainly the greater part of it went into rolling stock. So that my hon. friend will see that he is asking us to adopt a system of keeping the accounts which would not be accepted by any great railway in the country.

That might be the case, and yet it might not be a proper course to adopt here. There has been a great deal of difference between the two sides of the House as to what should and what should not be charged to 'capital account. We have that contention up every year, and it is for the purpose of doing away with it that we should adopt a system that would enable us to make a fair comparison. The hon. Minister of Finance says that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway' have been obliged to issue new stock, the proceeds of which have been expended on betterments to the roads. That is true, but the roads are worth more money, and they have thus added to the value of their pro-Mr. SPROULE.
perties. If our property were made more valuable by a million dollars than it is it would be quite different, because you would have an asset to offset the expenditure. But, in regard to ordinary running expenses, taking betterments into account, we should be able to have these accounts kept in some more simple and understandable way than that in which they are now kept.

I notice that the hon. Minister of Finance, in defending the present plan, states that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway have been adding to their capital, account. These railways would have a very poor show to get money upon the money market if they could not show that they were being operated at a profit. They must show a profit, and that being so, they are run much more carefully than a road which is being operated without any expectation, not only of making a profit, but of paying running expenses. I contend that this is a very vicious system. It may be excused by going to some localities and telling the people that: We are carrying our freight at rates at which we would otherwise be unable to carry it for. This is a most unbusinesslike thing for the government to do. We have been floating our bonds in the old country, and we have been representing that we are going to pay interest upon them. Just fancy going to the old country with a railwiay deal involving a hundred million dollars and say, taking into consideration the way in which the Intercolonial Railway has been managed, that the concern is not going to be able to pay interest on the capital invested In it. Although we are rich, and although the country is progressing, we cannot hope to keep it up for all time. Wie cannot have too many Pacific cables thrown upon this country when we have to pay $150,000 as our share of the loss yearly on working expenses in connection with the concern. Now, we are considering a railway out of which the hon. Minister of Finance tells us we should not expect to get anything. We are not getting anything out of our canals. There are no competing canals, and therefore we cannot tell what they might do. But I contend that after building a railway which is competing in many cases with other railways, it should be maintained on business principles, and the first business principle for any man who goes into any kind of business is to make a profit upon his investments. Otherwise, why go into business at all ? Why not let private enterprise take hold of it ? Yet the government have gone into a railway upon which they have expended $80,000,000, and the hon. Minister of Finance tells us that the intention was not to make a return upon it. If they had to raise that money to-day in England, and if they went before the financiers of England with the statement which has been made by the hon. Minister of Finance, that they were going into an

expenditure of $80,000,000 out of which they did not expect to make the interest or the running expenses, what would the financiers of England say ? It is all very well, with an abounding revenue, to take that view of the question, but when a period of depression comes, as the hon. Minister of Finance told us three years ago that it would come, how are we going to stand in the money markets of England ? We have been paying off some o-f our four per cent debentures. Let us go to England to-morrow and try to raise $100,000,000, even if the loan had the endorsement of the government of Canada. The endorsement of the province of Ontario could not get money the other day at three and a-ha!f per cent. If we could apply business principles to all the dealings of the government the better it would be, not only for the government, but for the country as a whole. The government are an example to the country, and if large corporations are going to go into business upon the same principle, that is to say, that they not only do not expect to get any return upon the money they -have invested,' but that they are not going to pay running expenses, it will prove to be a vicious principle in connection with the business of the country. I can understand that in exceptional circumstances, such as the building of a railway for military purposes, that you might not expect a return in money from that. That is, to a large extent, the position of the Intercolonial Railway, tout we are going to parallel that railway by another railway, and we do not expect it to pay running expenses for years. Under these circumstances, I contend that the less we do of this kind of thing the better, and quite endorse the contention of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) that the time should come soon when we should stop all further expenditure on capital account, particularly when we are getting no return upon it. I contend that is the plainest and the best way. A man does not require to toe a bookkeeper to understand that if there is a capital account of $100,000,000 which is stationary it should not toe added to, but the balance over and above that should be paid out of revenue or by vote here.

I am afraid I cannot 'quite see the bearing of my hon. friend's argument, or what real connection it 'has with the question under discussion. I pointed out that the Canadian Pacific Railway had issued a large amount of stock for betterments on its road. The hon. gentleman's reply to that is that the Canadian Pacific Railway could not have issued that stock unless it could have shown that it was going to earn the profit upon it, and he says that no capital should be expended in a transaction of this kind unless you can show that it is going to make a profit. I beg to differ with my hon. friend there. This country would never have been
built up on any such principle as he has enunciated. We have spent $83,000,000 upon our canals, and we never expect to get one dollar of return in the way of interest upon the money. Does my 'hon. friend say that it is wrong for us to carry on these canals unless we are going to have a book-keeping account and show every year that we are dragging money out of the canal traffic to pay for it ? I want to tell my hon. 'friend that this country was never built up that way.
That is the way it was built up.

The hon. gentleman insists that you must have profit in cash in the treasury, but the policy of the country has been to get the profit in the development of the business of the country. We do not expect that you should get the revenue into the treasury, because if the country prospers by the' development of public works, the country reaps a rich reward ; and even though you get no profit on a particular railway or canal, if these are instruments for the development of the trade of the country, it is absurd to say they are unprofitable investments. All the same, I have not said that it is not desirable to get a fair return where you can, without oppressing the business of the country ; I have not said that we should not have any advantage out of the Intercolonial Railway ; I have not said that we should not have a balance on the right side ; but I do say, that I would apply to any public work the larger view, namely, let us see that it is honestly and faithfully and justly administered, and let us get a balance on the right side if we can, but if we fail, let us comfort ourselves with the thought that by means of that railway system or canal system, we are getting our profit in the development of the trade of the country.
It seems to me that there is no fair comparison between a railway and a' canal.
Why ?

Because the canal is a water-way which every man who wishes to build a boat can take advantage of, whereas, a railway is given over to one individual or corporation and no others can take advantage of it. You do not give running rights to all other roads over the Intercolonial Railway and not charge them for the privilege, tout our water-ways and our canals are open to all the world. The canals of Canada and the United 'States are as equally available to the people of one country as of the other. A railway is entirely different.

The Minister of Customs recently denied a statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Osier). I say that the capital expenditure on the Intercolonial

Railway is $68,645,852, or an increase of over four and a half millions on capital account last year. My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) made^ tlie statement that when the Intercolonial Railway was finished, according to Sir Saudford Fleming there was about $14,000,000 charged to capital account, and the Minister of Customs said he was wrong. Can the Minister of Railways, through his deputy minister, inform the House whether the amount expended on the old European and North American road, and the Halifax-Truro section is' included in the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway ?
The deputy minister says that it is included.
Are you' certain of that ?
I was not present when the discussion arose, but I am so advised by the deputy minister, who speaks from recollection.

If that be the case, then I do not see how you can possibly balance your public accounts.
Rental to the Grand Trunk Railway, $112,000. Hon. Mr. HAGGART. I thought this was a statutory payment.
Now, that the hon. gentleman mentions it, I think it is covered by the statute, but the practice has been to vote it.

We were Informed on a previous occasion, that we would be given figures to enable us to ascertain whether the Drummond County Railway has enabled the Intercolonial Railway to pay better than it did before the extension to Montreal.

I have no statement which will enable me to answer that question. Possibly that is a little like the man who advertises and who cannot just tell on what particular advertisement he has had
his order ; although he knows that his business has increased generally. We know the business of the Intercolonial Railway has largely increased, and lam inclined to think that a very considerable portion of that ini' ' "se is due to the extension to Montreal.
There should be divisional accounts kept, and we ought to be enabled to make a comparison. >

They do not separate the different divisions, but I suppose a general idea could be had as to which section of the road has the largest traffic. I do not think it is possible to give exact information.

Any railway manager would be able to give that information. He is able to take the different stations along the road, make allowances for through-traffic, and tell to a dollar the earnings on each division.
My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) never had such a system in his day.
You can tell it from the present system of bookkeeping on the Intercolonial Railway.
The accounts are kept precisely ihe same n6w as in the time of my hon. friend.
I know that the accounts are kept in the same way, or nearly the same way, and I say that 'from those accounts', you can tell the earnings of each division on the road.
It could he only an approximate statement.
No, you can give it almost exactly.

We were assured over and over again by the ex-Minister of Railways, when he proposed to extend the Intercolonial to Montreal, that the future earnings of the road would show that the investment had been profitable. We desire to have this information now, in order to ascertain whether that statement was justified or not. Judging from the Canadian Pacific Railway report, this information ought to be easily ascertained. From that report we can ascertain the earnings and expenses, the profit or the loss on any portion of the road. If it can be done in'the ease of the Canadian Pacific Railway there should be no difficulty in doing it in the case of the Intercolonial.

I can see that it may be necessary to keep a separate account of the earnings and expenses of a leased line. All I can say with reference to the Intercolonial is that such statements have not been kept in the past and are not at present available.

In view of the debate which took place at the time the Drummond County Railway was purchased by the government, and the predictions then made as to the great increase in traffic that would come to the Intercolonial, it was naturally expected on this side of the House that the government would keep a separate account for that railway and be able to verify the statements they made at that time by producing the accounts. That can be done and ought to be done and we are entitled to receive that information from the Minister of Railways and Canals at any time, but especially when he is getting his estimates through.
I am afraid I cannot give it.
If that account is kept distinct that the minister promises to bring it down another year as a matter of course, we will close up parliament and go home.
Slow to promise, sure to perform.
I think we should have the promise.

I am sure the Minister of Finance would be willing to do this if he realized how easy it is. Every station has a statement of the freight and passengers handled at it. and that information is easily accessible. It is a simple thing when you come to look into it and the minister might fairly promise to do this. It would be of interest to know what part of the road is profitable and what part is unprofitable. You could tell what the working expenses of each station are and the amount of freight handled at it, then yon know the amount of through-freight that is shipped over the line and you can get the number of passengers who have bought tickets at each station and who arrived at each station. I think if the hon. Minister of Finance will think it over-
I will promise to think it over.

We got a promise of this kind from the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals when we w7ere voting the money for the purchase of the Drummond County Railway. The whole question was threshed out then and it was shown how easy it would be to keep an account of this and we had a promise that we would know whether the purchase of the Drummond County Railway proved profitable or not.

This is important to our side of the House because we venture statements on certain questions which only time can prove to be correct or incorrect. Our reputation is at stake and for the purpose of ascertaining whether our statements or those of the government have proved to be correct we should have that information. It is only a matter of a little book-keeping, because whether it is through-freight or local freight you know how many miles it has been hauled over the road and we also know exactly the passenger traffic that has taken place on it.

Supposing you had fifty passengers from Halifax to Montreal under the present system, how could you tell how many of these you would have had if you had not secured the connection through to Montreal ?

You know how many miles it is from Halifax to Quebec and how many from Quebec to Montreal and you deduct the one from the other ; you know the number of passengers passing over the Drummoned County Railway; then you credit a part of the price of each ticket to the Drummond County Railway in proportion to the length of that line so it is an easy matter to keep the account. Supposing you are sending a quantity of freight ; it passes over the whole road or over a few miles of it, but you know the train mileage and you know the earning per train mile on that road.

My hon. friend missed my point. Given the fifty passengers whom I have taken for illustration.then you can make a division of the probable portion of their fares which should be credited to the different sections of the road, but how can you tell how many of these would have left Halifax for Montreal by the Intercolonial if you did not have any road to Montreal and they were able to go only as far as Quebec.
Surely that would'be all to your benefit because the more traffic there is the more credit it is to you.

I have no doubt it would be of interest and value to the country if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) would order, that for the next few years at all events, separate accounts should be kept for that division of the road. I quite admit that as the minister has said, it does not follow that although you know a particular section of your road has been worked at a loss you would have got as much traffic on your main line if you had not had that section of road. A railway company may have a feeder and although the feeder may itself be worked at a loss it may bring in profit to the main line. Apart from that question, it may be of very considerable benefit to the country to know exactly what such a line as you now have running into Montreal costs you as a portion of your main system. It would be valuable especially if the government were disposed on some other occasion to enter into a similar contract. I did not understand the minister to dispute that it is possible to keep such an account with accuracy, there cannot be any doubt upon that * point, both as to earnings and expenses. We want no better evidence on that point than the clause inserted toy the government for the protection of tlie country in the Bill which we passed through the House last night in which it is provided that separate and distinct accounts shall be kept of the earnings and expenses of the eastern section and the western section of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. It is possible to keep a distinct; account of the earnings and expenses of the section of railway entering Montreal that has been the subject of discussion for the last half hour. There is no trouble about keeping the accounts ; -the extra expense would not involve more than the salary of one clerk during the year. The value of the accounts will be very great indeed, and I think it would be well if the minister would order that they be kept during the next year or two so that the country may know whether the acquisition of that line has been a benefit of not. After we get thh

accounts it will open to the government; to argue that although they may lose money on the particular section, that fact does not settle the whole question, because the road, may be of value for other purposes than, simply the revenue derived1 for traffic over that section.
Prince Edward Island Railway, $256,000.

Is it the intention of the government to have a second train a day between Summerside and Tignish during the coming winter, as was instituted by the Minister of Railways last year and which proved of such great advantage to the people.

I have not had before me any question of changing the general arrangements of the Prince Edward Island Railway. Whatever the present accommodation is will toe continued; and if necessity be ' shown for anything more, we shall be glad to consider it. We do not in the estimates contemplate any change.
What is the length of the road ?
210 miles besides 50 miles of the new branch.

Does the hon. minister think it prudent to construct a new railway to Moncton in the face of the results shown by the Intercolonial and the Prince Edward Island Railway ? What is the reason that it is not possible to derive a revenue from the Intercolonial, which traverses such a magnificent country as the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and from the Prince Edward Island Railway which runs through what an hon. gentleman described last night as the garden of the Dominion ? We find private corporations investing hundreds of millions of dollars in railways and paying large dividends every year, and in every case the capital is very much watered. I have here the report of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The aggregate capital of that road is said to be $341,000,000. I do not know how much of that is water, but we know that the capital Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
stock of $25,000,000 was originally issued and subscribed for at twenty-five cents on the dollar, so that out of that amount of $25,000,000, $18,750,000 is water. I do not know how much more of the $340,000,000 is water, but according to its report of 1903 the net revenue of that company gave five and nine-tenths per cent on its capital. If that be the case, there must be some extraordinary leakages on the Intercolonial which prevent its yielding any profit, and that shows the necessity of adopting some method of book-keeping which will show where those leaks take place. We ought to know what portions of the road are earning dividends and what are losing money. When a business man opens up a new branch he keeps a separate account for it. If he finds that it yields a profit, he keeps on working it; tout if not he gives it up. There are certain works on which the public money is expended in the interest of the people, in order to develop the resources of the country, and without any expectation of realizing a profit in cash. In this category are our canals, which are great national outlets for our commerce, and which could not be constructed by private enterprise. But the railways are in a different position. They may be constructed out of private capital, ana the railway magnates become millionaires in a few years. I am satisfied that the promoters of the Canadian Pacific Railway have all become multi-millionaires. But what I fail to understand is why the government should not be in a position to secure the services of men just as competent as those Who built the Canadian Pacific Railway. We are in a position to borrow money at a lower rate of interest. My idea would be for the government to build a road from Quebec, north of lake Winnipeg, thence through the prairie and the Rocky Mountains to Port Simpson. Such a proposition would have received my support. But this lengthening of the tail was what I seriously objected to, because I believe the present Intercolonial road is good for all the requirements of the section of the country through which it runs. And, with an expenditure of twenty-five per cent of the money which the government will spend in making the road from Quebec to Moncton, they could maintain a splendid harbour at Quebec which would enable them to do the business and would save the haul from Quebec to Moncton in the transportation of grain-if they ever hope to carry grain by that road.

I thank the committee and you, Mr. Chairman. In the calculations I have made I assume that the road will cost this country $100,000,000-that that amount will construct and equip the road. If the cost is more the figures will have to be revised accordingly. I have here a table ' which I have prepared, showing the cost to the country of this road at the end of 50 years. I assume that it will take five years to build the road, and that for ten years thereafter we shall receive no rent, as for seven years no rent is charged, and for three following years rent is charged at the rate of three per cent on the cost, but if not earned by the road) it is added to the capital account, and on that total capital the Grand Trunk Pacific pays rent thereafter at 3 per cent. I have proceeded on the basis of the experience of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Though that road has not yet been in operation for 20 years it is paying interest or dividends on the capitalization of $320,000,000 I have estimated that, for the first five years, after the ten years the proposed road should pay 3 per cent interest, the next five years 4 per cent interest, and so on, adding 1 per cent every five years up to the end of the fifty year period. This does not mean that a larger amount would not be earned, but that, as the capital expendture would be reduced by the difference between the interest we would have to pay-3*per cent-and the returns of the road, the amount of the capital account would be progressively reduced. So, at the end of 50 years the country would own the road at a cost of $22,754,559, with an earning capacity of $39,470,270 per annum, figuring it out on the basis of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not put any water into this $100,000,000 of capital expenditure-it is all cash properly and legitimately expended. It will he observed that I have shown an increased rate of dividend. So I cannot see anything wrong with the proposition. If I were in the position of the government and going into the building of this railroad I would look around and find some such man as Van Horne and get him to direct the affair. Supposing that, at the end of the period, the government were to give a man like Van Horne 51 per cent of the stock, retaining 49 per cent, they would have a 7 or 8 per cent dividend on the balance of the money, so that the road would be a good source of revenue. I am very much obliged to the Finance Minister and to you, Mr. Chairman, for giving me permission to present these figures.
Now, I believe the acting Minister of Railways and Canals will see the propriety of adopting some system of book-keeping by which he will be enabled to know how the operations of the road are being carried on. As a business man in a small way, I could not get along if I did not know at the end of each month how my business is <roins. I have to know how much I owe

12S96
andi how I am going to pay it, and then I can go to bed and sleep at night. But if I did not know that, I would worry all night. Which reminds me of a story. There was a man who had given "a note which was about due, and he had no visible means of paying it. He was very much worried over it, so much that he could not stay at home and face the trouble, but went away to a neighbouring town. He stopped at an hotel, but at night be could not sleep-turned and tossed in bed and at times got up and walked about his room and up and down the hall outside. The gentleman sleeping in the room alongside was prevented from sleeping by the other's restlessness, so he rose and asked the disturbed one what was the cause of the trouble. ' I don't know that its any of your business,' was the reply. ' Well,' said the good-natured neighbour, ' I thought perhaps I might be able to help you or afford you relief, so that you might get to bed and sleep.' Feeling that he had a sympathizing listener, the debtor said, ' I have a note coming due to-morrow, and I do not know where I am going to get the money to pay it.' 'Is that all,' said the other; 'well, you had better go to bed, and let the other fellow do the walking.'

1 am afraid, Mr. Chairman, you will not be so indulgent with me as you have been with our respected friend, therefore, I shall not be able to follow him in these figures. 1 am glad, however, to have his endorsement of the policy of building a transcontinental road, at all events through the northern part of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. The only fault he seems to find with us is that we go a little too far south ; that is to say, that while this has been called a sub-Arctic scheme, he wants it to be an entirely Arctic scheme. But coming back to the Prince Edward Island Railway, my hon. friend asked for an explanation why we have a loss on that road. He gave us some information about the Canadian Pacific Railway, and he said there was a lot of water in that. Well, in the case of the Prince Edward Island Railway, there is a lot of water round it, and this is largely the explanation why the Prince Edward Island Railway can hardly be expected to be a profitable enterprise.
A very large part of the traffic of Prince Edward Island is served by water communication. Still, a railway was necessary for the development of that portion of the country, and I do not think we can look forward at any time to finding it a very profitable undertaking. Many of the people live on the sea-shore, and' their means of communication are by water.

This item is to pay for the cost of necessary works now under contract, protection to
the north bank, installation of an electric system for operating the lock gates, new works, and repairs and enlargement, and regulating weir at lock 17.
Will the minister please give the name of the contractors to whom this money is to be paid, and the total cost of the electric light plant?

The contractor for the mechanism of the lock gates is M. P. Davis. Mr. J. J. Fallon is the contractor for some work on the wharf. I do not find the cost of the installation of the electric system separately. That is not for an electric light plant but it is for operating the lock gates, valves and workshops of the canal by electricity. The contract price is $35,496. That work is finished. There is an additional work of the same character going on by the same contractor.
I will get the cost of the electric plant later, if the hon. gentleman wishes.
I understood the work on the Cornwall canal was completed some time ago. Will this finally complete the whole work on the canal ?
Yes, the work that is contemplated this year. The shops are not yet done, but the canal work proper has been done.

A few years ago when these works were undertaken, and after they had been in progress for some time, the government decided that it was necessary to have a steamer to run from one end of the works to the other, that is from Cornwall to Prescott, through the Cornwall, Farran's Point, Rapide des Plats and Galops canals. That was for the superintending engineer, Mr. Rubidge, and when I asked for an explanation, some years ago, the answer was given that it was necessary for him to travel over these works. It cost $8,000 or $10,000 a year to keep that boat in operation, and now, although the works are practically completed, the boat is still employed. The boat is really idle as there is nothing for it to do. In fact, as I understand it, the only works that it would be necessary for the engineer to visit occasionally would be those in the north channel, which are being carried on by Mr. W. A. Cleveland, and I do not think that the engineer in charge, Mr. Rubidge, visits them very often. Now, there is an expenditure,
I suppose, of from $7,000 to $10,000 per annum for the maintenance of that boat.
I may say also at the same time that the position that Mr. Rubidge has held for so many years has been really abandoned, because of others being appointed to take charge of certain parts of the work. I want to ask the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals now, if, when the works are practically completed, this expenditure should not be done away with ? I do not think it is further necessary. The hon.

acting minister will quite understand that we have another steamer in lieu of the ' Scout ' that runs up and down the river, and that can readily do this work whenever necessary. I am not saying anything now in the way of fault finding with anything that has been done in the past, but it does seem a little unfair that this steamer should be allowed to lie at Cornwall practically all summer with a staff employed, and nothing to do. I would like to ask the hon. acting minister if it is intended to continue that condition of affairs ? I quite understand that he is not fully cognizant of the whole situation.

I think perhaps the explanation of the boat not being so busily occupied is due to the fact that Mr. Rubidge has not been in good health. The ' Scout ' has been transferred to the Marine and Fisheries Department and is being devoted to the lighting service. It will probably be necessary that there shall be a boat for the canal proper and it is very likely that the boat will be required for the superintendent after the work of construction is over and Mr. Rubidge no longer needs it,
Mr. REID (Grenville), Of course, as far as Mr. Rubidge is concerned, I can quite understand that he is not probably in good health. He is over eighty years of age, and I believe that he has arrived at an age when lie is hardly fit for the position. I would suggest that he be retired even at his salary for the balance of his days. I am not saying anything against Mr. Rubidge but the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals states that the boat may be required by the superintendent. I can hardly see how that will work because I understand that there is a superintendent who has charge of the Cornwall canal only. Then there is a superintendent who has charge of the Williamsburg canal, so that it would be impossible to manage this boat in that way and there could not be any possible use in simply having this steamer running up and down the canal. If it were necessary to have a superintending engineer for works of construction it might be quite different, but, these works are all completed now and there is no actual necessity for the steamer. I would like to have the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals explain how the superintendent could use the steamer in that way. There are two superintendents now.

My hon. friend has referred to the local officers. There is a general superintendent of the St. Lawrence canal system and if he is to continue his work and to examine the various canals he will probably need a boat for that purpose.

I would like (o know who the general superintendent is. I
never heard before that there was a general superintendent of canals.
I never had the pleasure of seeing him, but I am informed that his name is Stewart.

The hon. acting minister states that Mr. Stewart is the general superintendent. Mr. Stewart is in charge of the Williamsburg canal and there is another gentleman in charge of the Cornwall canal. I think his name is Daily. So that, there are two superintendents. Has Mr. Stewart charge of the Cornwall canal as well as charge of the Williamsburg canal ?

I am sorry, that, not having visited these canals myself, I am not as well informed as I would like to be in regard to them, but I am advised that Mr. Stewart's duties include the supervision of the Cornwall canal as well as of the Williamsburg canal.

That is news to me because there was a superintendent appointed for the Cornwall canal and he believes he is in the same position as Mr. Stewart. Is it the intention that Mr. Stewart is to have charge of this steamer for use on the Cornwall and other canals ?

For the present the steamer remains in charge of Mr. Rubidge. But, if anything should occur that Mr. Rubidge retires from the service and does not longer require the steamer we shall have to consider what shall be done. I would not like to make a definite statement to my hon. friend.

I can understand that the hon. acting minister is not thoroughly acquainted with the situation there. The people along the river have been making complaints for some little time about this steamer and I am satisfied it is not a necessity. I am, however, satisfied that if the matter were brought to the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals, whoever may be in charge of the department, it will be looked into and perhaps remedied.
Farran's point canal-enlargement, $9,600.

This is for work which has been done by the Canadian Construction Company for lowering the old canal bottom, repairing sills and pier and providing one pair of larger gates for old lock No. 22. The appropriation is $12,000, from which we have taken one-fifth.
This is to complete the contract ?	*
Yes.
That is wound up ?

Yes.
Rapide Plat, $20,000.
Who is the contractor ?
One of the Gilberts.
Is that at the upper entrance ?

Upper entrance ; extension of south pier.
Galops canal, enlargement, $102,400.
This expenditure is for the Iroquois section, $17,268 ; the Cardinal section, $39,000 ; the upper entrance, $46,350 ; and $25,000 to meet possible claims ; making $127,618.
What was done with regard to the slide that took place on the Cardinal section ?
The contractors, Wm. Davis and Sons, are making it good at their own cost.
Has the leakage on the bank between Iroquois and Cardinal been repaired ?
That has been repaired by the government.

There has been quite an agitation at Cardinal to have the government install some kind of machinery to swing that bridge, which is now being done by hand. If you do not put in a plant you should have two men more there, so that the work can be done faster than at present. It would be a great convenience.

It certainly would be desirable if some better arrangement were made for the swinging. That matter is now' under consideration.
North channel and dam, $64,000.
Where is this work 7
Between Prescott and Coteau Landing. Except for some surveys made by our own officers, no part of the work has yet been done.

In former days the steamer ' Alert ' was used for this work, and there is no better steamer on the river for that purpose. I think that the government might very well use the [DOT] Alert ' for the sweeping of the channel. No doubt she would come in very useful but she would be hardly adapted for the purpose mentioned by the acting minister. I quite understand that next year she can be employed very usefully in doing something of this kind and save the expense that would unquestionably be caused by employing another steamer. The hon. minister might use her for that purpose.

That is one of the services in which the boat might usefully be employed.
(Welland canal, to provide electric light plant, $44,000.
Is this being done by contract and has the contract been let ?

It will be done but the work is not yet commenced. We propose to take in this item $55,000 but we have asked in the supplementary estimates a further sum of $45,000, making the estimated cost of the whole undertaking $100,000 which we believe will furnish a complete electric light plant for the whole canal. This estimate is made on the report of an electrical engineer. We expect the work will be done by contract.
Has the contract yet been let ?
No.
Will it be completed in time for use this season ?
I am afraid it is too much to expect it for this season.
It is not a kind of work that will take a great deal of time to install.

It would not take a very long time but it is hardly probable that it would be done this season. It will be done probably during the winter

and will be ready In time for tlie opening of navigation next spring.

I would ask the hon. minister if there is any possibility of placing an electric light plant on the Iroquois and Cardinal section of the St. Lawrence canals at the present time. The Lacliine canal, the Soulanges canal and the Cornwall canal all have electric light plants and 1 see by the supplementary estimates that the Farran's point canal is to have an acetylene gas plant installed on it, although I understand the electric light is best. When this is done the only canal which will have no lighting system at all will be this Iroquois and Cardinal section and I think that it is absolutelv necessary, especially that at the head of the canal where the boats are coming in and out, that there should be good light.

No doubt the hon. gentleman is correct in the suggestion that an electric light system would be the better and I have no doubt that we will gradually introduce electric light on all the canals. In some instances we will be able to make arrangements with neighbouring towns having electric light plants to supply the light and in others we will have to establish our own plants, but the aim of the department is to have the electric light system generally employed upon the canals.
Is it not a fact that when this plant is placed on the Welland canal, every canal will have an electric light plant from the Lacliine to the Welland except the two I have mentioned ?
The [DOT]Welland canal is lighted by gas at present.
When this is done will not every canal have electric light except this one stretch to which I have referred ?

I am told that the Rapide Plat and Galops canal have no electric light. Of course the Iroquois and Galops are interchangeable terms. The Farran's point canal is being lighted by gas. The Rapide Plat has no electric light. However, there is no doubt that the electric light system is very useful and that it will be applied generally.

These two stretches which are on the Morrisburg section are the only two not lighted by electricity. There are electric light plants in each place, the electric light system could be installed at verv little cost and there is no doubt that it would be of great benefit to the maritime men. It could be done quite easily and it would complete the whole system.
We will have to consider it.

Is it the intention of the government to purchase the electrical 404*
energy necessary for the lighting of the Welland canal from one of the several electric light producers in the neighbourhood ? Is it the intention of the government to produce its own electricity or to purchase or lease from one of the companies that are in the locality ?
This estimate is for the plant, but it contemplates obtaining the power to supply that plant from one of the companies in the vicinity.
The contract has not been let to anyone ?
No.
Nor have tenders been called for V
No. nothing has been done.
Is the lighting of all these canals done by contract, that is the installation of the plant ?
I think it has been done by tender and contract generally.
What is the cost per annum of lighting the Coteau, Lacliine and Cornwall canals ?
What obstruction is this V
This is to deepen the rock cut at Ramy's point, the only shallow rock cutting left in the canal, which is the cause of considerable trouble in times of low water.
Is it expected that that will cost $217,000 ?

That is to cost only $5,000. In addition to that there are the votes.
To remove the centre pier ot three bridges on the long level and to rebuild the bridges at Welland, Quaker and Port Robinson, estimated cost, $130,000. .
To build new weir at Allanburg, estimated cost, $10,000.
Spillway old lock No. 2, $2,000.
This makes the total estimate of $217,000.
Improvements, Port Colborne entrance, $240,000.
What depth of water will there be when this is done ?
Sixteen feet.
Does that include the building of an elevator at Port Col-borne ?

No, we are asking an estimate in the supplement-aries to build elevator foundations on the two piers with a view to making some arrangement at once with some of the transportation companies for the erection of elevators. We propose to put in the foundations immediately, that is to ask the appropriation at once.
Will this complete the work ?
This will not finish it.
How much is it going to cost ?
The total cost of the improvements at the entrance of Port Colborne is fixed at $1,067,856. It would take another year to finish them.
Does the government intend deepening and enlarging the Welland canal ?
There is work for the deepening of the canal at several places where it was found the water was becoming low.
There is no intention to make it permanently deeper, generally speaking ?
Not generally.
Has the hon. minister any statement showing whether there has been any increase of the tonnage through the Welland canal on account of taking off the canal tolls ?

We have not particular figures, but there has been a considerable increase in the canals generally.
To deepen portion of summit level between Port Colborne and Tborold, $40,000.

That deepening already done has proved of great benefit. It will have to be continued until the very shallow portions are deepened. This work is necessitated by the fluctuations in the level of Lake Erie, and is intended to provide 14 feet navigation at all stages of low water.
Lachine canal-enlargement and improvements, pontoon gates, $116,800; slope walls, $17,600.
Mr. REID- (Grenville). Who has the contract ?
It has not been let, but will be by public tender.
