speechtext: Does this dry-dock at Montreal come under the Railway Department ?
Yes.

What reutal does the government get ?
The MINISTER OB'1 FINANCE. It is under lease, and I will bring down a statement.
Lake St. Louis-Hydrographic survey, sweeping channel, removing boulders, )c., $6,280.
Has this work been transferred to the Marine Department?

The lighting has been. The Railway Department still has the hydrographic survey.
Sault Ste. Marie canal-construction, $75,200.
This is for extending the lower entrance and deepening it, and also deepening and widening the upper entrance.
Does that complete the work ?

No.
Rideau canal-to rebuild swing bridge across the upper lock at Hog's Back (steel span), $2,000.
There was an old wooden bridge there, over twenty years old which requires to be rebuilt.
What is the total cost for rebuilding it ?

Two thousand five hundred dollars will complete the whole work.
Welland canal-stone protection to banks of old canal, $4,000.

I would ask the hon. minister if he would give consideration to the principle on which the government are to lease the water-powers of the old Welland canal? The old canal is not used for navigation. But there is a lot of valuable water-power on that canal, some of which is leased to manufacturers, and more may be leased in future. I think it would be in the interest of the country if the government had some stated scale of prices, so that those intending to go into the business of manufacturing and in a position to use this water-power, might be able to calculate on a certain scale of expenditure for power. If this canal were in the hands of a privatie corporation, of course it would be managed in that way. As matters are managed by the government in regard to this canal, those who think of locating on the canal are not able to know exactly what they will be called upon to pay. I do not wish to take up time discussing the point, but I. would urge upon the minister to look into this matter. Or if he has looked into it and can tell me now what the policy of the gov-

eminent is in regard to it, I would be glad to have him explain.

I do not know whether it will be found expedient to have a fixed scale. Certainly, there is none now. Still, no doubt, the matter is worthy of consideration. We are receiving better rates for water-power notv than we did some years ago, but fixed rates might not be advantageous under the varying conditions. For example, we are generally disposed to give power to municipalities for their own purposes on more generous terms than those on which we give it to private parties. The mattter will receive consideration.
Welland canal-to change valves and hanging gear of new lock gates, $12,000.
What changes are these ?

This expenditure is to change the Townsend valve, which never was satisfactory, as it is complicated and frequently out of repair and slow to operate. It is to be replaced with the Butterfly valve. The $15,000 asked for will complete the work.
Is it proposed to make the change all through the canal ?

Yes.
Welland canal-to survey and delimit government lands along the canal, $1,600.
This is a small item; still, I would like some explanation.
The canal boundaries along the old and new canals are very indefinite in many cases and require re-marking. A complete plan of the canal is needed to show the government's property and leaseholds.

I do not understand in what way the boundaries are indefinite. I never heard that we had any difficulty in ascertaining which was private property or the boundaries between the lands of private owners. I thought the lines were pretty well ascertained. They are magnetic bearings, and that ought to be sufficient.

There is a considerable quantity of land under leasehold, and it is deemed desirable by the officials of the department that the boundaries may be marked with stone monuments, as in the case of the Lachine canal.
Welland canal-to improve drainage along feeder, $1,200.
Does the bon. minister know what part of the feeder this is ?

This amount is required for cleaning and improving back ditches in order that land may be properly drained, and so avoid complaints of land owners with regard to drainage of their lands.
Lachine canal-to renew masonry wall basin No. 2, $5,600.
This is to renew and rebuild the old locks 1 and 2, Montreal. They are falling into decay.
I see a lot of work going on there. Will this expenditure complete it ?
Yes. The work has been going on for some time.
Who are the contractors ?
Coul-son, Quinlan & Robertson.
Was this let by tender ?

Yes.
Chambly canal-electric station by-wash, Ste. TherSse. $4,800.	.
What is a bywash ?

This sum is to be used to provide^ for rebuilding by-wash at Ste. TherSse and at electric power station for lighting the canal and furnishing power for the work shop. It is estimated for each by-wash, $3,000. The work will be done in concrete.
What is a by-wash ?

I heard the question asked before, but I was doing my best to dodge it by pretending that I did not hear. But my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) compels me to admit that I do not know what a by-wash is. The chief engineer tells me that it is something to let the water out.
How does it work.
I am sorry that I must acknowledge ignorance.

Well, I am in the same position.
Chambly canal-macadamizing tow path, $6,000.
Will the minister macadamize the tow-path on the Iroquois and Galops section of the canal ? This canal has been built, and it is all clay.
This is a highway, this is a regular traffic road.
In that case, it is being done for the municipality.
It is claimed we' have spoiled the road and we must make it good.
Spoiled the road by using this tow-path. There are no wheels going over it by reason of its being a tow-path.
It is a general public highway.
The minister said the road -was spoiled by reason of our rising it as a tow-path. Is that by reason of hauling heavy loads over it in vehicles ?

The
chief engineer informs me that we used their highway, and we are practically replacing it In this way.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say a moment ago that we had spoiled the road and this was done to repair it.

We
spoiled it by taking possession of their road, and we are now giving them this one.
This is not the same road, then ?
We are allowing them to use our tow-path as their highway, inasmuch as we took possession of their road.
Does the municipality contribute anything towards this work ?

No. The department thought tlhat inasmuch as we had taken possession of their highway we should give them a substitute therefor. We give them the right to use the tow-path, and we macadamize it for them.
Was it used in common before ?
It was used as a highway until we damaged it or destroyed it.
I do not quite understand how it was that we took possession of and destroyed their own road.

The damage to the road took place years ago, when the department used a portion of it. That was macadamized before, and we are now adding to the macadamized portion. That is the explanation of the department. It is not so clear as I would like it myself.
How many miles of this road are macadamized 1
Three miles, at $2,500 per mile.

Of course it may be all right, but I think we ought to have a little more information about it. We ought to know why so many years have elapsed without doing this. It is perfectly plain, I should think, that if you took a highway belonging to the municipality you should either put it back in the same condition, or give them another one. But I do not see that there is any obligation On the government to keep it macadamized. We have discharged our duty by giving the municipality another road in the same condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: We had a case in Cardinal where the government took the whole road, by the route of the canal, and it was absolutely necessary to make a new road. In that case it was macadamized.

The information is not as complete as I would like to have it, and I will let the item stand.
Item allowed to stand.
At six o'clock, Committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Chambly canal-land damages, $400.

This item is not correctly expressed. It is not actually for land damages, but for a wall to prevent land damages. I therefore beg to move :
That the words ' land damages ' he struck out and that the words ' wall to prevent land damages ' be substituted in lieu thereof.
Amendment agreed to.
Who owns the land ?
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman.
It is understood that the item just before that one shall be allowed to stand ?
Yes.
Is this to begin a wall or to cover the whole work ?

To cover the whole work.
St. Ours lock-stop	logs,	$800.The	MINISTER	OF	FINANCE.	This
is to renew the stop logs which are at present decayed.
Landing wharfs, $1,280.

What is the cost of the landing wharfs ?
The	MINISTER	OF	FINANCE.	The
item for landing wharfs amounts to $1,600. It is proposed to replace the present wooden wharfs with concrete piers and iron and wooden superstructures, which will make it a permanent work.
Are these wharfs owned by the government ?
Yes.

Is that the total cost '!
The	MINISTER	OF	FINANCE.	When
these estimates were prepared, some time ago, only a small appropriation was asked for this work, but since then it has been represented that we will have to engage in a much larger amount of work. It is almost a pity that this item is taken at all, because we will have to ask for a further

amount. X see that there is an appropriation in the supplementary estimates for $4,400, which will have to be added to this. The figures I have in regard to the item are not satisfactory, and I will have to ask it to stand.

I am not aware that there is any wharf at St. Ours excepting the wharf of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company. There is no government wharf at that point. If it is contemplated to build a new wharf there, when the item comes up, will the hon. minister have a little more information as to where that wharf is to be ?
Yes. It is represented here to be a government wharf.
I do not think there is a government wharf there.

We will let the item stand.
Item allowed to stand.
Carillon and Grenville canal, $18,400.

This is to construct a guide pier at the entrance of the canal and to renew the wharf at Grenville. The wharf or pier has been built twenty-one years, and the part above water is urgently in need of being renewed. It is proposed to substitute concrete for crib-work. The estimate is $23,200, and we are asking in this vote for $23,000.

In spending this $23,000 I hope the minister is keeping in mind, that before very long we will have the Ottawa ship canal built, and tha't this lock should be made of a capacity to suit that canal. This wooden pier having lasted for twenty years;
I suppose this new one will last for one hundred years, so the government ought to take into consideration that in five or six years perhaps, it may have to be utilized for the Georgian bay canal. Will the minister put that consideration before the transportation commission ?
The commission will have a free hand.
If you build these walls and spend money, the commission will not have a free hand except to tear them down again.
Is this a new work V
It is an old work which is being reconstructed.
Will it be let by public tender ?
It is under contract now to Messrs. Martineau and I.emoine. It was let by tender and the lowest was accepted.
When was the work commenced '!
It began last year.
This is the first vote.
No, there was an appropriation of $10,000 last year.
That is not shown in the estimates, and there do not seem to be any details regarding it in the Auditor General's Report.
There is evidently a printer's error in the estimates. The actual expenditure last year was $9,-77(5.53.

Is this contract given for a lump sum V The MINISTER OF FINANCE. The contract is for the' whole work on schedule prices. The total estimate for the work was $00,000. I should have said that the work commenced in 1901, and that it has been going on since that time.

Then it should be referred to in the Auditor General's Report.
The MINISTER CfF FINANCE. It ought. There was an expenditure in the year ending June 1902, of $16,998.
Why should a comparatively small work like this take five or six years to complete ?
As a matter of fact it is only two years under construction, but a good part of the work can only be done when the water is out of the canal in the spring.
Could it not be done in winter ?

It certainly is.
Miscellaneous-miscellaneous works not provided for, $4,000.

These items are the usual votes.
Salaries of engineers, draftsmen, extra clerks and messengers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $23,200.
This difference is accounted for by several increases given to various persons.

I understood that all of these engineers, draftsmen and clerks were paid out of the appropriation for any special work. For instance that the engineers and draftsmen on a canal or a particular piece of railway weie paid out of the estimate for that particular work.
These are officers on the headquarters staff, and that does not apply to them.
That is in Ottawa?
Yes.
And they do not come under any Qther vote, do they ?

No.
Cost of litigation in connection with railways and canals. $4,800.

These are costs which are incurred by the department in disputes which may arise in any part of the country which are taxed by the Justice Department, and then charged against the Department of Railways and Canals.	[DOT]

I would like to make an appeal to the acting Minister of Railways and to the Minister of Justice on behalf of a gentleman, a clergyman, residing in the village of Cardinal, who had a claim against the government for damages to his property. The case was tried in the Exchequer Court, and judgment for, I think, $1,200 was given in his favour. I understand the government are disputing his case in the Supreme Court.* The appeal to the Supreme Court is, in the opinion of a great many people, very very hard, as the gentleman is not a man of means. I would like to appeal to the hon. minister to try to see his way clear to accept the decision of the Exchequer Court and to pay this man the amount awarded to him. Could not the minister let this matter pass and give this gentleman the amount to which he is honourably entitled ?
I understood from this gentleman's solicitor that this case might be settled without prejudicing the other cases to which reference has been made.

That statement -was made by the solicitor of the reverend gentleman, but after considering the matter thoroughly I concluded that the interests of the government would be to some extent jeopardized by settling this claim, however, as I said a moment ago in consequence of representations made by my hon. friend, the matter is being inquired into further, and an effort is being made to arrive at some settlement.

I am frequently asked by the electorate to explain on what principle these law costs are paid, and I would like to know from either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Justice if they can tell me in what way this money is expended. Of course, I can tell at a glance that the amount being only $6,000, this cannot be more than the amount paid for the services of outside lawyers, and I therefore ask in what way business is given by the department to outside lawyers. I suppose that most of this money goes in counsel and solicitors' fees, and as it is a small amount in comparison to the amount of litigation every year, it is evident that some work must be done in the Railway Department and in the Department of Justice, where we know they have able lawyers engaged. As the electors frequently ask me and as I am unable to state on what principle the government act in having this business done by solicitors who are not permanent employees of the department, I would be glad if one of the minister's would give me as much information as possible on the subject.

Of course there is a law branch in the Railway Department, but in all matters of great importance we consult the Department of Justice. A good deal of the money is paid outside of Ottawa where it is necessary to obtain legal services. For instance very recently we had to send a representative over to the state of New York to interest himself in a very important matter with regard to the Galops dam, a part of which rests upon American territory. Occasions of that kind sometimes arise.
I see that you employed as a medical man, Dr. T. C. Ga-boury, to act as attorney in re Lafleur et al.

That was a case of land damages, and Dr. Gaboury, who lives in the locality, was employed specially to go about and settle claims so as to avoid lawsuits. He was not employed as attorney at law but as agent, with power of attorney to act for the government.
In a certain case of Stewart against the King, over $2,000 were paid Blake, Lash & Cassells for fees. Were they acting for the government ?

Yes, this was an unfortunate ease which arose out of Stewarts quarry on the Soulanges canal. It went to the Exchequer and the Supreme Courts and we succeeded in getting the claim reduced by a very large amount.
Was the Deputy Minister of Justice associated with Mr. Blake ?

No, not in that case. A conflict had arisen between himself and Mr. Stewart, and it was alleged at one time that Mr. Newcombe had shown personal hostility to Mr. Stewart, and we thought it was well to allow the matter to remain in the hands of a third party.
Did the Solicitor General act ?
No, none of the officials of the department.
Was there a junior counsel ?
Yes, a man named Lawior, who was connected with the case at the locality where the work was dome.

He drew $1,500 in connection with this case. $3,500 were paid out in law fees by the department in this matter although we have the Minister of Justice, the Deputy Minister of Justice, and the Solicitor General, and one of the pledges made by the hon. gentlemen when in opposition was that the law costs would be very much reduced. Are they decreasing or increasing ?

The business of the country in litigation, as in other respects, has increased very considerably, but with respect to law costs there has been a gratifying decrease. When I was Solicitor General, I appeared in almost every case for the Grown, which I could attend to personally, and my friend the deputy minister has appeared to such an extent that it is a grievance to the bar at large that he is employed too frequently. As far as I am personally concerned, it is looked upon as improper for me to go to court, although my desire is to appear as frequently as possible.
Is this six thousand dollars more than the amount paid last year for law costs ?
I have not the figures paid last year. But the preceding year the expenditure was close upon the $0,000. This has been the annual vote for several years.

Before 1896, one of the great grievances in the province of Quebec was that there was the amount of money spent on law costs despite the fact that we had a perfectly organized Department of Justice. I recognize the propriety of what the Minister of Justice has said with regard to his
not appearing in every case in which the Crown is concerned, but it seems to me that that reason existed before 1896 as well as to-day. Very far from decreasing, the amount we expend in law costs has increased considerably. Last year over $87,000 were paid to legal gentlemen, and I notice that friends of the government were employed exclusively. Whether it be that they are better versed in the law than Conservatives I cannot say, but out of that $87,000 only $5 were paid to a Conservative, a lawyer in Montreal. I shall not go as far as my hon. friends opposite did in 1896, when they utterly condemned the late government because it spent a much smaller amount under this head, but $87,000 paid out in law costs during the year appears to be a very large amount, and we are justified in asking if this $6,000 is over and above the $87,000.
It is part of the $87,000.

I do not think so. I think that $6,000 is over and above the $87,000 paid last year, and I have no doubt the amount will be considerably increased this year. In that connection I would ask the minister to give us the names of the parties [DOT]to whom this $6,000 was paid last year.
My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) must not be alarmed at the magnitude of the costs last year, for, after all, $87,000 is but a small sum compared with the $116,000 paid in 1896.
Not as much as that.
Just as much as that.
I contradict my hon. friend.

And in 1897 the sum was still larger, because we had to clean up the old accounts. If my hon. friend will bring this up on the supplementary estimates, I will give him the facts and show the decrease in these costs, although the business has increased. When I speak of costs, I mean solicitors' fees. Seventy-five per cent of the solicitors' work that used to be done outside exclusively is now done in the department. The enormous fees, amounting to as much as $18,000 paid in one year to a firm in Ottawa- and running each year from $15,000 to $18,000-are not seen any more. My hon. friend says that we limit ourselves to our political friends in the distribution of this patronage. Of course, other things equal, he would not blame us for preferring our friends. But if he will look at the items of expenditure, he will see the names of a good many gentlemen who do not belong to the Liberal party.
Precious few.

A good many, and some of the largest items. And

This subject was such a constant theme of discussion in the province of Quebec before 1S96 that my memory of it is thoroughly good. We were told on the platform that we were actually keeping alive a number of these dangerous people called lawyers, and I recollect that tbe sum we were said to have spent was much smaller than $116,000 mentioned by my hon. friend. But, if it was wrong then-and that is the point I wish to make-to carry on these expenditures, if it was a scandal then to spend the money of the people in maintaining lawyers when it should be devoted to public improvement, why is it right now ? We have a long list in the Auditor General's Report, making up a total of $37,941.53 paid to lawyers. Here is one lonely Conservative lawyer in Montreal, who, probably, had a claim against the government which they could not dispute, and he received $5. C. Johnston, Regina, bore up against the enemy and received $1,456. Mr. W. B. Ross, of Halifax-I suppose, not a relative of my hon. friend from Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross) -was paid $4,524. Hon. A. speechtext: No. If the custom which the hon. gentlemen opposite so violently condemned is to be kept up, I would suggest to my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) that there are in Montreal, and no doubt elsewhere, competent lawyers of a Conservative faith, and that he ought to divide this patronage between the parties.

many of us got a chance previous to 1896, except when we came with our guns after the enemy ?
But my hon. friend knows the golden rule.
The Minister of Justice says that the payment of amounts to legal gentlemen in Ottawa has been done away with.
Not done away with, but the amounts largely decreased.
Quite a large amount was paid to one firm-several thousand dollars.
Chrysler & Bethune, I suppose, the hon. gentleman refers to. But the amount was not $18,000 or anything like it.
I see that Hon. A. S. White was paid $2,375 for drafting the Railway Act.
The hon. gentleman does not hold me responsible for that ?
Surely that work could have been done in the department. And in comparing amounts spent by this government and the previous government for legal fees in Ottawa this amount should not be overlooked.
Do I understand the Minister of Justice to say that all the law costs paid by the different departments are summarized under the Justice Department ?

The practice is that when an account is rendered for professional services for any department the account goes to the Department of Justice ; we tax it, and then it goes to the particular department that is charged with the case and that department pays it. But it is all under the head of legal expenses, and legal expenses are all summarized on page 327.
Is this account of Chrysler & Bethune on page W-54 of the Auditor General's Report, $615-is that included hi the summary ?
That would appear to be an item in connection with the arbitration in the case of Mackenzie & Mann vs. The King, the judge of the Exchequer Court acting in that matter.
Is there any regular fees that we pay solicitors ? That some are paid at the rate of $25 per day.

The amount varies. Some receive $100 a day ; but the regular agents of the department, those who do solicitor's work for us in different parts of the country, are supposed to receive $25 a day. But when you come to employ counsel they charge much higher. Christopher Robinson, for instance, who acts for the department occasionally, Mr. Sam Blake, and Mr. Ayleswortli. get $100 a day. There are others who get smaller fees, varying from $25 to $100 a day.

In this case of the Hon. A. S. White, we are entitled to some explanation why the department had to send so far to get a gentleman to draft this Railway Act. I should think that required some gentleman with exceptional ability. But when he is only paid $25 a day, it would seem to indicate that he was not considered a light in the legal profession.

The drafting of the Railway Bill required to be done by a specialist. In the Department of Justice our hands are very full, and none of us would assume the responsibility of drafting an important Bill of that sort. There might be gentlemen in Ottawa capable of doing it, but it is not unusual to take professional men elsewhere. For instance, the Manitoba School Bill was prepared by a gentleman who came to Ottawa from Winnipeg for that purpose.
In that case it was the province of Manitoba who was interested, and therefore it was proper to send for a gentleman from Winnipeg.
He was paid by the government, though.
That may be, but inasmuch as it was the Manitoba people who were interested, it was perfectly right to employ a gentleman from Manitoba where the Act was to be enforced.

I do not think the Minister of Justice is doing justice to himself in his explanations with regard to the legal expenses. It is a very flimsy excuse for him to make, when he is challenged in connection with the expenditure of public money, and in failing to employ local talent, to say that the old government did the same thing. He might do something and be perfectly conscientious in doing it, but when the Minister of Justice sees fit to condemn something that we did, and when he does the same thing, I think he is a doubleqlyed hyprocrite to pretend to say that he was justified because we did it. Where is your Solicitor General now ? Where was he all this time ?	_

During part of the time that these expenditures were being incurred the Solicitor General was busily engaged in the Supreme Court and in the Exchequer Court. I happened to be Solicitor General myself at that time. The present Solicitor General is now abseut attending Exchequer Court cases that are being tried in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. He was away during the past summer attending the Privy Council in England ou government business. I may add to that, and I make the statement in all seriousness, that in my opinion it is in the interest of the government, and it. is desirable, to concentrate as much as possible the litigation of the government in the hands of the Department of Justice. It has been my desire to do that, and I venture to say that seventy-five per cent of all the litigation in matters that are now pending, is controlled in the Department of Justice here. The solicitor's work is done by the Deputy Minister of Justice and it is only when it is necessary to engage counsel outside that we engage them. I would like to go fuiv ther and say that it is impossible, when you have cases from Halifax to Vancouver, and when local knowledge is necessary, when vou want a local solicitor who knows local conditions, I say it is impossible for all that work to be done here, and it is m the interest of the government that local men should be employed. Still, it is made a grievance against the government that we keep too much of the work in our own hands.

I sympathize with the Minister of Justice. I understand how his followers are very hungry to get their share of what is going. But that does not justify him in doing what he condemned when we were in power.
You did not do any of the legal work.
That is rather a sweeping assertion, as I think the Minister of Justice will And if he looks over the Auditor General's Report.
No, I know what was done in the department.

But I was not inquiring where the Solicitor General was now, I was not finding any fault that he was not doing his duty. I was only pointing out that when we are paying these enormous fees for legal counsel, it seems to me the Department of Justice might do some of that work themselves. If litigation is increasing so fast, that shows the government must be at fault ; they must be doing business very loosely, or they would not have so much litigation. They canribt be a business government as we have been led to believe they are or they would do the business in such a way that they would not have so much law.

I can see where the seriousness of this legal business comes in. It might be well to have two or three very able gentlemen connected with the Department of Justice to look after the government's interest at the courts which are held. It is a well known fact that when a case is tried in the court the hon. Minister of Justice employs a local solicitor to take charge of the case in the interest of the government. I think I can safely say that in many cases the solicitor employed is not generally the ablest solicitor in the locality and is not able to cope with the gentlemen who are employed in opposition to the-government. If this were all centered in the department at Ottawa and gentlemen of ability were employed to plead the case on behalf of the government I think it would pay the government better even to pay the local solicitors the amounts that they receive now, because, I believe in a great many cases, the judgments rendered against them would not be rendered if the government employed men of ability to plead their cases.
I know of cases in which men have been employed on behalf of the government that I would not have employed on my own behalf and I say that without saying anything disrespectful to these gentlemen. I knew the men who were employed on the other side and I knew that those employed on behalf of the government were not able to cope with the situation. I believe that two or three men should be employed to do nothing else but plead the cases of the government. Of course, it might be necessary to have the assistance of a local solicitor to get up the brief. At present the government do not send any person to do that. They allow the local solicitor to go ahead and carry on the case and in nine cases out of ten judgment is rendered against the government.	[DOT]
No.

Is it not a fact that in nine cases out of ten judgment is rendered against the government, whereas it would be rendered in favour of the government if they employed men of the ability of those whose names 'have been mentioned, such as Mr. Christopher Robinson, Mr. Ayles-worth and men of that calibre ?

I do not know about the local cases. Perhaps my hon. friend may be correct because I suppose he would not speak without knowledge, but I can tell him in reference to the cases that I have personal knowledge of that you can go to the Supreme Court and find that 75 per cent of the cases have been successfully contested by the government.
In the Supreme Court.
The government have generally turned the other i side down pretty successfully.	I '

The amount involved was exceedingly large and on the other hand we had against us Mr. B. B. Osier, Q.C. assisted I think by Mr. Hogg and another legal gentleman in this city. What was the result of this case of Battle vs. the Crown ?

I do not remember the details of that case, but I think the case never'went to judgment. I think the case was compromised and as a result of the compromise a very large reduction was made in the claim. '

Canals - repairs and operating expenses. $585,540.
There is an increase of $54,216. We would like to know what this is for ?	'

The increases on the Cornwall canal amount to $5,270, and the decrease to $2,264. leaving

a net increase of $3,000. I have the details of the increased cost of the services on each of the canals here. While the total increase of $54,000 is in one sense considerable, yet it is a very small percentage of the aggregate.

I understand that the minister is not providing for an increase in the salaries of the lock tenders on the Welland canal. If that be the case, I want to put in a word for them, because I believe they are the most underpaid men in the services of the government; too much underpaid in fact, to enable them to render proper and efficient service. We have heard a lot of the prosperity of the country and the increased cost of living, and while I do not object to increasing the salary of a civil servant who gets $2,000 a year, if the increased cost of living requires it; yet, I think we begin at the wrong end, when we leave the men who are only getting $400 a year out in the cold. These men who receive small pay, feel the cost of living much more than the gentlemen who get high salaries. I would remind the minister that several petitions have been sent here from the Welland canal employees, urging on the government that they are justly entitled to an increased wage. As these employees cannot come to the House themselves, and as they are my constituents, and whether they voted for me or not, are entitled to justice, and, as I am the only person who can represent them on the floor of the House, I want to impress upon the government some reasons why these men should get an increase of joay. To commence with, they are getting exactly the same pay as they got twenty-five years ago and we all know that $400 does not buy as much today in the Niagara district, at all events, as it could buy a quarter of a century ago. Other employees than the lockmen on the Welland canal have had their wages increased. I do not believe that the carpenters are paid as much as they ought to be. They get less wages than are paid by contractors, and they get less than the union scale in St. Catharines, Merritton and other places along the canal. I believe that this government can afford to pay its servants just as much as any private contractor pays them. It is a poor government if it can not. While saying that, I must add that the carpenters and labourers have had their position improved during the past fifteen years, by shortening their hours as well as increasing their pay. The labourers on the Welland canal get $1.50 for nine hour's work, which is 10 2-3 cents an hour, but the lock tenders, who require to be more skilful men, get $45 a month for a day of twelve hours, which is only 14^ cents per hour. The lock tender at $45 per month can only get about eight month's employment in the year, and the minister can see what that figures down to. I do not think it is in the interests of the country that these men should be kept at such low wages, while
civil servants in Ottawa who get five times their pay, have had their salaries raised because of the increased cost of living. The lockmen must be sober and steady men; their eyesight and their hearing must be good, and they must be trustworthy. To pay men of that class $45 a month for eight months in the year is penurious, is mean and is stingy. My remarks will apply to the bridge tenders as well. Let me point out also that the government have now made the canals free, no doubt with the object of getting more vessels to pass through them, and that being the case, it must necessarily increase the work of the employees to whom I refer. These men, when they are at work, have to work extremely hard, and their calling is only made comparatively easy because of the fact that many vessels may not lock through in quick'succession. I can assure the minister that if he lived on the Welland canal and saw those men at work he would come to the conclusion that they have no easy job of it. The fact remains then, that the pay of these men has not been increased for twenty-five years, and as you have lately adopted a policy which increases their work, they, therefore have a double claim to the consideration of the government: first, because of the increased cost of living; and second, because the canals having been made free, their duties will be largely augmented. The matter I suppose will receive the attention of the government; but I am bound to say that I do not think that the ordinary justice is being done these men which they have a right to expect. If we are to err at all on the side of liberality it should be in regard to the $300 or $400 men and not the $1,500 or $2,000 men. You talk about the increased cost of living and increase the salaries of the judges who are receiving $5,000 or $0,000. I am not objecting to that, I am in favour of increasing the salaries of county court judges particularly, but while I am Th favour of increasing the salaries of county court judges, we must remember that they get from $2,400 to $3,000, and I am that much more in favour of increasing the salary of the man who gets $300 or $400 and has to support a wife and children. If we are to err on the side of liberality let us begin with the poor man to whom $25 is a great deal and not with those who receive much larger stipends. The lock tender on the Welland canal gets $45 a month. If you multiply that by eight you get his annual income, or less than $400 because a man who is working on the canal cannot expect to obtain employment in the winter months. If he is working for the government during the summer he is not the subject of much commiseration and people naturally give the preference to the men whom they want to work for them in summer so that practically the income of these men for the whole year is simply the $45 a month which they get for eight months

of the year. It is sometimes said that it does not take much of a man to be a civil servant. That ought not to be the case and I do not think it is. I think we should have the best men in the country as civil servants, and I say that you cannot retain good lock tenders unless you pay more than $45 a month. Many of these men have become accustomed to this work and I think in all fairness they should have an increase. I would not object to a higher standard of qualification, and if the government think that some of these men should not be employed because they are not fit for the work, I would say that the proper business method would be to get rid of them and to get others but while the government are employing these men to do the work and are increasing the salaries of gentlemen in the civil service running up into the thousands, I think they are making a mistake and doing an unfair thing to the workman in not increasing his salary. The government shonld begin with the $400 men and not with the $1,500 or $2,000 men. It is not alone these men who are interested in this ; the whole shipping interest of the country is concerned in the proper tending of these locks and swing bridges. If a man is careless in looking after one of these swing bridges where a railway crosses the canal an awful loss of life and property may result and carelessness in working the locks might also result in flooding of the adjoining lauds and in great destruction. It must be remembered too that these men are on duty in twelve hour shifts night and day and the salaries which they receive are not at all fair in proportion to their work.

I understand that the workmen on the Welland canal had the good fortune to get their increase in advance of the others. I think my hon. friend must be mistaken when he said that they had received no increase for twenty-five years. I understand that complaint was made that the lock tenders on the other canals were not receiving the same pay as those on the Welland canal and that the increase had to be made to bring them up to the standard of those on. the Welland.
The Welland canal lock tenders did not receive an increase.

They were getting higher pay than those on the other canals and the increase had to be made to bring the others up to the Welland standard. However, I have not had this matter brought under my consideration since I have been at the head of the department and I quite sympathize with the view that those who are receiving very low salaries should be considered. We are making the labour of these men less arduous by the use of the electric system, but that makes no difference as their time has to be considered and they are entitled to fair remuneration for their work.

The hon. minister says that the increase In the repairs to the canals is very slight. I would like to call his attention to the fact that last year the total paid for repairs on the Morrisburg canal, with which I am more familiar, was $13,700 and the total amount paid to the Morrisburg staff was $14,403, altogether in the neighbourhood of $28,000. At the time the Liberal party icame into power the amount expended on repairs was about $8,000 and the amount paid the staff was about $7,000, or a total of $15,000, so that the expenditure has been actually doubled. Now, there is no excuse why the repairs should be doubled. During tlie last three or four years these canals have been In the hands of the contractors, and have all been put in good order. There was no necessity for placing a dozen more men on the repair gang. I know for a fact that pressure was brought on the government from the local committee in each village, and the result was that from each and every one so many men were taken and employed on the repairs, and in addition the government put more men on the locks than were actually required. Take the locks at the head of the Galops canal, they have got an overseer there and a iockmaster as well, or more than they actually require. That is one of the reasons why the repairs staff have increased, and I think that the acting minister will also find very material increases on the other canals because I hear the same remarks about them. He will find too that in distributing the patronage, the government are very good to their friends.
I see no objection to that save in this respect that they go outside my constituency, in which this canal is situated, for supplies, and I think it is hardly fair to do so when they are not inviting public tenders. And they pay big prices when they go and give the' orders to their friends. For instance white pine timber sixteen feet long at $25 per thousand feet, and pine plank $20 per thousand feet.
Knots included.

Yes, knots included. These prices were paid to the Alexandria Wood Exporting Company of Alexandria, and if report he true, the Alexandria Wood and Export Company is the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell).
The report is not true.

1 see that this company received a large amount in connection with the Cornwall canal, and in connection with the Williamsburg canal it 'received $813.18. Here is Mr. Cameron of Iroquois who received $602.47. He lives along the line of the canal, and I have not the slightest hesitation in saying that he could have supplied all that stuff. But Mr. Stewart, the superintendent, came from the county of Glengarry, and I have not the slightest

doubt that the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell) recommended him for the position, and he has returned good for-
For evil.

I can give no other assurance than that whatever is necessary to maintain the canal in good condition, we will have to provide, lhe mere fact that somebody supplied lumber at certain prices does not show that the lumber was too high or not needed. But my hon: friend has helped me to meet the argument of the hon. member for Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) who says that the men on the canals are worked too hard. My hon. friend says that, on the contrary, there are too many men for the work.
I spoke of the Welland canal.
The hon. member for Leeds and Grenville (Mr. Reid) spoke of all the canals.
He does not^ know how his neighbours work on the Welland -canal.

I referred entirely to the Cornwall and Williamsburg canals, the only ones I know anything about. There are practically double the men on the Williamsburg canal to-day compared with [DOT]six years ago, and there is no more to do. The" canal is in first-class repair, and there is no reason why the number of men on it should be doubled. I might also draw the attention of the acting minister to the fact that there are several men who were employed *on the construction staff-I do not refer to the engineers themselves because they have do be kept on to finish their final estimates- but there are several men kept on the staff drawing their salary when the works are practically completed and their services might be very well dispensed with. There are none really necessary except the engineers and their assistants. Are those men to be continued right along indefinitely ?
If I find any men employed on the canal unnecessarily, of course they will not be kept on.

They will be kept on unless the department takes some action, because a great many of them are members of the Liberal committee in that locality. It is on the recommendation of that committee that they were appointed and will Tie dismissed.
That is where my hon. friend is wrong.

1 know of one Liberal committee, composed of about six men, of whom five are employed by the government. They appoint themselves each and every time and they are still on duty drawing their salary and doing no work whatever. The work is practically completed.
In the village of Curran where that work is going on, is it necessary to have any men employed around there now ? The work is practically done, there is nothing but a dredge there, and yet the staff is kept on.
1 do not refer to the engineer himself. I think that there are two or three engineers who have to be kept on to Amish the final estimates.
Mr1. SCHELL. The hon. member for Leeds and Grenville (Mr. Reid) has been kind enough to mention my name in an entirely unwarranted manner. What were his duties ?
I do not know.

I understood he had been a school teacher, and at the time of his appointment was a clerk in the employ of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Montreal. Marine men are anxious to have a man appointed who is qualified for the position. If the hon. minister could hear the opinions expressed by Liberals along the canal, as well as by all marine men, it would not take him very long to make up his mind to get some person qualified for the work.
I am suspicious of the Liberals who would complain to my hon. friend (Mr. Reid, Grenville).
They are members of the Liberal committees in towns between Cornwall and Kingston.

They should keep better company.
Additional to pay persons employed permanently in the public service and remuneration to any other persons for services rendered for and In connection with passing vessels through the canals of the government of Canada from midnight on Saturday to midnight on Sunday, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $14,400.
This is the usual vote.
Is this for lock labourers and lock-masters, to pay them extra ?
Yes. They are paid extra when employed on Sundays.
Is that the sum that is expended each year, or approximately so V
I have not the actual expenditure of last year. It is the regular sum taken year by year.
Now that the canal tolls are abandoned, is it necessary to keep a collector at the head of the Cardinal canal ? There is no duty for him to perform there.

The making of the canals free, as announced at the time, was more or less experimental, and it has been thought well to keep the collectors there to keep accounts as usual, so that we may ascertain what the revenue would have been. But I think the increase of trade has been so considerable that we may look forward to adopting that policy as a permanent one.
Do they sign the shipping reports and make reports exactly the same as they did previously to the tolls being abandoned ?
The accounts are kept in precisely the same manner.

What is the object of keeping a collector if there is nothing to collect7 Could not a tally of the boats passing up and down be kept just as well by some other employee on the locks ? The function of a collector is to collect money, but if it is merely a question of counting boats, cannot that be done by the lockmaster ?

Well the functions of a collector are not entirely to collect, that is a part of his duty. A collector is also an accountant, and it may be 405
that a man who is otherwise well qualified to be employed on the canal might not be an accountant. However, no definite policy has been adopted.

I understand that the government are going to carry out the policy of freeing the canals from any tolls whatever. A collector has only one duty to perform, and that is to collect tolls and to account for them to a government official who goes around from time to time and examines his books. That is what the collector does on the Lachine canal, on the St. Anne's lock, and every other canal. If you abolish the' toll what is the object of keeping, a collector ? There is no object except that you do not wish to dismiss him.

In this case at Cardinal, all the steamers go straight through to Montreal, and there is a collector at Cornwall and one at Lachine, and the latter gentleman could do all the work that is necessary. The collector at Cardinal would simply issue a pass and the collector at Montreal would pick it up. It seems to me it is really a useless expenditure to keep a collector. The lockmaster could keep an account of .the one or two local boats that pass up and down. I would like to know if it is the intention of the government to keep that office going ?

For the present we think it is desirable to have Collectors there for statistical purposes. The lockinasters may in some cases be able to keep these statistics, but not in all cases. 1 am not prepared to say what the policy may be in future. I shall give the matter consideration, or whoever may have charge of the department will do so.

This is not a large item, but it seems preposterous to keep collectors of tolls after you abolish the tolls. The reason is probably because the government does not like to abolish the office. If you give as a reason for keeping the collector that it is for the purpose of collecting statistics, that can be done perfectly well by the lockmaster. I can tell the minister that there is not a lockmaster who is not able to furnish these statistics to the government, not one of them, I believe, who does not do that duty at the present moment. If these collectors are kept on, it is because the men who were collectors in 1896 were dismissed without any reason, and partisans were put in their places, and the government do not want to dismiss them, although they have abolished the tolls. So the country is put to the expense of paying collectors who have nothing to do.

In this case at Cardinal, the collector lives a mile and a half from the locks ; the lockmaster is the one who collects the statistics for him now. You are simply paying the collector a salary for doing nothing, at this point in particu-



lar, where the vessels go right straight through.
Is the toll abolished on the Murray canal ?
On all the canals.	.
Then I presume the collector is kept on there also ?

I hardly think the explanation the hon. gentleman has given is quite satisfactory. Now, the hon. gentleman has some policy on the subject, we have a right to suppose. I do not know whether he is to continue to hold his present dual position of Minister of Finance and Minister of Railways and Canals. It is difficult to say just when the government will have sufficient courage to appoint a Minister of Railways. It is currently reported that the Minister of Finance is about to give up the position that he has adorned for some years, to become Minister of Railways. If he thinks of retaining the position of acting Minister of Railways which he now holds, has he formed any policy as to what he is going to do with regard to these collectors ? Now I do not advocate the taking away of a man's position from him unnecessarily, if he is required in the public service. Even though he may not be employed all the time, I would not think it the proper thing to take his living away from him. But this is a case in which it seems, as far as the discussion has gone, that there is no necessity for it. The hon._ gentleman, looking forward to possibilities,' probably, will tell the committee what his policy is.

I must confess that I have not given any special personal attention to the matter. I am simply adhering to the policy which my predecessor established, assuming that he had good reason for it. If it be found that there are persons who do not perform any work and are still drawing salaries, I think that is a matter that should be looked into and if a case of that kind is brought to my notice I will make inquiry into it.
I have given the hon. minister a case to inquire info now on the Williamsburg canal.
We will see.	*

Will the hon. minister say that we are going to keep on paying collectors of tolls during the whole of this year on the canals when my hon. friend is surely aware that these men will have nothing to do ? It seems to me, that, although, as indicated by my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is on the eve of assuming a different department, he would not be so indifferent to the policy of the department Mr. REID (Grenville).
which he at present occupies and it seems to me that some kind of defence ought to be given to the committee for the fact that the salaries of the different collectors of tolls on the canals are being continued although the tolls themselves are abolished. My hon. friend says that these officials are retained for the purpose of keeping the statistics, when he knows perfectly well that these statistics are kept irrespective of the collectors. We know even without the collectors exactly what traffic passes through the canals because these statistics are kept by other officials.

I have already stated, without undertaking to define a policy for the future that for the present it has not been thought well t^o dispense with the services of these officials and that we are utilizing them for statistical purposes. If these statistical purposes can be as well served without those officials that is a matter that I am willing to inquire into, but for the present we do not feel warranted in dispensing with the services of these men without inquiry.
What statistics ?

They keep precisely the same accounts of all transactions which lake place on the canals as if they collected tolls. They keep accounts of the vessels which pass through and of what the dues would be if they were charged, so that we will have at the end of the year an idea of what the dues would have been and of what the concession is that has been made.
Do boats have to stop and report to these officials just the same as if they collected tolls ?

There is ho change whatever in the manner of operating and keeping the accounts. It is the very same as if the tolls were collected.
. Mr. TAYLOR. How about the case of the collector at Cardinal who lives two miles away from the locks, and never goes near them ?
I confess I cannot answer that. That is a proper subject for inquiry.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. member for Cardinal says that he never goes there. His office is at the locks, he visits his office only once in a while and draws his pay.
That we will have to look into.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if there are any reports made by collectors since the tolls have been abolished.
Yes, they are making the usual reports.

Would it be asking too much of the hon. minister, as he is going to bring down some information before the supplementary estimates are passed, to bring down a memorandum, showing the amount of the tolls that the collector at Cardinal would have collected from the 1st of May to the 1st of October of this season ?
I will inquire as to what reports are made by the collector and I will be very glad to bring them down if they are there.

If he makes out the reports as heretofore there should be no trouble about it. These reports are sent every day to the department, and the department could tell up to last night what he should have collected. One of the clerks could get it in ten minutes.
I do not anticipate any trouble. I will try to have the reports.
Would the hon. the minister bring down the reports of the collector at St. Anne's and the collector! at Lachine, so that we can see what has been done by these officials ?

Yes.
Salaries and contingencies, collectors offices. $28,546.40.
I notice that there is an increase for these collectors who are not performing any service.
There is an increase of $464.
It is not very great, it is true, but it is not the sum that is involved.

This increase is divided as follows : Williamsburg canal, $23S; Soulanges, $550 ; Lachine, $100; Chambly, $5; St. Anne's, $1; an increase of $494, less a decrease of $30, making the net increase $464.
Is this $35,683 paid for the salaries of the collectors ?
Salaries and contingencies.
Counected with the collectors' offices ?
Yes.
I heard the hon. minister mention that there was an increase in the salary of the collector at St. Anne's ?
No, the item of salaries and contingencies shows an increase of $1. The amount of the estimate happens to be $1 above last year.

Are the salaries of collectors in no cases increased this year ?
405J
In Montreal, I am told, some of the clerks may have been, increased.
Surely we are not increasing the salaries of collectors when there is nothing to be collected ?
There are several clerks in the office at Montreal and it is quite possible that some of the salaries have been increased. They are keeping statistical accounts.
Is the salary of the collector at St. Anne's to be increased ?
I should say not. The increase for salaries and contingencies is $1 and I am sure that the collector has not got the $1.
Has the salary of the collector at Lachine been increased ?
There is an increase for salaries and contingencies of $100, but I have not been advised as to whether the increase is in salaries or contingencies. I will have to ascertain.
There is an increase on the Williamsburg canal of $238. What is that for ?
I cannot say what part is for salaries and what is for contingencies.
Then the item should stand until we get the information, because I think that the salaries should not be increased under the existing circumstances.
I do not think there is any increase in salaries, but I will bring down the informaton.

Last year the collector got a salary of $700, Sundays, 345 hours at 20 cents an hour, making $69, rent. $[DOT]->3.87 ; postage and express, $9.84 ; and horse-hire, $169.75 ; I cannot understand how lie could have worked 345 hours on Sundays. That lock is closed on Sundays from 7 a.m. until 9 p.m. It seems impossible that he could have put in that many hours.
In the latter part of the season the canals are open on Sundays without limit as to hours.
This would pay him for every Sunday during the whole season. Was his horse-hire to take him up and down from the village to his office, which is about a mile and a half.
He is allowed a dollar a day for horse-hire.
And in addition to that he is apparently paid $5 a month rent for his own house down in the village.
In some cases houses are furnished to flie canal employees and it may he that he Is allowed rent.
This seems an extraordinary case. Why should he be allowed rent for his own house ?
It was never allowed before this gentleman was appointed.
If rent is to be allowed at all, I do not think that S5 a month cau be complained of.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is he allowed to attend to his medical duties as a doctor, and is this horse-hire for driving him to his patients or to the canal.
The deputy tells me that the understanding with these officials is that they are to give their whole time to the public service.
Is the rent not allowed on the theory that a man should be where his work is ?
Probably that was the origin of the system.

For thirty years the former collector got a small salary, and of course the government could not give the new collector an increase and so they got over the difficulty by giving all these extras which makes the salary over $1,000. I do not refer to this case in particular. There are other cases of the same kind. There are employees on the work of construction that has been practically completed, and if the minister wishes to find out he can ascertain that the increase is accounted for by employing men who have been forced on the government.
I will make inquiry into all these things.

This is rather a fishy case. It appears that this gentleman is employed as collector, and that he is at liberty to practice his profession as a physician. The canal tolls have been done away since that gentleman was appointed and he has no longer any duties to perform as collector. He lives in a house of his own and receives rent for it, a thing hitherto unheard of and he is paid $1 a day for horse-hire. Is that to go to see his patients or is it to go up and collect tolls where there are no tolls to collect ? The acting Minister of Railways had better allow that to stand until he gives us that information.
We will give the hon. gentleman the information, but there is no reason to let it stand.
I am afraid that after the item is passed it will be a little too late, rt might be a proper thing to strike out this whole item and the acting Minister of Rail-

ways might come to that conclusion himself.
I can hardly think that he is prepared to justify a case of that kind ; I am sure he would not and I think he had better let that item stand.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
According to the Auditor General's Report that gentleman has charged for 345 hours of Sunday work, at 20 cents per hour, $09. During the seven months which constitute the season of navigation, the canals are open on Sunday from 12 to 7 and 9 to 12 o'clock, making ten hours on Sunday. That for thirty Sundays would make the total number of hours of Sunday work 300, but this gentleman charges for 345 hours, and yet no boat could pass through that canal on a Sunday night or any other night in the dark. Therefore there was no necessity for night work at ail.
I think the minister should allow this item to stand until he finds out why this gentleman put in a charge for 345 hours when he did not put in an hour's work. Why should lie go up there and sit from 7 until 12 o'clock in the morning for the sake of drawing his pay when this canal is so situated that a boat must approach and leave it by daylight.

If I should find that any officer on the canal had been guilty of misconduct that would not be a reason why the others should not receive their money. These are proper matters for inquiry, and I shall see that they are inquired into.
Is there anything in tlie Order in Council appointing this gentleman providing that he should be paid for house rent ?
I do not know.
Would he be entitled to house rent if it was not provided for in the Order in Council appointing him ?

Not unless tlie minister of the day allowed it to him. I am not sure if he was appointed by Order in Council, but it would not be a very great stretch of authority for a minister to allow house rent; that is speaking on the principle, not on the merits of the case.
Is the minister going to allow this item to stand ?
I do not think so. This is the last item in the estimates, and I would like to have it cleaned up.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
You will have a similar item in the supplementary estimates, and perhaps the hon. gentleman will then bring down the information asked for, and give to the House the number of hours of Sunday labour that this gentleman put in on the ca nal.

1293S
I will give tlie hon. gentleman whatever Information we have in our possession.
We have been very fair to my hon. friend and he might drop the two items which have been allowed to stand and clear the thing up.

My hon. friend is right, the criticisms have been fair, but if there are two or three cases where some one gets $10 or $100 more than he should that is no reason why the rest should not have their money.

The hon. minister did not catch my point. I stated that as we have been fair in the criticism of his estimates, he might allow these two items to be dropped, and then he could clear up the whole thing now.

I will have to come back with some information for the hon. gentleman in any case, so I think it is better not to drop them.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved tlie adjournment of the House.
Before we adjourn, I would ask the minister what business will be taken up to-morrow.

We have made such good progress in the last day or two that the Order paper is pretty well cleared. There are several Bills on the Order paper which are not yet printed, and therefore we are not in a position to proceed with them, but so far as possible, we will take up the Bills which are in order before the House.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Shall we take up the Audit Act amendment Bill ?

Not tomorrow, we will postpone that perhaps until the first of the week. If there is no objection we can proceed after disposing of these Bills to deal with the supplementary estimates, although they were only laid on the Table to-day.

maintopic: DEATH OF HENRY CARGILL, ESQ., M.P.
DEATH OF HENRY CARGILL, ESQ., M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deem it
my very sad duty to refer to the lamentable event which took place last night, and which has deprived us of the companionship of one of the most esteemed members of this House. The Conservative party were certainly fortunate in having in their ranks such a man as Mr. Henry Cargill, for he was in every possible sense of the word a good man-a good citizen, a good father, a good husband, a good and warmhearted friend. During the long years that he was associated with us in this House he had endeared himself to the hearts not only of his own political associates, but of those who held different political views. Not only was Mr. Cargill a good citizen, but we know from long acquaintance with him that lie was a man of exceptional ability in the profession which he followed, and followed with much success. His sudden demise, coming under such sad circumstances, is another lesson to us, which is as old as the world, but always new, of the uncertainty of our lives. Those who apparently are frail and seem to live under tlie shadow of death may live long, while those who appear to be in robust health may be suddenly called away. We on this side of tlie House join sincerely with our hon. friends opposite in conveying to the mourning family of Mr. Cargill the frank and true expression of our deep condolence with them in their sad bereavement.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: DEATH OF HENRY CARGILL, ESQ., M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members on this side of the House, I thank the right hon. gentleman most sincerely for the very kindly words he has uttered. Coming as we do from paying the last tribute of respect to a very dear friend, we are reminded, I am sure, how frail and uncertain is our tenure of this earthly life. Yesterday Henry Cargill stood amongst us in all the vigour and strength of mature manhood ; he spoke in this House with unusual animation, and none of us would have supposed for a moment that within a few hours we would be following his remains to their last earthly resting place. He has been a member of this House since' 1887, with the exception, I believe, of one session ; and during all that time I am sure that not one word nor one act of his failed to inspire the deepest respect and confidence of every member of this House. His great generous heart was perhaps not known except by those who were most intimate with him ; but those who had that privilege knew of many acts of whole sonled kindliness on his part which were not known to the public at large. I am sure it can be said of him that against his warmest political opponent his soul harboured no bitterness. He was too_ great a man for that. He was listened to in this House with deep respect. His great abilities. as a business man, and the sound common sense and breadth of view which always characterized his remarks earned for

him the sincere respect of every member of this House. I join heartily in the kind and generous words of my right hon. friend the First Minister, and in the assurance which he has conveyed to the bereaved widow and family of Mr. Cargill that they have in this hour of their affliction the deepest and most sincere sympathy and condolence of every member of this House.

I would like, Mr. Speaker, to bring to the notice of the House a paragraph in the Montreal ' Star ' of yesterday, allegiug negligence on the part of the government with reference to sending military protection to Sault Ste. Marie.
The paragraph is as follows :
Much indignation is expressed among all classes of citizens over the manner in which the Dominion government ignored the repeated demand that the troops be sent to protect the town properly, as it became apparent that the presence of the militia was necessary. That the troops are now guarding the town and the company's property is something for which the militia authorities at Ottawa are not entitled to any credit. In fact the Ottawa authorities have not even yet countenanced the sending of the militia. The story of the government's negligence to comply with the town's request for troops is an interesting one, as related by Mayor Plummer. When the attitude of the men began to predict trouble the mayor promptly wired to Ottawa, asking that fifty troops be sent without delay. He received a reply directing his attention to a clause of the Act which empowered him to call out the troops on his own responsibility.
I think that the question is of sufficient importance to be brought up in this way, because it is not a party question and it is exceedingly desirable that the community at large should understand what the law is, and that the government has not been neglD gent. This paragraph admits that the mayor of the ' Soo ' did receive an answer to his telegram. As a matter of fact, telegrams were sent by the representatives of the company there and the mayor, to the Prime Minister and myself, and the only answer was sent which could be sent, and that was an answer calling to the attention of the authorities that paragraph of the Militia Act under which they could claim and secure the protection of the militia. That telegram was promptly sent and others were receivedi afterwards, but they were all to the same effect. I would like to read the provision of the Act to which the authorities at the ' Soo ' were referred :
1. The active militia or any corps thereof, shall be liable to be called out for active service with their arms and ammunition, in aid of the civil power in any case in which a riot, disturbance of the peace, or other emergency requiring such service occurs, or is, in the opinion of the civil authorities hereinafter mentioned, anticipated as likely to occur, and, in either case, to be beyond the powers of the civil authorities to suppress,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Sir. F. W. Borden).

speechtext:
or to prevent or deal with,-whether such riot, disturbance or other emergency occurs, or is so anticipated within or without the municipality in which such corps is raised or organized:
2. The senior officer of the active militia present at any locality shall call out the same or such portion thereof as he considers necessary for the purpose of preventing or suppressing any such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance, or for the purpose of meeting and dealing with any such emergency as aforesaid, when thereunto required in writing by the chairman or custos of the quarter sessions of the peace, or any three justices of the peace of whom the warden, mayor, or other head of the municipality or county in which such riot, disturbance or other emergency occurs or is anticipated as aforesaid, may be one ; and he shall obey such instructions as are lawfully given to him by any justice of the peace in regard to the suppression of any such actual riot or disturbance, or in regard to the anticipation of such riot, disturbance or other emergency, or to the suppression of the same, or to the aid to be given to the civil power in case of any such riot, disturbance or other emergency.
The civic authorities acted under this provision of the law. They applied to the senior military officer on the spot, Col. Elliot, and Col. Elliot took such steps as he deemed necessary to deal with the situation. As a matter of fact, the government has no authority to do anything. The power is given, under the Act, to the civic authorities who are on the spot, and who must be presumed to know best what the requirements are and what the necessity is for taking a certain course. The government is powerless to act at all. One can see how absurd it would be otherwise. Suppose that riots were imminent or believed to be imminent and some alarm was felt, are (roops to be sent hither-and yon throughout the Dominion? The thing would be utterly absurd and never was contemplated by the law. As a matter of fact, the law has been literally complied with, the government has done its full duty, and I think it is in the public interest that this matter should be understood once for all.
Will the municipality be expected to pay the cost of transportation and maintenance of these troops ?
That is a matter of law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Surely the government, under the Act, are responsible entirely for the number called out to suppress a riot. The mayor makes a requisition, and then the military officer on the spot has the authority to call out, not the number of troops required by the mayor, but the number he thinks may be required. The responsibility is upon him.
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
He calls out the number required for the suppression of the trouble so that the responsibility as to the

number and the time they will be engaged is entirely in the hands of the military authorities.

As a matter of fact, the requisition does not necessarily call for any particular number of troops ?
The MINISTER OB' MILITIA AND DEFENCE. No.

That must be determined by the senior officer. Would the minister read the portion of the statute which places that within the discretion of the commanding senior officer and also the portion which limits the period during which the troops are required ?
The MINISTER OB' MILITIA AND DEFENCE. There is no limit.
Have the government taken any steps to do anything towards providing that these unfortunate men shall be paid their wages ?

I need not tell my hon. friend, for he is aware, that the government can do nothing of that kind. But I may say that I have information from a private source this morning that arrangements have been made, and the men will be paid to-morrow.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I rise to a question of privilege. And before going into the matter to which ' 1 desire to draw your attention, I beg to ask the indulgence of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, as I intend to speak in the English language, with which I am not so familiar as with French, my mother tongue. Last week several petitions were presented from different constituencies of the Dominion asking this parliament not to proceed further with Bill (No. 235) relating to a National Transcontinental Railway, as the petitions pretend that this parliament has not enough information

petitions from the county of Bagot there is one from the parish of St. Theodore d'Acton, with whose electors I am well acquainted, and in which I have the honour to be well known. One reading these petitions and assuming them to be correct would, no doubt, form the opinion that a certain number in the county of Bagot are opposed to this transcontinental railway. Let me say that I Was particularly surprised to read a petition from St. Theodore d'Acton presented to this House by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin).
I have not done that Mr. Speaker.
The name of my hon. friend (Mr. Morin) is endorsed on the petitions.
I did not put the names on the petition.

I may call the attention of the hon. member (Mr. Marcil, Bagot) to the fact that, in a few moments, there will be a motion for Committee of Supply, and, if he does not intend to conclude with a motion, he might wait for the motion for Supply, when he will be free to speak.

At the conclusion of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall move the adjournment of the House. I was saying that the petitions presented pretend that this parliament should not proceed with this Grand Trunk Pacific Bill. Many such petitions have been presented, particularly from the county of Bagot which I have the honour to represent in this House. Amongst the
That we have never placed signatures, nor authorized any person whomsoever to inscribe our names on a petition addressed to the honourable Senate and House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled, protesting against a measure now submitted to parliament concerning the subject of transportation facilities. We declare that we approve of the attitude taken by the government of the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in regard to this project. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) drew your attention to this matter, Mr. Speaker, and I thank him for having done so. In ' Hansard ' of the 30th of September, I find the following attributed to yourself, Sir, in reply to the hon. member for Bellechasse :

It certainly would be irregular that the signatures on petitions presented to this House should be signed by the same person. Petitions should be signed by those whose names are supposed to be attached to them. Rule 84 says :
Petitions to the House shall be presented by a member in his place, who shall be answerable that they do not contain impertinent or improper matter.'
If an hon. member when presenting a petition is answerable that it does not contain anything impertinent or improper, I should think he should be responsible if there is anything impertinent or irregular In the petition presented by him. I have no [DOT]doubt that these petitions have been sent in order to mislead the House and the hon. the Senate; and I may be permitted to say that if enough time were allowed to see all those whose names appear on these petitions,
I am sure it would be possible to obtain from a great majority of them the same testimony as I have read here from some.
