I should think that, for the honour of the hon. member for Dorchester it would be well for him to ask permission to withdraw these petitions. If the law of our province permits of the vindication of the honour and the rights of the electors of the county of Bagot, I may say at once that as soon as the session _ is over, I have the intention of taking the opportunity to do so. This is all I have to say, and, I hope that,1 in saying it, I have not been offensive to anybody. I move the adjournment of the House.

I would like to say a few words in regard to these petitions. I may say to the House that in regard to this Transcontinental Railway Bill I took no part directly or indirectly in any of the counties of this country. Petitions have been sent here from the county of Dorchester,

but I know nothing about them, I do not know Who sent them here, I do not know who wrote to the county of Dorchester to have these petitions signed. Some days ago a gentleman was here who had a handful of those petitions, and he said to me : Will you present them 1 I never read them, I do not know where they came from. I took no part whatever in procuring those petitions, and I have nothing to be sorry for. I can throw the first stone therefore in regard to that matter.

Before the hon. gentleman takes his seat, I desire to ask him if he knows anything about these petitions from St. Prospdre and from St. Malachie, in the county of Dorchester, which petitions I now hold in my hand ?

Very well, am I guilty because the hon. gentleman holds them in his hands. I have already stated that I took no part directly or indirectly in procuring these petitions. I have said that petitions have been sent here from the county of Dorchester but that I know nothing about them. The hon. gentleman may hold whatever he pleases in his hands or in his lint, he is responsible for them himself.
Amendment (Mr. Marcil, Bagot) negatived.
Bill (No. 258) to amend the Act respecting the Department of Railways and Canals, was read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.	.
We have no copy of the Bill.
This Bill is in the exact words of the resolution (page 11189 of the ' Hansard,' which has already passed the House.
Is the Bill printed in French ?

No.
On section 1,
1. Advances may be made from time to time, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, to the Minister of Railways and Canals, to enable him to obtain, produce, manufacture, use_ and dispose of all necessary materials, equipment and stores required or used in connection with the construction, renewal, maintenance and operation of the Canadian government railways, and for the establishment and conduct of railway stores.

It seems to me this is giving new powers to the minister. I understood that everything used iii the construction and maintenance of that railway, that was ordinarily charged to capital account, would have to be voted by the House. This is simply for the purpose of balancing the stores account. You did not intend to make any purchases uuiess the money was

voted by tlie House, purchases either chargeable to capital account or for improvements.
When stores account is depleted, then there is a credit to the Intercolonial to the extent of the depletion.
Charged to the Intercolonial. If goods are taken out of stores then they are charged against the revenue expenditure or capital expenditure, as the case may be, against the appropriation of the year.
No, you get a straight credit of the stores account. Suppose there is $1,200,000 at the present time, and you deplete that stores account bv $300,000 ?
How ?

In any manner you like, by payment, or sales, or in any other way, out of stores account. Does not that leave you a credit between the difference of the sales and the actual amount of the credit ? Then you have the absolute disposition of that.
You would credit the stores account.
You have the absolute disposition, for the use of the Intercolonial, of the difference.

We cannot spend any money for any purpose that has not been appropriated by parliament. What we do by this Bill is simply, if I may use a homely illustration, to open a shop. We have goods in stock for which we get
credit, and as they are used out of stock, they are charged up against the particular service in which they are used, and when they are so taken out of the stores account and charged against working expenses or construction, as the case may be, there is a credit to the stores account.

In connection with what my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has just said in connection with the statute, it may be as the hon. Minister of Finance has sugested. but I would hardly think so. The words of section 1 of the Bill are very plain, it seems to me. They are :
Advances may be made from time to time, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, to the (Minister of Railways and Canals, to enable him to obtain, produce, manufacture, use and dispose of all necessary materials, equipment and stores required or used In connection with the construction, renewal, maintenance and operation of the Canadian government railways, and for the establishment an! conduct of railway stores.
Is that not equivalent to a parliamentary appropriation ? Does it not permit the government, in the absence of an appropriation, to make advances to the Minister of Railways and Canals out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund ?
That Is correct, but the advances have already been made and the goods are in store now.

While there may be some goods in store as to which some advances may have been made, the section seems to be a general one which would operate at any time in the future, and which would therefore - permit future . advances to be made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund as advances without a parliamentary appropriation.

The only authority that would be given the government would be this : Suppose the stores account is $1,500,000 to-day and we took out of it $100,000 and put it into the track, it is credited to the stores account and charged to working expenses or capital account, as the case may be, according as parliament has appropriated the money. Then we have reduced the stores account to $1,400,000 and if we desired to do so we would have the right to put in another $100,000, but as long as the stores account remained as it is at present, we would not have purchased anything on this account. It is intended to give the government a standing credit for the Intercolonial Railway, but we cannot take out of the stores one penny's worth of goods except it be applied for the purpose for which parliament has appropriated the money, unless we sell the goods to outsiders, in which case they become a credit to the stores account. We might sell our goods and credit them to the stores account, or, if

we take rails out of the stores and put them into the track, we charge them against the appropriation for the year for that purpose.

Where is the limitation in the Bill to which the bon. minister refers, to the effect that if there is a balance to the stores account of the Intercolonial Railway the balance shall only be applied to the ordinary working expenses of the road, or to capital account, as parliament has authorized ?

You cannot use the stores account for any other purpose than for the purpose of the Intercolonial Railway, and you must charge it against the particular service for which the money has been appropriated. This account is not a new one. There is absolutely nothing new in this proposal.
I know there is not.

We are simply doing what my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) did for many years without law, but we are now proposing to do it with law. He had his stores account for a long number of years. He bought what he liked, and charged it to stores account. He did not require an appropriation from parliament to buy goods and put them into the stores account. That method has prevailed for a quarter of a century, and under our system of government anything which has become a custom begins to be almost regarded as a matter of law, but when my attention was called to this matter,
. I thought that it should be put in a proper legal shape. We have exactly the same principle now, though on a smaller scale, in connection with the King's Printer. The King's Printer has to buy and keep on hand a stock of materials for which he has no especial parliamentary appropriation. The appropriation for the printing is given to each department or to parliament, as the case may be, but the King's Printer must have his material on hand to do the work, and therefore he has a standing credit. He has had it for years, and last year we gave him by statute a credit of $100,000 for this purpose. He is authorized to buy goods, and these goods are charged to the stores account. If in my own department, for instance, I want some printing done, I have a vote of parliament to provide for the printing, and I buy that printing from the King's Printer, jlist as if I bought it from an outsider. In that way we simply provide the King's Printer with a means of carrying his stock. The same principle applies to the Railway Department. We provide the Railway Department with the means of keeping a stock on hand.

There is no doubt as to what the intention of the hon. Minister Hon- Mr. FIELDING.
of Finance is. The only doubt in my mind was as to whether when there was a credit to the stores account you limited the expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway to the amount which had been appropriated to operating expenses or capital account. I suppose it is so, as the hon. minister says that any credit that is given to the stores account should be used for the purpose only for which it is voted, that is to say, for the ordinary expenses of the Intercolonial Railway, or to be applied to something for which it has been voted on capital account.
Certainly, it cannot be applied to anything except that for which parliament has made an appropriation-either to working expenses or to capital account. There is no qualification as to that.

I really cannot so understand it. It seems to me to be in the same position which was mentioned the other day by the hon. Minister of Finance when he inquired whether the statute for enabling the government to make certain increases in salaries would enable payments to be made without a special appropriation. The hon. Minister of Finance took the ground that the Bill itself was a parliamentary appropriation. and that no further parliamentary appropriation would be required. I am not dealing with the book-keeping methods of the Intercolonial Railway, but I think I can understand the words of the statute fairly well, and while section 2 deals with some book-keeping matter in connection with the Intercolonial Railway which I do not profess to understand as well as the hon. Minister of Finance or my hon. friend from South Lanark, nevertheless, section 1, which stands by itself distinctly states, that advances may be made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada to the, Minister of Railways and Canals for a certain purpose, and there is no limit upon it. It is true that you have at the end of the section the words :
And for the establishment and conduct of railway stores.
But the use of these words does not place any limitation whatever upon the words which precede. These are supplementary to the language which precedes, and not in limitation of it. You have the distinct provision, as far as the word ' railways ' in the last line of the clause is concerned1, that advances may be made, and if you have a statute to that effect, what need is there of any parliamentary appropriation ? It stands in the place of a parliamentary appropriation. I do not know anything about .the usage or practice itself. If it be true that moneys have been used in this way in the past without parliamentary appropriation, that is a matter to be considered. What we are dealing with now is the question as to

whether or not we shall authorize that by statute. I must confess that, after having given the best possible consideration to it,
1	am still unable to construe the statute in the way in which my hon. friend has done.

If we had section 1 authorizing the advance without section 2, I think the criticism of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) would be just. There must he a parliamentary appropriation to allow of the purchase of goods to the extent of $1,500,000. Section
2	goes on to say that the existing stores
account is to be taken as part of this. It says :	~-
Stores accounts shall be established, as of the date 30th June, 1903, in connection with the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway.
And that these accounts shall be charged with all the different items in the different accounts as respects that. Section 2 is intended practically to say that it is not intended to enlarge your powers of purchase, but it gives you in addition the power to take your existing stores into account, and when you have taken your existing stores into account you have exhausted your powers of purchase. That is what it means, and if there is any doubt about the matter, I shall be only too glad to accept any suggestion that will make it clear.

I am most anxious to appreciate the arguments of the hon. minister, tout I cannot see anything in section 2 which limits the "broad language of section 1 in the way he thinks it is limited, and I would suggest to my hon. friend, in order to make plain what he desires, if I thoroughly understand his intention, that we should add a clause to the Bill providing :
Nothing herein contained shall be construed to authorize the advance of moneys in the absence of parliamentary appropriation.

Oh, no, that would not do ; this is a parliamentary appropriation, 'but we have already expended it.
Mr. BORDEiN (Halifax). I am dealing with the future. We can arrange about the past as you like. I think that in the future we should provide that no money shall be paid out for capital account or operation of the Intercolonial Railway, or anything else, unless you have a parliamentary ap-propiation for the purpose. It seems to me to be a perfectly workable proposition to add a provision to the clause of this Act that in future advances shall not be made in the abj sence of the parliamentary appropriations.

That would not do ; that would defeat the purpose of the Bill. It would not do to say that no purchase shall be made without a
special parliamentary appropriation. Undoubtedly if we did not have the stores on hand, this would be a credit in advance for the Intercolonial Railway of one and a-half million dollars. The only reason why it is not now an advance Is that the ex-'penditure has been made without any legal authority. Under the old system the goods are now in store. But it is intended to be, and should be, a credit to the Intercolonial Railway to the extent of a million and a-half dollars. That is to say, the officials of the Intercolonial Railway should not have the right to pay out money to the extent of one dollar without a parliamentary appropriation, but it will not do to say that they cannot have a stores account until you have provided for every particular item. The Intercolonial Railway officials must be able to carry on their business just as a merchant does. A merchant must have stock on hand to meet the demands that may arise. Just as the King's Printer, for instance, must have stock on hand to do business, so must the Intercolonial Railway, and it is now intended to give, in a legal way, the credit which they have had for twenty-five years past. But the Intercolonial Railway has no right to apply these goods to any purpose until parliament has authorized their use. The fiscal year closes on the 30th of June, and let us suppose that you have then a large stock of coal on hand. That stands in the stores account, and you have no authority to pay that out of the appropriation of that year. You can only take out of the appropriation for that year as much as will pay for the coal used up to the 30tli of June. You must have the balance of the coal on hand, and' where is your parliamentary authority ? This is your parliamentary authority ; by it the Intercolonial Railway officials are allowed to keep on hand a stock of- various* articles aggregating $1,500,000.

How would it do to put at the beginning of the clause :
For the purposes of a stores account advances may be made.
I have no objection to that, but It will not make it any better.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the acting Minister of Railways tell me that this is not placing in the hands of the Minister of Railways power to spend $10,000,000, or $15,000,000, or $20,000,000 every year, if he sees fit to do so, for the purposes of the railway, without coming to parliament and asking an appropriation ? You have $1,500,000 capital in stores on the first of July.
They are not necessarily on capital account.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
But they are paid for and are there in store. During July the minister!

can use half a million dollars' worth of these stores, spreading them out over the different works. On the first of August he can go to one of his political friends and buy that half a million dollars' worth of stores and put them in store. On the first of September again the stores may have run down SI,000,000, so that there will be, only half a million dollars' worth on hand, and then the minister can go to another friend and buy one million dollars' worth of stores, put them in store, and he can repeat that month after month.
What is he to do with the $15,000,000 of stores after he takes them out of the store ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He takes them out for the purposes of the road.

But he cannot do that unless this parliament has appropriated $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 for that purpose; he cannot take a dollar's worth of goods out of store except for the purpose for which parliament has authorized the expenditure.

Does the Minister of Finance mean that the proposition is to convert a portion of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada into a supply of stores for the Intercolonial Railway, and then to use the stores only so far as you are permitted by a parliamentary appropriation ? Is that practically the object ?
That is it. That has been the practice for twenty-five years, but there has 'been no authority for it.

What I want to know is why there should be power to convert a portion of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada into stores' supplies for the Intercolonial Railway without a parliamentary appropriation for that purpose ?
This is the parliamentary appropriation ; this Bill is a parliamentary appropriation.

Then, I was right in the view I first took, that you are doing away with the necessity of a parliamentary appropriation for the purpose of converting a portion of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada into a supply of stores for the Intercolonial Railway. I am not criticising the proposal, I am only endeavouring to understand.

A merchant will not sell all his stock within one year ; lie must have a surplus to carry him over the year and to meet new conditions that arise, and just in the same way the Intercolonial Railway could not possibly order exactly the quantity of goods required to serve it for the twelve months after the end of the fiscal year, closing on the Mr. TAYLOR.
30th of June.' The fiscal year closes on June 30, and in May or April you may find yourself in want of coal. You could not figure out the exact amount you would require for the balance of the fiscal year, so you buy a lump amount, and if you are wise you look a little ahead. How are you to pay for this coal ? We want to give a legal authority for carrying it in stock, but before one ton of it can be taken out of store and used on the Intercolonial Railway there must be a parliamentary appropriation.

The difficulty, suggested by hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) is the difficulty of knowing the quantity of stores that will be required ; but is that not a difficulty" which we meet every day in making parliamentary votes 7 We are told by the government : We do not know how much will toe spent, but every dollar will be accounted for. Could you not do the same thing with stores, making a liberal appropriation, and then using such stores as may toe necessary? You would, of course, have to make a generous appropriation, and then if an emergency occurred, could you not resort to Governor General's warrants ?

What we are now proposing lias already been done in another branch of the service, and it seems reasonable that it should be done with regard to the Intercolonial Railway. The condition in regard to the railway service is not exactly the same as in those services to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has just referred. We have had to do, in the case of the King's Printer, what we are now proposing to do in the case of the Intercolonial Railway. The two cases are exactly alike only that the appropriation for the King's Printer is a modest sum, and for the Intercolonial Railway you must have a larger amount. With regard to tlie particular words of section 2, to which my hon. friend has referred, I am afraid I am open to the criticism-although I may not get the credit for it-of allowing the Auditor General to have his own way.
It is his suggestion that a clause should be worded in that way. In this whole matter I am trying to meet his wishes.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

With the explanations that lmve been given of section 1, so far as I have heard them, I do not see any great objection to it, except that I think that the words in the last line, ' and for the establishment and conduct of railway stores,' are somewhat indefinite. The words, ' produce and manufacture,' in the third line seem to me to cover everything that is necessary. I do not know what is meant or intended by establishing and conducting railway stores.
I do not attach any importance to those particular words. I think they are superfluous. I may say, however, that the clause was largely the work of the Auditor General himself.

Then I would suggest, so as to bring all the advances and payments that may be made clearly within the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, the addition of these words:
' The making of such payments shall be subject to all the provisions and regulations in that behalf of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.' I think that is important, because there are provisions made for the safety of the government and the people with respect to advances of all kinds, and it would be well to use such words here so as to make the meaning perfectly clear. If it is essential that there should be the utmost care and scrutiny about anything it is with regard to stores.

That is certainly the intention of the Act, and if my hon. friend thinks the addition of those words will make it clear, I have no objection. As I have said, the wording of this Act is largely that of the Auditor General, and I thought that if he was satisfied with it, the rest of us might be. But I have no objection to the addition of those words.
I spoke to the Auditor General about them, and he thinks they would be an improvement.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section '1,

I think that this section requires more consideration than would at first sight appear necessary. ' These accounts shall respectively be debited with the balance of stores then held on account of each railway.' I presume that means that the amount of stores to the debit of the accounts shall be accepted under this new arrangement as final.
Not necessarily. They will be subject to audit like everything else.

They were audited presumably in the past. On the 30tli of June, 1903, say there is $1,000,000 of stores to the debit of stores account. That will have to be transferred at once to the debit of the new account. It is quite true that every year an audit takes place when the Auditor General counts the stores on hand, what may be called an ordinary stock-taking, but that goes on generally speaking in all railway companies. Yet I think there are very few companies that will not find, in the course of years, a large amount of material on hand which may be worth only one-third or one-fourth of what they are valued at In the accounts. I very little doubt that
if a thorough stock-taking of all the materials in the stores on the 30th of June, 1902 were made by an expert railway man, he would cast aside all obsolete materials as so much waste iron, and there would be found an enormous difference between what appears in the stores account and the actual value. I would therefore object to this clause being supposed in any way to settle the stores account. I would object to its being held, assuming that $1,500,000 be transferred to stores account in pursuance of this resolution, that that should end the account. I think it is of the utmost importance that there should be a thorough stock-taking of all the materials in the stores of these two railways. I would prefer that the hon. minister had provided in this section that before a new account is established, there should be that thorough stock-taking, and placed to the credit of the stores account only the actual value for railway purposes of every article. I recollect very well that on the change of administration in the Western Railway a thorough stock-taking was made of every item in the stores, and it certainly did a very great deal of good.
I think that there ought to be such stocktaking on the Intercolonial and the Prince Edward Island Railway at present. No merchant or manufacturer would be content with a perfunctory stock-taking, just carrying the items on from year to year at cost price, though many of them, may have become obsolete and have to be sold as old scrap. It does strike me that this second clause may be used as a very convenient way of getting over that under the plea that the Act of Parliament authorizes the amounts to be passed and charged up as they stand on a particular day. I would therefore suggest that this clause should be revised, and that before the new Act is started, there will be a thorough stock-taking, under the supervision of the Auditor General, and that the accounts shall then be started with the actual values of the materials.

I fail to see that there is any need for a revision of the clause in order to serve the purpose which my hon. friend has in view. That there should be frequent stock-taking at proper intervals and that these should have due regard for depreciation, I admit. This is not the creation of a new account. This account will have in the books precisely the same value, force and effect as it has to-day. It has been examined and audited by the Auditor General, with all the unlimited powers he possesses, and we have no reason to doubt that it is fair and correct. We propose to take that account because it represents the cost of these stores to the department and has been examined in the usual way. We are opening a new account but giving legal authority to the account as it exists. My hon. friend says we should

take stock and see whether there is depreciation, and he adds that that would be a very proper thing to provide in connection with this Bill. I do not see that by opening up a stores account under the name of ' new stores account ' you do wrong by taking the figures exactly as they are in the old stores account, unless you suppose that those figures are not correct. But we have no reason to doubt their correctness. We are simply taking an existing account and giving it legal authority. It does not diminish anybody's rights to examine, criticise and condemn. We have to take the account as it stands until somebody shows there is something wrong in it. All that my hon. friend says with regard to stock-taking I admit, but I cannot see that it has any particular relation to this Bill.
The reason I suggest that there should be stock-taking, now that the hon. gentleman is making a new departure-
No. lie is mistaken.

I regard it as a new departure. The hon. gentleman tells us that an audit has already taken place under the supervision of the Auditor General. Well, the Auditor General told us in the Public Accounts Committee and he has told me outside that he has nobody who knows anything about the value of these things capable of going into the stores and picking out wliat is obsolete and what is not. Such an audit for the purpose of stock-taking is absolutely valueless, and as you are passing an Act of parliament to start a new stores account and are making a new departure, starting fresh in the year 1903, upon a balance appearing on the 30th of June, it is important that you should start that account upon a proper footing and that the debit to it should be the actual value of the stores taken over. That is especially necessary having regard to what the Minister of Finance says, that in the past everything has been accurately audited by an auditor who tells us he knows nothing about it. If it has not been audited by the Auditor General that is the Auditor General's own fault. This happens to be in that branch of the Auditor General's business in which we admit his right to deal with matters as he pleases. There are some things in which,
I think, the Auditor General takes authority which does not belong to him, but, in this case he has complete authority to deal with the matter, and, if he has not carried out the audit, the fault is liis own. Of course,
I do not say this as reproaching the Auditor General. All I say is that he is responsible.
If lie says lie does not know anybody who can do that work, that is not the fault of parliament or of the government. The statute-and we are dealing with amendments to the statute-gives him unlimited

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: power in this matter-there is no limitation as to time or the person he shall engage for the work. If the audit is not satisfactory, we shall be glad to have him make it satisfactory. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) is quite mistaken when he says we are opening a new account or creating anything new. There is nothing new proposed. This account has been in existence tor years. But attention has been called to the fact that it rests on no statutory authority, and we seek to amend the law in that regard. But, by creating statutory authority for the account, you do not create the account. That account is there, and we take it as it stands. If there is anything wrong in it, hon. gentlemen are as free to point it out in the future as they are to-day-. The passing of this Bill dees not change the situation one iota.

The object is plain. Those stores stand charged to the Intercolonial according to their valuation in the stores account. I can see that there would be a 'difficulty as the stores account has been kept in the past. Suppose that there is a sale of stores to the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk. The amount of money received for the stores is paid into the consolidated fund of the Dominion, and not into the fund for stores. Flow are you going to get it back to the stores account unless you have a credit ? You must have a credit account somewhere.
We have it now.
You are constituting it under this Bill.
No, we have it. We are giving it legal authority by this Bill.
I do not see how you can possibly have it.
My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) may not see how we can have it, but all the years he was a Minister of Railways he had exactly tins system to such an extent as he saw fit to use it.
Then, the government seek to legalize what was in vogue before. I can see the need for the system in order to get money back into the stores account in case of a sale. .

We are not worrying about the legal authority to sell, it is the legal authority to buy that is causing the difficulty. If we had $1,000,000 worth of stores and sold $100,000 worth to a railway or anybody else, that money would go into the consolidated revenue fund, as the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says. It is then credited to the stores account of the Intercolonial, and we have the right to buy $100,000 worth of stores in place of what we have sold.
That is what you want to do-to give credit to the stores account. You may have done that before, but you have no legal authority.

We have no legal authority to buy-to spend the money. We do not worry about legal authority to receive money ; we are ready to receive it without legal authority, if the owners will give it to us. But the legal authority to buy is what worries us.

The hon. Finance Minister has stated the course pursued in these matters in the past, and, no doubt, has stated it accurately. I can understand, as I say, that this credit has been necessary in order to get back money into the stores account in ease of a sale. To give legal authority for that, I understand to be the object of the Bill.
Yes.
There is no doubt about what the intention of the Bill is. The minister has been speaking of what has been done hitherto.

I would again call attention to the question of the audit of railway stores and other matters of that kind requiring technical knowledge. The Minister of Finance tells us again and again that the Auditor General has had every officer, every clerk that be requires for the purpose of such an audit. I can only say that the Auditor General tells me the direct opposite of that. He says that he considers it of very great importance that he should have an auditor of technical knowledge for such work, and that he has no such officer. It is absurd to say that you can take a clerk out of a merchant's office or a bank and set him to audit a railway stores account. He does not know that he is dealing with. You might as well ask me to go down and audit a druggist's stock in trade. I might find some stuff in a small bottle worth .$10, and in the next bottle, twice as much in bulk worth 10 cents, and, having no technical knowledge of the value, I should have no means of knowing that there was a differ-, ence. You may send an ordinary bookkeeper to audit the stores of the intercolonial if you like, but you might as well keep him at Ottawa and save his expenses. The store-keeper might show him thousands of tons of metal represented in the books by a certain amount, and the auditor might take that material as good value for the
money, and yet, it might be mere scrap iron and unfit for use upon a railway or in railway construction. For a thorough audit there must be technical knowledge on the part of the auditor. The Auditor General has no such officer. And I wish to say further, on this question, that we do want the audit of an officer of the government. The Auditor General is not a servant of the government, but a servant of parliament, and so represents the whole people. The auditor at Moncton is simply an officer of the government of the day, and can be dismissed by the government of the day. He has no independent authority.
What we want is am officer, a clerk, an auditor, solely under the authority of the Auditor General, that he shall have such a man on his staff as will have sufficient knowledge to enable him to make an audit such as is required here. Now, the Auditor General has not such a man, he has told us in the public accounts that he has not any expert of that kind ; he has told me personally that be has no such person. Yet the Finance Minister speaks as if the Auditor has everything he requires. The Auditor General perhaps has not asked for another clerk. We know the difficulty that heads of departments have in asking for extra expenditures for their staff. Even if the Auditor General has neglected to ask for it, in parliament we have the right to ask for it, and I say that the Auditor General should be supplied with an officer of that character, and that the accounts of the Intercolonial and the Prince Edward Island Railway should be audited in the future in a way they have not been audited in the past.

I have not made any allusion to the audit of any government official at Moncton or elsewhere. My observations this afternoon have reference to the auditing of the Auditor General. Now, there is a question of fact between the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and myself. I stated the other day that we had supplied the Auditor General with all the officials he had asked for. My hon. friend says the Auditor General tells him now that is not true. Now I am bound to say that if the Auditor General staled that to my hon. friend, I cannot understand it, for it is at variance with the Auditor General's own statement to me within the last fifteen minutes, and I am bound to believe that there is a misunderstanding between the Auditor General and the hon. member for Hamilton. I again say that we have supplied the Auditor General with every official that he has asked for. Now he is the judge of how many officials he wants. We have a right to refuse, we have not exercised that right. But I say that the auditing of the public accounts is the business of the Auditor General ; I say that while there are certain things that I think

the Auditor General is undertaking which do not properly belong to him, in this particular business he has a right to determine how he will audit the accounts of the Intercolonial, and they have been audited in the way that suited him. I say he has asked for no official who has not been given to him. If he says, I have not got an official- I cannot help that. AVe cannot go and thrust officials upon the Auditor General, we have no desire to do so. I say that he has audited all these accounts in such manner as he thought proper, and if he wanted any more officials it is not my business to go and thrust officials upon him, it is his business to say, I require further help. He has not been unduly modest in the past in asking for help-I do not say he has asked it improperly ; but whenever he has found it desirable to have an additional staff he has asked for it, and got it. I want to repeat again without equivocation, that we have given the Auditor General every official he has asked for. He has audited these accounts in the past in the way that was pleasing to himself, and it will be quite time enough when he asks for further officials to supply them.

I did not say that the Auditor General had complained that he had been refused any official by the government, any clerk, or any auditor-I said nothing of the kind. I simply said that the Auditor General had told me, and he had told the Public Accounts Committee, that he had not an auditor of the expert knowledge that was necessary to inspect these particular accounts.
I say it is a farce to attempt to audit railway accounts by a man who is a mere bookkeeper, without any railway knowledge. A man cannot audit these accounts without information that would enable him to do so. I endeavoured to point out a few minutes ago cases where his audit would be absolutely useless unless from want of knowledge. As I said, he may come across tons of materials in store that are absolutely obsolete ; he has no knowledge whether those should be classed as scrap-iron or not, or whether they should be charged up in the accounts for use upon the railway. He should be a man able to say to the general manager : Are not these obsolete articles ? are they of any use ? what is the use of lumbering the stores with them ? should they not be sold as scrap-iron ? Naturally a general manager may say : I do not want to sell these articles as scrip, they stand in my stores at five cents a pound, and if I sell them I will only get three-quarters of a cent a pound. But that is just what we want an auditor for. He should say :	I
cannot value these as railway articles, as railway appliances, they are of no value except for scrap-iron. That is the kind of audit we want. I am not complaining that the Minister of Finance has refused the application of the Auditor General for such a man, I say' we ought to have such a man, and I say again that the Auditor General has told me several times that such an auditor would be of great value to him, because he himself is entirely unacquainted with that subject, and he has nobody in his department that is acquainted with that subject.

Does not the hon. member for Hamilton mean to say that the Auditor General told him that he had not an officer who was a judge of the value of material, instead of saying that he had not an officer capable of auditing the accounts [DOT]?

Precisely, that is what I am talking about. I have endeavoured over and over again to explain what the Auditor General says with regard to the auditing and inspection of the railway accounts, that he has not an official on his staff with the technical knowledge necessary to enable him properly to audit those accounts. I have never said nor pretended to say that the Auditor General has asked anything that had been refused. He has stated in the Public Accounts Committee that he had no person with a technical knowledge that would enable him to do this, and I claim it was the business of the government, having heard that, to provide him with such an officer. Has the government done it ? I have taken the opportunity on more than one occasion, both in the committee and in the House, to say that he ought to be supplied with such an officer.

Aly hon. friend appears to me to have extraordinary views of the duty and jurisdiction of an auditor of accounts. Take his own illustration. He says : How could any one audit the books of a druggist without expert knowledge. Now does my hon. friend say that a professional auditor must have expert knowledge of the values of every item that a druggist would purchase ? A man who has experience in the prices of all kinds of goods may not be able to make up a financial statement, may not be able to go through those books. I think my hon. friend will admit that the officials of the department are responsible for the purchase of these things needed on the railway, they are responsible for the prices they pay for them. It is not the duty of an Auditor General to go over the accounts and say whether he thinks the prices paid were fair market prices ; that is surely not what an auditor is for. The banks have a professional expert auditor, but he does not go over all the securities of the bank and say whether they are good or bad ; the auditor of a loan company does not inquire into the value of the assets or the nature of the securities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Does he not inquire into the value of the securities ?
The auditor does not A'alue the securities. How could any professional auditor go over every item of the stock and say whether it was purchased at the proper value ? That is not his duty.

If an auditor is going over the_books of an investment company and he finds stocks valued in the security list at par, and he knew that they were only worth fifty cents on the dollar, do you mean to say that it is not his duty so' to report them ?

I think my hon. friend would, if he was an auditor. My hon. friend being an honest man, if lie was drawing money from a company to audit its books, and he noticed anything of that kind, no doubt he would report it to the president and directors of the company. That is the only duty he would have to perform. It always appeared to me that the Auditor General does not need a staff of experts for each department.
I did not say that.

Practically that is what it comes to. My hon. friend knows very well that an auditor of an investment company does not go over the value of each piece of property on which they have a loan, and say whether the value is a fair one or not.

Is the hon. gentleman not aware that the expenditure on both capital and income account for one year on the Intercolonial Railway is about $10,000,000, and should we not have an expert auditor for that one item alone ?
.The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, lou might keep an expert auditor for one item and not for another. The officials of railway departments are charged with the administration of the department. They are responsible for the conduct of the department. The auditor audits the accounts to see whether the stores have been purchased and the accounts properly kept. We are to be the judges of the conduct of the officers of the department. I think it would be a very proper thing for the Auditor Gen-eial, if any of his staff in going over these accounts noticed any amount as having been paid which was excessive or extravagant or irregular, to report the fact to this House. But to say that the Auditor General should be the judge of the prices is an altogether different thing and it would be impossible that such a state of affairs could exist. In each department there are officers specially attached to each branch who have to certify before the auditor will pass an account that the price paid is fair and just. It is upon that expert that we place the responsibility and the minister assumes responsibility for 406
his official. The minister comes before parliament and the country and is required to justify the conduct of his department. The Auditor General could not very well be called upon to judge in regard to every item as to whether the price paid is too much or not.
How should I know as a member of the Public Accounts Committee anything about the values of the commodities in store if the auditor did not act as an expert and did not know the values ?
The official of the department has to sign the account. He is an expert. He is our employee. He is the man we hold responsible.
If he is the man who is held responsible what is the use of sending an auditor there at all ?

The auditor has a different duty to perform. It is liis duty to audit the accounts but that is a different thing from fixing the values. Each department could not wait to consult the auditor as to the price or value of goods before making a purchase. If the auditor notices anything excessive or unfair it would be his duty to report, it would be the duty of the officer who is responsible to give an explanation to his minister and the duty of the minister to explain to the House as to whether there was anything in the charge or not. The conditions and circumstances are so different in different sections of the Dominion and in different seasons of the year that nobody not familiar with the conditions at a particular time could judge as to whether the prices were fair and just or not. The chief engineer of the department is responsible for that. He has under him on the spot, in the locality where the work is going on or where the purchases are proposed to be made, a man in whom he places confidence and who reports to him as to values and whose accounts he endorses. It seems impossible to hold the Auditor General responsible for the conduct of every department. There would not be much use in having any departments at all if he were to be the sole judge as to how, when and at what prices articles are to be purchased. We have a large staff in each department and it is to the judgment of these men that we must look to determine whether the accounts are fair or not. The Auditor General simply deals with the money part of it. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker), on second thought, must see that the proposition which he makes Is thoroughly impracticable. There is a responsibility upon the head of the department to see that his department is properly and economically managed and he has to answer to the House for the expenditure of the money which is appropriated to his department. The Auditor General should not be expected to become



responsible for tbe prices paid for goods. If, as the hon. member for Hamilton suggested, they were taking stock and if for that special purpose the Auditor General wanted a technical officer to place a value upon the stores at the time of stock-taking I could understand that there might be some force in what he has said, but to make a general proposition that the Auditor General is to be responsible for the prices paid for stores is to suggest something which is impracticable and impossible.

It does not seem to me at all impossible because the auditor might be an officer who had all the qualifications of an auditor and still have in addition to those technical knowledge that would enable him to perform the duties that have been referred to by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). My hon. friend pointed out a very striking case, namely, that in the stores account there might be the accumulations of years that were charged at the price at which they were originally purchased. Every person knows that many of the stores might not be worth one-tentli of what they cost. During the time that the accumulation is going on there must be a false account in regard to them.
They might be worth more.

Possibly, they might be in some instances. My kon. friend from Hamilton pointed out that there should be a technical officer who was an auditor as well. It is a case of stock-taking once a year. It is just the same as if an auditor were auditing the accounts of an insurance or a loan company. One of the things he would look into particularly would be the securities and the values of these securities and lie would have to value them for what they were worth at the time. Why should we not have the same system in connection with the Intercolonial Railway ? It is a very large concern. There are immense sums of money expended from year to year. I can quite understand that neither the government nor the general manager is at all anxious that these accounts shall be cut down. It is no reflection upon them at all when I say that. The general disposition is to make the best showing possible. The lion. Minister of Public Works says that the government are responsible, but I think he is going too far with his responsibility. The responsibility of the government only goes to the extent that we can turn them out of office when they do wrong. They do not redeem the losses that are made; their responsibility is not in dollars and cents and therefore there should be an officer to stand between the people and the government, I do not card* how well meaning they may be. To have a he-''thy state of things you must have business carried on in a business way. There is absolutely no difference between

auditing the Intercolonial Railway accounts by a technical officer who understands values and who would go into the stores and take stock, valuing the goods that were there, separating those goods that might be sold for purposes other than scrap iron from those that will be nothing more nor less than scrap iron
That would not be an auditor.
My hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) does not seem to understand yet. He would be an auditor with technical knowledge.
Where can you find an auditor with that technical knowledge ? You cannot do it.
My hon. friend has a very much smaller opinion of the possibilities of men of ordinary intelligence than either I or this committee have.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us the difference between the functions of an auditor and of a valuator It strikes me that he is confusing the work of two different classes of officials.

The difference is, in general terms, very distinct. The valuator is one who has a knowledge of the goods he is valuating. He must be an expert and a man of knowledge in that particular line, but it does not follow that he may not be a first-class accountant, an auditor in every sense of the word. Auditing is not a mere matter of seeing whether there are receipts for all the expenditures ; an auditor must see whether the accounts were authorized how the money was provided, and whether the payments were legal or not. It does not follow that because a valuator has technical knowledge he may not be an auditor as well. It is possible to have a trained officer, as the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has pointed out. It may be quite true that we have no officer of that kind now, but I reiterate what I said before, that it is very' easy to get a man who is a first-class auditor in the true sense of the word who would at the same time go into the stores and say :	Here, we will take
stock ; we will go through your accounts afterwards, but let us see what your stores are like. This seems to me so plain that it is not worth arguing.

I would again place myself on record so that there may be no misunderstanding that on this question there has been no difference whatever between the Auditor General and the government. The Auditor General has unlimited power to audit these accounts. He has exercised that power. He has had all the officials he has asked for, and has had the most full and complete control of the accounts. I do not admit that it is the duty of this government to thrust officials on the Auditor General if he does not want them.
Not in this instance, because he is the party who must make the application.

1 do not think the fact that the Auditor General has not made an application to the present parliament would prevent parliament from doing what it thinks to be most in the public interest. I do not propose to give up my independent judgment. There may be things that are in the public interest for which the Auditor General does not ask, and he may ask for things which I would think were not in the public interest. The question is whether or not there should be some audit with respect to stores and supplies of the Intercolonial Railway, made by an officer who is independent of the government.
That would be a valuator, not an auditor.
Does not the hon. member recognize that the present functions of the Auditor General are something more than what is popularly called auditing ?

Would my hon. friend say that the Auditor General is called upon to value the supplies covered by the accounts which he has to audit, and has to decide whether the beef, the pork, and the various other articles were bought at proper prices V He lias nothing to do with that. He simply audits the accounts, sees that they are entered properly and that there are vouchers for the payment. He has nothing whatever to do with the values of the articles to which the accounts relate.

I desire to express as distinctly as I can my absolute divergence from the view expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Charlton). Not only has the Auditor General that power, but he has exercised it over and over again. If my hon. friend will look over the Auditor General's Report for the last half dozen years he will see that the auditor more than once has sent out officials to measure work which has been done, and has made a report that he does not think that it is worth the amount sought to be exacted from the government. Did he not, under the late administration, send down to value some work on the Curran bridge.
He was not called upon to say whether the work was worth so much a yard, but to ascertain if the work was performed. It was a scrutiny of the accounts.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) is not aware of what the Auditor General has been doing during the last eight or ten years. If he will look 406i
up the Auditor General's Report, he will find that whether or not the Auditor General has the power to do it he has at least been exercising that power frequently. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) seems to think that because there was an auditor in the Department of Railways and Canals, there was an end to the question. It does not put an end to the question, because the functions of the Auditor General are entirely different from those of an auditor who is under the control of the government. If the argument of the Minister of Public Works were carried to its legitimate conclusion, it would result in the abolition of the Auditor General, because every department of the government has its auditor. The Auditor General is the servant of the people through parliament, removable only by parliament, and not by the government. The point taken by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is that we should have an audit of the same kind as that made by the auditor of the department performed by an officer who is not dependent on the government, and who cannot be dismissed at the will and pleasure of the government. That seems to me to be a reasonable proposition. I do not suppose the Auditor General can value every dollar's worth of supplies, he cannot push this work to extremes, but you can give the Auditor General power to investigate where he has reason to believe, for example, that work at a particular station is being done at an excessive price or that the work for which a claim is made has not been done, or that the work is being improperly divided as between capital and maintenance accounts. Investigation of that kind must be performed by some one if you are to have any check. It may be done by officers of the department at the present time, but there should also be power in the Auditor General to supervise that work.

There is very little, if any, difference between the hon. leader of the opposition and myself. In closing my remarks, I said to the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that if he had advocated for this stores account a valuation by an officer not under the control of the Railway Department, but under that of the Auditor General, I did not think there would be any difference between us. But he spoke of an audit in a general way, and it is in a general way that I thought and stated that it would be impracticable. The hon. leader of the opposition and myself agreed ; I did not take the position which he says I did. The logical conclusion of the principle he has enunciated in his remarks would be to abolish parliament and the departments, and to leave the whole thing to the Auditor General. That would be a more logical conclusion than the conclusion which he drew from what I said. I quite agree with my hon. friend that if the Auditor General

thought it desirable in. any particular matter to have a valuator in his department, he should have one. I can quite understand in this particular case that if parliament was not satisfied with the way that stores account was being kept, or with the values put upon the stores by the department, parliament should ask their own official to make a valuation and report. But it seems to me impracticable, and ridiculous for any one to argue that the Auditor General and his branch must be held responsible for the value of the goods purchased, Ac. X agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, that the people of Canada do not want to have the Auditor General control all the aff airs of this country ; they look to parliament, to their representatives here. They must leave the power in the hands of parliament, even over the Auditor General.
The officials of the various departments, who are supposed to be perfectly capable and. honest, must certify the accounts before they are passed by the Auditor General ; just as every business man has to depend on the officials of the various branches of his business to certify to the correctness of ' the accounts for goods purchased. I would go so far as to say that if, for example, the Auditor General found accounts coming to him from the Public Works Department for lumber at $30 or $40 a thousand, which was purchased at some point where the ordinary price was $20 a thousand, I think he would be neglecting his duty if he did not report the matter to the minister, and inform him that he would report it to parliament if it were not properly explained. But to say that the Auditor General must be responsible for the prices paid by the department, I think every one will admit is a ridiculous position to take.
Do I understand the minister to say that a proper inventory of these stores is made at stated intervals ?

I presume there is. In so large a department as the Department of Railways and Canals, there must be a proper set of books, and the accounts must be properly kept, although they go through the Auditor General's department. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) suggested, as did the hon. member for Bothwell, that the officials of the department, or the minister, would desire to show that their purchases had not been improperly made, or that they had not bought more than they required.
The hon. gentleman, I think, misunderstood me. I did not enter into the question of whether purchases were wisely or unwisely made.
That would be the result.
No, no.

It was suggested that if they had overbought, and prices afterwards went up, they would try to hide the fact. In such a case the Auditor might appoint a valuator to go over the account ; but as an expert book-keeper he could not value the goods. A man might have an expert knowledge of certain goods and be unable to read or write. In the same way, it would be improper to hold the Auditor Genera] or his department responsible for the prices paid. On that point, there is no difference between the hon. member for Hamilton and myself, that if in stock-taking there was any doubt.about the prices paid, the Auditor General might appoint an officer separate from the department to report whether the prices charged were fair or not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WOK NS.

speechtext:
Nobody would pretend to go so far in either direction as the Minister of Public Works has suggested. No one would go so far as to take away ministerial responsibility by making the Auditor General responsible for anything but neglect of duty. The Auditor General cannot be responsible for the payment of excessive prices. All he can do is to call attention to it. It is no new thing to have an account certified with the statement that the prices are reasonable and fair. I have often seen that certificate when I knew that the prices were not fair. Without attempting to place any wrong-doing at the door of any minister, we know that the tendency under all governments is to pass these accounts. It becomes largely a mere matter of form. The hon. gentleman may ask, have you no confidence in the officers ?	1
do not think I need enter into a discussion of that phase of the subject at all. Confidence or no confidence, goods have been purchased, under former governments as well as under the present government, for which too much has been paid. That will always be the case under our system, where party favouritism is shown in the purchase of supplies. Let us not close our eyes to that fact, it is one of the evils of our system. It seems to me that it is a fair proposition that when goods are purchased at an excessive price, the minister and the general manager should be informed of the fact. The officer who makes the purchase or the officer who values the goods in the store, is not going to call attention to it; and the minister and the general manager will have no means of knowing it unless they get the information from some other source. It seems to me it would be of substantial benefit to both to have a technical officer who knew values. I think it is going too far to say that you could not get a man who had technical knowledge and was an auditor as well. There would be no difficulty about that. The hon. member for Hamilton has pointed out the great advantage of such an officer

in tlie department, where there are so many chances of leaks, and great leaks, in spite of the energy and close scrutiny of the general manager, upon whom the minister must rely. We must give him very wide scope. It is a very natural state of things. You destroy his usefulness if you do not do that. He cannot always run to the minister for advice. He must be a man capable of taking responsibility on himself. The minister, it is true, is responsible for the conduct of the general manager, but would not this greatly facilitate the work in the department ? Let us shake off all the rid usages that cease to be useful and enter upon a new, enlightened and intelligent method which will best serve every interest in the department. I think my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has called attention to a question which is not to be disposed of by saying : this is impossible. It is quite possible. Everybody knows that there is not one department in which goods are not purchased at too high prices. It is not possible for the minister to always guard against that, but let us guard against it as far as we can.
Do I understand the Minister of Public Works to say that the Auditor General has no responsibility as regards the fairness of the prices charged ?

I do not think parliament would expect him to be responsible for the prices. If he had reason to suppose that the prices were not fair, his duty would be to report that to parliament if he did not get satisfaction from the department ; and it is for the people to punish their administrators for having paid excessive prices. Nobody would hold him responsible, except for not reporting.
He exercises his powers in every case to prevent a recurrence ?
Of course.

I thought his duties extended further than that. In looking over the Auditor General's Report of last year, I see some correspondence that indicates something altogether different from the understanding of the minister. For example, some printing was done outside the Printing Bureau. The account was sent into the Auditor General, bearing a certificate that the prices were fair and just, but he refused to pass it, because he said it required another certificate.
From the King's Printer.

It had a certificate from the King's Printer, but he said it required a further certificate that the prices did not exceed those which would be charged in the Printing Bureau. Therefore, the Auditor General must consider that he has some
responsibility with regard to the prices charged by outside parties. If that be not the case, the officer of the Railway Department, whose duty it is to find out if the prices are fair and just, could send in an account in which the prices were double what they should be, and the Auditor General would be justified in paying it. Surely he must have some option, or he would pay every account that came along, and the responsibility would not rest in ms department.
The hon. gentleman says that the Auditor General would joay the accounts. It is not his business to pay accounts at all.
The hon. minister will admit I am right in saying that no accounts are paid -without the Auditor General's certificate ?

The point taken by the Minister of Public Works, that the Auditor General ought not be held responsible for prices is correct. If the other view is correct, if he is responsible for the prices, and if what the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) says is correct, that many claims have been paid where the prices are excessive, then the Auditor General should be dismissed as incompetent. But he is not responsible for the prices. In the case of the King's Printer, the Auditor General claimed that a certain certificate was required ; and if that had been attached, he would have passed the account.
What certificate was it ?

The Act requires that the prices should not only be fair and just, but correspond with the prices at the Printing Bureau. A certificate to that effect -was not attached ; but if it had been, the Auditor General would have passed the account, and nobody would say that he was responsible for the prices. All he had to do was to see that he had the proper vouchers according to law. To hold him responsible for the prices would be to impose on him a responsibility which was never intended, and which he would not accept himself.
That contention is not justified by the letter of the Auditor General himself. The Auditor General did receive a certificate that the prices were fair and just, and still refused to pass the account.
He required another certificate that the prices were not in excess of those charged by the Printing Bureau. Under the Act, he must have that certificate, and it had not been given him.

That is what the Auditor General's letter says :	I quote only part
of it :

Please make no further payments for printing out of your letters-of-eredit, except on vouchers whose certificate includes the fact that the prices do not exceed those which would be charged for such printing at the Government Printing Bureau.
I do not understand that the Act under which the Auditor General discharges his duties calls for such a certificate. If it does, the responsibility for correct charges of goods rests with the Auditor General.
In that particular case.

There is a distinction between being responsible for the charges and being responsible for the getting of a certificate. One involves judgment as to whether the prices are reasonable or not, and the other involves seeing whether the certificate is attached or not.

Of course, I do not wish to euter into controversy with the Minister of Finance on this subject, but I would like to understand it. I take it, from the letter 1 have read, that the Auditor General felt responsible for the correct prices in the accounts which I have referred to, for the reason that the account, when it went to the Auditor General, bore the certificate of the officer whose duty it was to certify that the prices were fair and just. That measured up to the requirements of the law
The Auditor General says it did not.

I feel sure that I do not misunderstand it, because the Auditor General does not say that the law requires a further certificate, but, as an officer feeling some responsibility in respect of the prices, he calls for a further certificate, not only that the prices are fair and just, but that they do not exceed those charged in the Printing Bureau.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) has misunderstood it. The Auditor General sometimes claims pretty wide and generous powers, but it is only just to him to say that I do not think he claimed in this case to judge whether the prices are fair and just. I speak from recollection, and, having none of the papers before me, subject to correction, but I think I am correct when I say that the Auditor General had been passing these accounts for many years with the certificate in the same form in which the hon. gentleman has quoted it, but it suddenly occurred to the Auditor General-I do not say he was wrong-that the statute under which he was acting required another certificate, and that certificate he demanded. We have passed an Act this session to make it clear that the additional certificate is not required.

The point that my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) has raised is this : This was a class of work similar to that being done in the Printing Bureau, and it was being done outside. As a gauge of what was a fair and reasonable scale of prices, he fixed the prices that would have been charged had it been done in the Printing Bureau.
Parliament fixed that.

I quite understand. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has not enlightened me at all by his remark. The Auditor General is not guided merely by the statutes, but he must have some discretionary powers which it would be impossible to embody in a statute. This printing was being done outside, and the Auditor General said :	I do not care what your certificate
may, be as to prices being fair and just, what I want to know is that the cost to the country is mot more than it would have been if the work had been done in the Printing Bureau. It was not a question of complying with the statutes

Will my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) permit me a question ? Is he sure that the Act does not require that the certificate accompanying these accounts should be that the price is not in excess of the price that would be charged in the Planting Bureau ? I am not certain of the matter, but my recollection is that the Act under which printing is done outside the Bureau, as it was before the amended Act of this session was passed, required that the prices for work done outside should mot be in excess of those in the Printing Bureau. That was got over by the legislation of this session.
If that were the law,' it is not necessary to cure a difficulty or an imaginary difficulty
Yes, it is necessary to cure an imaginary difficulty. I will give my hon. friend the case.

I was pointing out to the Minister of Finance that the Auditor General might take the course he has taken in the exercise of powers which should properly be his. Where work is done outside, he should make sure that it does not cost the country any more than work done in the Bureau. No one would imagine that it would require a statutory enactment to authorize the Auditor General to do that- it would be within the proper exercise of his powers. And the case to which the hon. member for Peel calls attention seems to show that the Auditor General felt that it was not enough for him to see to it that the prices were reasonable, but that the cost to the country was not made greater through the work being done outside. That is the essence of the whole thing. If the hon.

minister will point out where I am wrong I shall be glad to be set right.

I do not think it would be well to be drawn into a discussion of the merits or demerits as to this question of the cost of the printing. But I state my recollection of the case. Many years ago, in the time of the late government, an Act was passed intended to permit certain printing to be done in portions of the Dominion far from Ottawa, and it was provided-or seems to have been so intended-that if the prices were deemed fair and reasonable from the point of view of the local conditions under which the work was done, they should be accepted and approved. That appears to have been the spirit of the Act, and for many years the Auditor General allowed that spirit to prevail, under the late government and under the present government, and accepted and approved accounts which bore the certificate that the prices were fair and .iust. The accounts did not bear any certificate comparing the prices with those in the Printing Bureau. In fact the whole intention as I understand it was to recognize the fact that the prices might not be those of the Printing Bureau, the work being done under different conditions. But the Auditor General, after passing such accounts for many years, came to the conclusion-I do not say he was wrong-that the statute under which he was acting required a further certificate, and lie recently demanded that certificate, claiming that it was required under the statute. I have not the Act under my hand, but I think lie was correct. This year an amendment was introduced to carry out what was intended to be the spirit of the Act from the beginning, the spirit under which the Act was administered for many years under both governments.

Does that mean that excessive prices may be paid for the work done outside. If I understand the Finance Minister correctly, it means that the Auditor General has lost control in these matters. It means that the Auditor General has passed accounts for years, possibly at excessive prices-I am going to admit that, fox-, these things are as likely to have happened in the past as to happen ixow; let us be fair and frank about it. The Auditor General of course, like any other man, learns from experience. He had passed accounts year after year under both governments without inquiring whether excessive prices were being paid. Then, I fear, he made the discovery-a very useful one and one that should be within his powers without direct statutory authority-that his duty was, not to prevent work being done outside the Bureau, but to see to it that the. cost of the work to the counti-y should not be more than if it were done in the Bui'eau. That is plain. The govei'nment has relieved the Auditor General of that portion of his duty
and of the exercise of that authority. It means no more and no less than that they have taken away the power from the Auditor General, and that now accounts are to be paid at such prices that, I repeat-and I regret to repeat it-the certificate is little more than a matter of form in some cases. But the conditions may have been such as did not warrant any government in getting it done there. The Minister of Public Works tells us that the government is responsible. That is a kind of responsibility we do not understand as having force in this country. Ministerial responsibility never repaid nor restored one cent to the people from whom it has been taken away, under any government. The moi'e power you give an officer to pi-event these excesses the better for the country and the more will the ministers be relieved of trouble.

We are getting away fi-om the real point involved. But I may inform my hon. friend that the change that was made with regal'd to the printing did not necessarily imply that an excessive price had been paid. This printing being done in different portions of the Dominion at places where it suited the convenience of the department to have it done, prices that were fair and just according to the rates current in the place where the work was done, would be the fair and just prices for that work. That is the point of difference. The Auditor General understood it that, way for many years, and approved the accounts as not excessive, as being fair and just according to the standard prices of printing in the places where the work was done. That was the spirit of the Act, that was the way in which it was interpreted for many years. But when the Auditor General took it into his head to make a different interpretation, even though he had a statute to support him in doing so, it was thought well to make a change. However, that is going into the merits of the question. The origin of this part of the discussion was whether the Auditor General was responsible for the prices being fair and just. I say I do not think the Auditor General is responsible, or should be held responsible: that a part of ministerial responsibility. His duty undoubtedly will be to call attention to any case in which he thinks there was fraud, or dishonesty, or excessive charges, and so forth. But the responsibility is not his, the responsibility is the minister's. His duty is to call attention, to remonstrate if he likes, to blame, to spread the story out before parliament- that is the limitation, in my judgment, of his authority ; he is not responsible whether the prices are fair or not.

I think the Minister of Finance will agree with me that it is the duty- of a responsible minister of the gover-ment to place every power In the hands of an official to prevent these improper prac-

tices. That is the best way for the ministers to shield themselves, to protect themselves from tlie matters to which we are now calling attention. I quite agree that it would be impossible to make the Auditor Geueral responsible for the prices. He could not help excessive prices being paid, and to censure him for that would be wrong, and impossible to carry out in practice. But what my hon. friend from Hamilton is pointing out is the desirability of placing at the disposal of the Auditor General every means of preventing these improper practices.
Mr. BLA1N. As to whether the accounts require a further certificate, as the Minister of Finance thinks they should, let me read three or four lines from a letter from the King's Printer, Mr. Dawson :
I have given the certificate the Audit Act requires. I have certified that the prices are fair and just. According to the rules of equity there should be no hesitation to pay such prices.
