The King's Printer says that he gave merely a certificate that the prices for printing were fair and just. I do not know whether the minister would go so far as to say that the King's Printer is wrong, and that it does require a further statement that the prices do not exceed the prices that would be paid for such printing elsewhere. The King's Printer says that he has been doing this for ten years.

Speaking from recollection, I think the Auditor General took the ground that there was another Act somewhere dealing with the matter, which required an additional certificate, and that was the certificate he demanded.
When was that Act passed ?
I cannot say, it has been in operation for many years.
The King's Printer says there is no such Act.

1 think tne Auditor General was able to show that there was an Act somewhere which required that. He was merely acting, as he claimed, within the limits of some statute, and asking for certificates in accordance therewith.

The point is that the King's Printer says, over his own signature, dated December 26th, 1902, that the accounts have been paid continuously upon the simple certificate that the prices were fair and just.

That is no doubt correct, that was the form of audit for a while. While the Auditor General accepted that certificate for many years, he recently required something else, and clai ned that he had statutory authority to demand it.

My opinion is that the Auditor General was quite right I Mr. CLANCY.
in requiring that the prices should not exceed those of the government office. I can understand that If the printing was given by tender there would be no necessity for the Auditor General making such a reference ; but from the fact of the printing being farmed out, it was necessary to have some basis upon which to arrive at the proper cost. Would the acting Minister of Railways and Canals tell me when the last inventory of stores was made, what was the value of the stores, and by wborn was it made ?

The inventory is made on the 30th of June every year. According to the books of the Auditor General for 1901-2, the value was $1,500,000; the value at the last inventory, at the close of the year 1902-3, was about $917,302.24.
By what official was that inventory made ?

The manager informs me that the inventory of the track stores along the line is taken on the 31st of October, and of the rest on the 30th of June. The general stock-taking is on the 30th of June but they prefer to take stock of the track stores at the end of the season.
The hon. gentleman has not yet given me the information I have asked for. Who has charge of the stock-taking ?
The accounts are taken by the officials of the Intercolonial Railway, men in the department specially assigned to make that investigation.

I have sent for the Act respecting the Printing Bureau, and I see that there is nothing in it requiring a special certificate, and that the amendment made this session does not do away with such a certificate, -because there was no certificate required. The amendment made this session provided that:
Nothing in this Act shall require that stationery and printing tor the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway or the Prince Edward Island Railway shall be obtained or done in the said establishment in any case where such stationery and printing may be more conveniently procured elsewhere at a cost not exceeding customary and fair commercial rates for similar work or supplies in similar quantities.
That section was brought in, not to do away with any certificate that had previously been required, but to enable the government to get its printing done apart from the Printing Bureau. Therefore, the Auditor General was acting within his right in demanding the certificate required by the statute.

My recollection is that the Auditor General d'd claim that he was acting under the

statute. Howevei, tlie point is not of much importance, because I am simply contending that the House cauuot expect* to hold the Auditor General responsible for the prices paid for stores being fair and reasonable. All you can expect the Auditor General to do is to see that the accounts are correct, and that if in any case he has reason to believe that the accounts are improper, it is his duty to call attention to them and to investigate. But we could not hold him responsible for the pfriees paid1 for goods throughout Canada, and I do not think he would be willing to accept that responsibility.

I cannot understand who the official is who makes the inventory of stores. There will no doubt be an official in charge for the stores department, but these supplies will be scattered along the railway and will be at the different stations. Who makes out this inventory ? Is it the gentleman in charge of the stores or some other official ?
The inventory is taken by the store-keeper, with the assistance of such officials as he has in his own branch and of others from other branches of the railway service as may be required.
Who fixes the valuation of these stores ? Is it the gentleman in charge of the stores ?

The valuation of these stores is based on the prices which were paid for them, subject to any loss that may occur in keeping or handling them. The general manager has given me this illustration for instance : If a quantity of oil was placed in the store, in measuring it out there would be a certain amount of loss that would be charged up against revenue. You could not measure out exactly the same quantity of oil as you put in. In that case, the books would be balanced by charging the loss against the revenue account for the year.
On section <3,

I would like to ask the hon. minister if there is any classification of this large amount of money that is expended on the Intercolonial Railway ? If there is jilaced to the credit of the Department of Railways and Canals $1,500,000 for the Intercolonial Railway, do I understand that the minister would have the right to say that it should be expended in any way he wished ? Would it be apportioned in such a way that so much money would be voted for the purchase of steel rails and so much for the purchase of locomotives ?
No, it would be general.
Could the minister take the million and a half and purchase whatever kind of goods he wished ?

It is a very extreme case, but he could. But what would he do with them afterwards ? He would have to make use of these goods. There would be no great pleasure in having them in store, and he could only use them on the Intercolonial Railway at such places and for such purposes as parliament had, authorized.
Mi-. BLAIN. I do not think it is fair that the department should have the right to apportion the full appropriation made by parliament, or that the minister should have the right to expend the money in any manner that he wished. The minister should come forward and say that so many thousand dollars should be applied to one part of the railway and so many thousand to another part. But to give the minister carte blanche to expend this money seems to me to be giving him very extended powers.

I do not think, if my hon. friend were starting a shop and wanted $100,000 to carry his stock, that he would find it convenient to state that so muqh should be devoted to goods of one colour and so much to goods of another colour. I would like to call the attention of the committee to the wording of the Act of 1S93 respecting the Department of Public Printing and Stationery. It contains these words :
Provided that nothing in this Act shall be held to require that the printing for the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway or the Prince Edward Island Railway shall he done in the said establishment in any case when such printing may he more conveniently done elsewhere at a cost not exceeding that which would be charged for such printing at the said establishment.
Therefore, what the Auditor General asked was that a certificate should be given in accordance with the words of the statute. His demand rested on the statute.
May I ask if the Auditor General objected to these accounts without that special certificate ?

I do not know what the Auditor General did before the Act was passed in 1893, but I know that for long years afterwards he passed these accounts without the certificate.
Mr. I?LAIN. The Auditor General did not enforce the Act in respect to the special certificate which the hon. gentleman has referred to ?
I believe that is the fact.

That is rather suspicious. It looks as if somebody was trespassing in regard to the accounts, when there was no such trespassing in days gone by. Perhaps my hon. friend can tell us why the Auditor feels it to be his duty to enforce this law to the very letter now, when he felt it to

be his duty for many years not to enforce it at all ?
Prices were fixed toy Order in Council, and that Order in Council was passed by the late government.
And these were to be the prices not exceeding those charged at the Bureau ?
No, they were not.
That is what the Act says, and they could not pass an Order in Council contrary to the Act.

The hon. gentleman says they could not. An hon. gentleman said a few minutes ago that whether tlie Auditor General has power to do a certain thing or not, he does it. That Order in Council was passed. We will take another illustration. Twenty years ago the Superannuation Act was passed, whereby a man was entitled, upon his retirement, to receive an allowance in proportion to the number of years of his sei-vice. After the Act was passed a case arose where a man had a few months over the year' to his credit, and the question came up as to how it should be dealt with. The government of the day passed a very sensible Order in Council to the effect that if the number of months was less than six they should not be counted, while if there were more than six they should count as another year. For twenty years the Auditor General accepted that Order in Council as a good law, but a few months ago it occui'red to him that it was not good in law, or in common sense, and he cut down the allowance of a lighthouse keeper, saying that this was not what the law, said, and this year we have had to change the law.

The hon. gentleman will, no doubt, find cases of that kind. It is not to be expected that after years of experience, the Auditor General would not find out that in some respects he was not acting sti'ictly according to the law, but the strange thing about the matter now is that just as soon as the Auditor Geuei-al acted up to the law passed in 1893, the Minister of Finance comes in with a Bill and says to the Auditor Genei'al : The law of 1893 provides that while printing may be done outside it shall not cost this country any more than it would cost if it were done at the Pl'inting Bureau at Ottawa ; it will not do for you to insist on a strict observance of the law, for if you do we will repeal that law so that we can close your mouth, and we will give such prices as may be charged to suit the conditions in outside towns. The government of the day is not justified in getting one line of printing done where the conditions are as favourable for economical work as they are in the Printing Bureau. You may say that it is more Mr. BLAIN.
convenient to have it done here or there, but hon. gentlemen opposite know very well the evil tendency of pursuing a course of that kind. The pressure of party friends under our system is a great danger to the public, and the moment you take away the Auditor's power, and say to the Auditor General : True, you are living up to the Act of 1893, but under such circumstances we cannot give our friends any printing because their conditions are such that they cannot compete with the Bureau, and therefore we cannot give it to them. The government are not justified in doing this. There can be any number of conditions under which yoxx can pay anything you like, and say that it is a fair price, that a mani is not making any undue profit. One man may not be able to make even a living where another man can make a profit. The minister is taking a dangerous step in this, and one that he will have reason to regret.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE, i'lie hon. gentleman finds great danger in things that ai-e done by this government, in which he saw no danger when his own friends were in power.
Mr. ClANCY. I am talking on general principles, and I said it was wrong if it was done under the late government.

The merits of the printing question do not happen to be connected with this Bill, but let me state briefly the facts of the case. The late government passed an Order in Council; the hon. gentleman said they could not do so.
I said they had no authority to do so.

The hon. gentleman is now proving that his friends set the law of 1893 at defiance when they passed an Order in Council declaring that this work might be done in different parts of the country on certain terms and conditions having regard to local conditions. For years that system was carried on under both governments and the Auditor General allowed it to be done, accepting the certificate of the King's Printer that the price was fair and just. Then the Auditor Genei'al makes the discovei'y that this was not consistent with the statute, and says : I will live up; to the statute. Then, we come in and say -I did not introduce the Bill, but I accept my share of responsibility-that that which was the understood policy of both governments for many years, and to which the Auditor Genei'eal did not object, should continue to be the system in force. In regard to the superannuation, much the same thing occurred. For 20 years the Auditor General paid the odd months to the poor lighthouse-keepei', but at this late stage he awakens to the idea that it is not legal and refuses to give the lighthouse-keeper the
benefit of these months. We step in and say that we will give the lighthouse-keeper the odd months, because it is fair and reasonable.

The hon. gentleman cannot take shelter under that. The hon. gentleman is too intelligent not to know that when I said the late government could not pass such an Order in Council, I meant that in so doing they exceeded their authority. The Auditor General had a perfect right to call attention to the fact that if such an Order in Council existed it was contrary to the statutes. The fact that the former government did that does not justify the present government in doing it. We should adopt such a policy as will inure to the best interests of the country. X am not here to defend any act of the former government that is not defensible, I do not think it is the business of any man on either side of the House, because his party may have made mistakes or have gone too far, to justify these mistakes. Ret us, I say, adopt such a policy and such rules as will inure to the best interests of this country. The hon. minister is trying to take shelter behind what ? Behind the fact that the former government did it. Is he adopting all the virtues as well as all the vices of the former government ? Has he laid down the rule that because a former government did this, whether it be good or bad, that he is to adopt it. Is it in the interests of'the country to take this power from the Auditor General by repealing the Act of 1803, notwithstanding that the Order in Council has n >
legal effect ? I ask him. too. if it is in the public interest to take that power out of the hands of the Auditor General and to permit printing to be done anywhere in Canada at prices which, under the conditions, can always be justified as being fair ?

My bon. friend (Mr. Clancy) has criticised the action of his friends in the late government. I will be more generous. I am going to defend the late government. I will not allow them to be maligned by the hon. member for Botbwell (Mr. Clancy). When the late government passed the Order in Councillor, I think, the Conservative government dealt with both of these questions, with printing and superannuation-it was a common sense Order in Council. Tn relation to superannuation, where the statute had failed to take account of the odd mouths, it was reason and common sense that the government should say : where a man has seven months to his credit, we will count it as a year, and if he has only two or three months to his credit we will not count it at all. That was common sense and in carrying that out we have been simply doing what is fair and reasonable. The late government for years allowed their friends to do the printing. Our predecessors did it as
we do it. I am here to defend the principle of giving our friends the preference every time provided the prices are just, and I am not in favour of concentrating all the work into the Printing Bureau at Ottawa If a portion of that work has in the past been done in other portions of the Dotnimon,
I do not think we should concentrate it all in Ottawa. There has been no change in regal'd to method or price. The Conservative press did a certain amount of work for the Intercolonial Railway at a price settled bv Order in Council. If that system has been continued by the present government at prices which are fair and just, I say there is no wrong to the public treasury, and I am here to defend the action of the late government in that respect.

I wish to differ from the policy of the government in respect to giving out printing to any other office than the Printing Bureau. I am not here to say whether the late government did what was right or what was wrong. In my humble opinion they did what was wrong, and I believe that where the government has a Printing Bureau, as they have in the city of Ottawa, capable of doing a large amount of printing, it is not wise to give the Railway Department authority to get their printing done in any part of Canada they choose. Whether the prices are fair and just or not, I do not express any opinion at the moment. I wish to express my dissent from the policy of the government in this respect. I do not think it will receive the endorsation of the people of this country.
It is a little late ; the Bill is passed.	.
I think it is the duty of the government to take away such power from the department.
I do not think there was a division on the Bill ; so I am afraid my hon. friend is bound by it.

Perhaps I should not say what is in my mind about that sort of criticism. The hon. minister sought to drag the superannuation question into this discussion. We are not responsible for that. I want to remind him of the promise he and the minister who sits behind him made to this country, that if they were put in power they would abolish the Superannuation Act. Yet. tlie charges to the country under that Act are now greater than they were under the late government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have been waiting with great patience and expectation for the last ten minutes, thinking that the committee would stop this irrelevant^ discussion ; but finding that they are widening it, I am constrained to ask them to he good enough to return to the question.
I hope the Minister of Finance will take notice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, both sides.
It is very kind of the chairman to show so much patience ; but I notice that his patience generally ceases when a member of the opposition has the floor.
Order.

However, I bow at once to liis ruling. I do not think the superannuation question should be discussed at this time. We are not responsible for the introduction of that question, and I have said all I have to say upon it. In my opinion this Bill gives too wide powers to the Railway Department. I do not think that department should have placed to its credit ?1,500,000, with tire right to purchase for the Intercolonial Railway whatever kinds of goods they wish, in whatever quantity, wherever they wish, and at whatever price they wish. I think the Act should specify that a certain amount should be placed to the credit of the department to purchase steel rails when required, a certain amount to purchase locomotives when required, and so on. I do not think such great powers should be given to the minister. The new minister seems to require very great liberty.
I do not know whether his predecessor would think this a proper measure; he is not in the House. For myself. I think it is very dangerous legislation, and I wish to express myself as against it.

This morning I raised a point with regard to the first section, which I did not press very strongly, because the Minister of Finance and my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) both seemed to entertain a somewhat different view to that which I expressed. But I must say that I am not quite convinced yet. I think I understand the intention of the section, and the difficulty I have in regard to it is owing possibly to some lack of care in the way in which it is drafted. As the section reads at present, with the last line struck out, it provides that advances may be made indefinitely. There is no necessary connection between section 1 and sections 2 and 3. My difficulty would be to a great extent eliminated if you added after the word * advances,' in the first section, the words ' on railway stores account.'

I have no objection to adding these words though I do not think they change the meaning of the section. I move that section 1 be reconsidered, and that these words be inserted.
Motion agreed to; Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

Bill (No. 200) to amend the Act respecting certain works constructed in or over navigable waters, read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister to let this stand over until next session so that we may have time to consider it. This government has never given a dollar for the purpose of erecting a wharf on either side of Howe island there. The farmers, in order to get over from that island, have established a ferry service operated by cable, and have built a row of docks along both sides. Why should the government compel these people to take out a license and pay $5 for permission to use the ferry they have established themselves? This Bill will apply to ferries which have been running for the last fifty years.

I do not see why we should not have a law to regulate the use of these cables in order to protect life and property. In the case of certain ferries which have been long established, we might not charge any license, but it is necessary, that they should be subjected to some regulations. There have been a number of accidents owing to the absence of any regulations. Nearly a whole family was drowned at Bout De L'lsle near Montreal a few months ago. A cable had been stretched aci'oss the channel without license. It was under water, not seen, and there was nothing to indicate its presence. These people came across this obstacle and their boat was upset and they were drowned. The only recourse their successors have is to sue in damages the parties who laid the cable. In Manitoba repeated accidents of a similar kind have happened.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's argument is not sufficient justification for the

course lie intends to take. There are many accidents on steamboats which are licensed and carry licensed engineers, captain and pilots. I do not see how there can be any danger in leaving these cables undisturbed, because they run along the bottoms of rivers. If the hon. gentleman will allow the Bill to stand, he will find that he will get representations against it from many of the provinces.

Does this Bill refer only to navigable waters ?
The MINISTER Oh' MARINE AND FISHERIES. Yes, I do not intend to regulate the use of cable across waters which are not navigable. I am going as far as it is possible to go under the present circumstances, and am acting on the recommendation that has been made. If the hon. gentleman wishes to apply it to non-navigable waters, the Bill will be found still more objectionable to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor). The principle is not new at all., but is involved in chapter 92 of the Revised Statutes of Canada respecting certain works constructed in or over navigable waters. This Act was passed in 1886, and the present Bill only expands the powers which are given under that Act and provides for the regulating of some things which are not regulated under the law as it stands. The non-regulation of which has led to loss of life and property.

I have in mind navigable rivers on which ferries are established by municipalities. If the present Bill becomes law, these municipalities will have to get licenses from the minister for a ferry, and, no doubt, he will send out an inspector to see that the work is done according to his regulation. If the hon. minister wishes to apply this to the North-west Territories, where they have no municipal institutions, I personally, would have no great objection. But if he wishes to interfere with the work in this respect now carried on by the municipalities in Ontario, I think lie is going altogether too far. How does the hon. gentleman intend to provide for the proper arrangement of these cables ? Is he going to send out a travelling inspector ?
A lot of them.

I am afraid it is only a means of providing offices. I have not had an opportunity to study the Bill closely, but from the hon. minister's explanation, I am led to believe that he is not warranted in taking charge of ferries now controlled by municipalities and properly managed. Nor is there any reason why he should demand a license fee of $5 from a municipality for carrying on such a work.

Supplementing what the hon. member for Botliwell (Mr. Clancy) has said-the hon. minister can answer both of us when he speaks. I understand that in the North-west Territories they establish these ferries and maintain them for the- convenience of the settlers. Would not the hon. minister run foul of the North-west council there as well as of the municipalities in the ease my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) has referred to ? And, if a license is charged, would not the government be responsible for seeing to it that these ferries are kept in proper condition, and be liable in case of accidents V

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) surely is not serious. If a bridge is constructed over a navigable water according to plans which have been submitted to the Governor General in Council and approved, and an accident occurs, would the hon. gentleman contend that the government is responsible ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Certainly.
He will not pretend that before a court, I am sure.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In support of what my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) lias stated, I may say that one of the cables from Howe island to the main shore is owned and controlled by the municipality, and a man is paid by the municipality to operate it. The other, at the end of the island, is owned by a private individual. I do not know whether the hon. minister intends to provide that these ferries cannot be operated without making application to his department and paying $5. He says that this does not apply to non-navigable waters. Will the hon. gentleman define navigable and non-navigable water ?
The hon. gentleman must know that as well 'as I do-everybody knows what is meant by navigable water.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Well, will the hon. minister explain ? In referring to the remarks of my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) lie spoke of non-navigable waters. What are non-navigable waters ?

Waters on which boats cannot be used for regular transportation. The statute makes it very clear what is navigable water and what is floatable water. I do not see any object in having a debate on the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What, in the hon. minister's opinion, is a non-navigable water ?
One that it is not possible to navigate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: With what kind of a boat ?

With a canoe ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Even the smallest pond in the country can be navigated with a boat of some kind. So this would apply to every patch of water we have.

The minister ought not to dismiss this question with a nod of his head. He seems to think that everybody ought to know what is a navigable water, but, being a layman, I confess that I do not know as much as the minister does on these matters. What is a navigable water ? The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) suggests that any water is navigable on which you can float a canoe. Does the minister agree to that ? Take the case of a river with an island in it. On one side is the boat channel, but on the other, between the island and the shore, boats do not go. Would the part not used be navigable under law ? Or, take the case spoken of by the hon. member for South Deeds (Mr. Taylor). The island lie mentions, if I remember well, is at the foot of Lake Ontario. The farmers have stretched a cable across to the shore in order to work a ferry. That channel may not be used for steamers, but is it or is it not navigable water ? Where municipalities have established these ferries, of course, the ferries are as well managed as they could be by the Department of Marine and Fisheries or any officer the minister might send. If the minister takes this under his control, would lie insist upon the municipalities carrying out certain regulations made by his department, and would he insist upon their getting a license ? These are questions which should be answered before we pass this legislation.

I think that nobody will deny that the Dominion has jurisdiction over all navigable waters, and that it would be a defiance of Dominion authority for any person to lay a cable in navigable waters that would interfere with navigation. As I understand it, the object of this Bill is to fix the liability. If my hon. friend or some of his friends happened to be navigating a river and met with an accident in consequence of these cables, and if he could not fix the liability anywhere, he would say that the government were neglecting their duty. As I understand the object of the Bill, it is simply to provide that these people shall pay a nominal fee, so that there will be some' responsibility, and in order that this work may be carried on without interfering with navigation.
Would the minister consider the River Trent, for instance, a navigable stream ? It is not navigable in its present state, but with certain improvements it may be made so.

Laymen like the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) and myself would Mr. HEYD.
get into deep water if we undertook to explain the legal meaning of a navigable stream. It may be, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says, that a stream is navigable on which navigation can be carried on for commercial purposes, unless it has been declared not to be so by Act of parliament.
Mi-. CLARKE. Declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.

There are streams that are navigable, and might be construed to be navigable unless they have been declared by Act of parliament non-navigable streams. In such a case the jurisdiction over them would fall within the province instead of the Dominion. There are other streams where, at certain seasons of the year, not even a canoe could be paddled over them, and yet they are legally navigable streams, as I have found in my experience.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: As I understand the Act defining navigable waters, it places jurisdiction over them in the Department of Public Works. Now, why is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries going to take charge of these ferries when they properly belong to the Department of Public Works ?

That may be correct in a general sense, but my hon. friend knows that fisheries and navigable streams are under the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and the old government. I think, put ferries under the Inland Revenue Department. But in a general way, I think my hon. friend is right, and it would be better, in the public interest, that the granting of licenses to these parties should be in the Marine Department rather than in the Public Works Department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
If a party wants to build a wharf on any navigable water he must make application to the Department of Public Works, which has control of all navigable waters. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries may think that these cables are interfering with the fish that may resort to these waters. That may be the object of introducing this Bill, for fear that these cables stretching across these waters may interfere with the fisheries; otherwise, I do not see that it has any justification unless it is to bring some grist to his mill, and give him some more patronage. I do not seq why we should have legislation spliting up departments, putting one part of a navigable stream under the control of Public Works and another under Marine and Fisheries. If the government have promised to give the Minister of Marine and Fisheries more patronage, let them come down with an Act and define what jurisdiction he has, instead of running in these little annoying Bills, taking parts of jurisdiction away from the

Department of Public Works tliat properly belongs to it. But aside from that, take the Rideau canal from here to Kingston, I know several of tliese cable ferries running from one side of the Bideau canal to tlite other, that have been working for years. Have these people got to stop using these ferries ? I ask the minister to point to a single accident that has ever happened to anybody navigating the waters of the St. Lawrence or of the Rideau canal, in consequence of these cables, or point to any other place in the Dominion, or cite one case where a family was going across in a row-boat and ran against one of these cables and were upset. That happens every day in the week without a cable. People get upset in row-boats and lives are lost. But merely on account of one accident, is he going to put the people of this country to this great inconvenience ? Does lie pretend that if a rowboat is paddled over the water that makes it a navigable water ? Then, every stream in the Dominion is a navigable water.
I never heard of an accident happening to a steamboat or a sail-boat coining in contact with one of these cables. These cable ferries are a great convenience to the people in all parts of the country, and the people, in order to have communication with each other, have a little boat which they pull across with a cable. That cable lies at the bottom of the river when it is not in' use, and will not interfere with anything except when it is used to pull the boat across. Then the people see the ferry moving and can keep out of its way. But the minister wants to make a place for some half dozen men to go round and inspect these cables and collect tolls, putting the public generally to great inconvenience.
Has the minister had any demand from the province of Ontario for this legislation ?

This legislation is not new at all, the principle was adopted nearly 20 years ago when the first Bill was passed regulating the use of navigable waters. That was a consolidation of many previous laws then existing. I refer to chapter 92 of the Act respecting navigable waters, which provides that bridges, booms and so forth shall be regulated in a certain manner, and when a bridge is destroyed and has to be renewed, or when a bridge needs repairs, the plans therefor must be submitted to the Governor General in Council, who will not sanction them unless it is made clear that they will not interfere with navigation or render navigation more difficult. Therefore, this legislation is not at all new. I did not expect, of course, that all these questions would be raised, otherwise I could have looked more deeply into past legislation. But I find that chapter 35 of 49 Victoria, refers to a number of Acts previously existing, which it repealed. Those Acts are the following :
45 Vic., c. 37, respecting bridges over navigable waters constructed under the authority of provincial Acts; 40 Vic., c. 43, respecting booms and other works constructed in navigable waters, whether under the authority of provincial Acts or otherwise ; 46 Vic., c. 44, to amend an Act of the present session respecting booms and other works constructed in navigable waters, whether under the authority of provincial Acts or otherwise; 48-49 Vic., c. 6, to amend the law respeetng bridges, booms and other works constructed over or in navigable waters, under the authority of provincial Acts. This law of 1886 is a consolidation of all those statutes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Not a word in those Acts about ferries.

Not about ferries, but about all the rest. At that time probably accidents which have occured since had not occurred and it had not been deemed necessary to pass such a law. I have cited accidents on the St. Lawrence river. There was also an accident on the Red river by which a man in a yacht lost his life because the yacht passed at a point where a cable was laid and there was no notice that the cable was there. I do not see that it would be a bad principle to protect the life of a citizen against such accidents as these if at the present time it is a good principle to protect the property only of the people. The law regulating booms, bridges, &c., on navigable waters is in the interest of protecting the life of citizens. It is in the interest of navigation pure and simple. I do not understand the hon. gentleman's argument. The hon. gentleman says that this law is introduced to create some patronage. I do not see where the patronage comes in. You might as well use the same argument whenever you undertake to regulate any matter affecting the public interest. In cities you might as well contend that there should be no police to maintain the law because it might involve a question of patronage. Some one has to see that the law is executed. It is not provided in the Bill that any officers shall be appointed to enforce the Act. It will be executed by the officers of the department. We have officers all over the Dominion and it will not be very much trouble to see that these cables are laid in accordance with the regulations. At the present time telegraph companies lay cables across rivers and streams and for their own protection they lay them in such a way as not to interfere with navigation because it would only be damaging their own property if their cables were interfered with. But, it is not so in regard to movable cables. The hon. gentleman says that they remain at the bottom of the river. That is not so. When the ferry passes from one shore to the other the cable is lifted and that is 1 where the danger comes in. The hon. gen-

*12992
tleman says it is very easy for those who navigate those waters to see when the ferry is coming across and that they should guard against danger. Perhaps it is impossible for them to guard against danger if there is a very swift current because there may be no indication that there is a cable at the point at which their vessel or boat is. I think, for all these reasons that this legislation is reasonable and that the objections raised by the hon. gentleman should not be allowed to stand in the way of it. I think that he makes these suggestions only for the sake of wasting time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Because legislation has been passed regulating booms and bridges it is no justification for this legislation. We all know that if a man puts a boom across a navigable water a boat cannot pass. The boom is there and may be an obstruction. The same remark applies to a bridge. Legislation lmd to be passed to regulate the building of bridges over navigable streams in order that they might be placed at a proper height above the water. But, these cables do not interfere with navigation at all. They are generally put in a narrow stream and not in swift waters.

I have seen them in swifter waters than are to be found any place in Ontario or Quebec. I have seen them across the Yukon river and if there is any swifter river in the Dominion of Canada I would like to know it.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
If they cannot get them anywhere else they may put them in a swift current, but they are generally put in a narrow stream and where the current is not swift. Those at Howe island are less than one-eight of a mile long and there is no boat navigating that water except possibly a row-boat or sail-boat. They can see the ferry as it is starting out and they can remain where they are until the boat reaches the opposite shore. The ferry at Howe island has been operated for the last thirty years by the municipality. I think the city of Kingston furnished the cable and that the municipality of Howe island operates it. At the lower end of Howe island a farmer has a little ferry operated by a cable and if any one wants to get off the island he runs the boat over. It is not operated every hour of the day but only as there is a demand for it. It has never interfered with navigation, there has never been an accident and why should this poor farmer be obliged to come down to Ottawa to see the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in order that he may keep up this ferry for the purpose of accommodating the people of this little island ? Why should he have to come down and ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to give him a license and pay him $5 in order that ho may be be able to oblige the farmers of Howe Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
island ? This government has never contributed a dollar to build a wharf for the poor people of Howe island. The Municipality of this little island built the wharf there, and the hon. minister now says that he will oblige them with a license and take $5 from them. I think it is an outrageous proposition. What is happening there will happen in almost every municipality in Ontario where the people have these little ferries which are operated with a chain or wire cable. I think, as I have said, that it is an outrageous proposition to demand that these people must take out a license to operate these two ferries or be liable to a fine of $100 or more if they fail to do so.

I am at a loss to understand the opposition to this Bill. This Bill provides that nobody shall interfere with navigable streams or navigable rivers. Any man who puts a chain across a navigable river puts an obstruction in the river which is liable to cause accident. There may be places where this may be tolerated without any serious inconvenience being caused to anybody, because, although the stream is navigable, it may not be navigated, but there are places where it would be a serious inconvenience to the public if a party were allowed to put such an obstruction in a navigable river. Under such circumstances it seems to me to be only a wise precaution that nobody should be allowed such a privilege without having permission from some authority who can go and look into the circumstances of the case- and see whether it is advisable to grant such permission or whether it is inadvisable to allow such a cable to be laid. There may be places where it is advisable and there may be other places where it wmuld not only be the reverse of advisable but perhaps dangerous. Nobody could find fault that it should not be within the power of any man, however meritorious his intention might be, to put an obstruction in a navigable river because the consequences might be very injurious. The statement made by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) that there are places where little ferries are kept is very true. It does not follow that the owners of these ferries shall be obliged to come to Ottawa and take out a license. It does not follow that they will be obliged to pay $5 for if because the Bill says that the license fee shall not exceed $5. it may be $1. or it may be twenty-five cents. But, the principle of the Bill seems to be a proper one.

I do not think that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or perhaps the right hon. gentleman <Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier), has quite considered how far-reaching this is. I may point out a case that comes under my notice almost every day. There are two branches of the river Sydenham, which is navigable for from 12 to 16 miles of its length, and on each of these branches boats are being operated con-

stantly during the season of navigation. This river does not separate municipalities, tout it runs through municipalities, and each municipality maintains ferries instead of (bridges, as the construction of bridges would entail a greater expense on the municipalities than they could undertake. Under the Ontario Act, there is a provision by which ferries may be established and controlled by municipal councils, and provision is also made for the establishment of ferries between two municipalities, tout in that case, of course, the assent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council is necessary. I am putting the simple case where the ferries are established by the one municipality, and on this river there are five or six of these. That is not an interference with navigation, and these ferries are under the control of the municipality, which is responsible for them, and is more concerned than even the department hero could be to secure the safety of life and property. The intention cannot be that the municipality, after operating one of these ferries for half a century, having the greatest care for the protection of life, should have to come down here to ask for consent.

On section 1,

On section 2,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman was to give us the recommendations of (lie British Board of Trade in regard to this matter on the second reading of the Bill, or, as we would have preferred, at some previous stage.

The object of the amendment is to enable the minister to appoint a permanent commissioner. An accident happens, it is reported to the department, and the minister^ happens to be absent, or for some reason or other he cannot be reached at once, and the matter is delayed. On the representations made to the department by tlie British Board of Trade, we have thought that it would be in the interest of navigation and for the improvement of the St. Lawrence route if in such cases it should not be necessary for the commissioner to wait the arrival of the minister to get the necessary authorization. speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
My hon. friend promised us, when the resolution was going through the Committee of the Whole, that



lie would, produce tlie request of the British Board of Trade. It is that I was referring to.

I have not with me to-night, owing to the absence of the deputy minister, the representations which were made to the department on this subject. But I suppose the hon. gentleman will take my word that this amendment has been demanded in the interests of navigation and shipping.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Of course, I would be happy to take my hon. friend's word, although he has hardly kept his promise with regard to producing the document. On section 3,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This is intended to apply to masters, mates or engineers. Wliv not apply it also to pilots ?
Because there is a Pilotage Act which deals with them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What provision is there in the Pilotage Act to cover such cases ?
Chapter 180 of the Revised Statutes of Canada contains all the provisions respecting pilots.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
As I understand it, this Bill is intended to provide speedy means of Inquiry into marine casualties, but the power given the officials appointed to investi-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
gate only covers certain officers. Why not make it competent for them to inquire iuto the conduct of the pilot ?
Because all that is dealt with in the Pilotage Act. We have special legislation as regards pilots.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Take the case of a stranded steamer in which it is perfectly clear the stranding is due to the fault of some one. There is a dispute as to whether it was due to the fault of the pilot or the captain or some of the officers. You are taking power to investigate the conduct of the officers, but can you use the investigation for the purpose of dealing with the pilot. If not, why should you make any distinction between the masters or officers and the pilot.
Especially as it is not likely you could know in advance who is responsible. It might be the pilot.

Investigation into the conduct of pilots is provided for in chapter 80 of 49 Victoria. And I may say that one of the reasons advanced in favour of the Department of Marine and Fisheries taking charge of the pilotage between Montreal and Quebec and the River Saguenay is precisely the reason advanced by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke). In order to put the whole thing under one control, another Bill has been introduced ; the consideration of which has been postponed until Tuesday next. This Bill will have the effect of putting under control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries investigations to be held as regards the conduct of pilots. That is under chapter 74 of 49 Victoria.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But this Act contemplates the appointment of an official to inquire into cases of stranding and so on. Why not give this officer power to deal with the pilot as well as with the master, mate and engineer V

I cannot do it under this Bill, and that is why another Bill has been introduced. If that passes, then, under the amended law, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would be authorized to make regulations and give power to an officer to investigate casualties, and to take cognizance of offences of the pilot as well of the other officers. I think it is a good move and, as 1 stated when that Bill was under discussion, it has been recommended by the Board of Trade of Montreal, the shipping interests, and the harbour commissioners. And, to the credit of the pilots of the district, I must say that they have unanimously asked to be taken under control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. That is the reason for bringing the Bill before the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Suppose that an investigation is held under the provisions of the Bill now before us and the investigating officer iinds that the master, engineer and mate are blameless, but that it is the pilot who is responsible, what will be the modus then ?

Under the Act which I am proposing to amend by this Bill, the investigating officer will have no authority, because it is a different class of people who have to be dealt with and they must be dealt with in a different manner and under a different law. But, in order to attain the end that the bon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) desires, the Pilotage Act also will be amended so that the commissioner who is called upon to investigate casualties under the Act may investigate, at the same time, the conduct of the pilot but with a little difference because there are certain provisions which will be followed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Is the Bill to which the minister refers printed ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AN1) FISHERIES. Yes. It is the Bill, the consideration of which has been postponed until Tuesday, at the request of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax), in order to allow the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) to be present when it is discussed). And Quebec too V

No, as regards Quebec, I have to say that we have been unable to come to an understanding. And we do not care to coerce them. After all, as everybody consents to the change that is proposed respecting pilots between Montreal and Quebec, it might be just as well to wait and see how this law works. If it is satisfactory, no doubt the pilotage authority of Quebec will come to the same conclusion as that of Montreal, and so the authority of the Department of Marine and Fisheries will be extended, with the consent of the harbour board and pilots of the district of Quebe.

Yes.
