speechtext:
In what way do the provisions of this Bill bring the pilot who m y be in charge of a vessel below Quebec, for 407i
instance, and who may be found to have been derelict in his duty in case of stranding or other accident, under the discipline-if I may use the term-of the commissioner who is to inquire into cases of marine accident ?

It will not bring the pilots below Quebec under the authority of the 1 >epartment of Marine and Fisheries, for the reasons I have explained, that we could not come to an understanding with the pilots and harbour commissioners of Quebec. So, the law regarding casualties cannot be adopted to apply to those pilots. But, under the authority of the law that is proposed, it will apply to the pilots from Montreal to Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not think the hon. minister has quite met what is suggested by my hon. friend form West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The Bill (No. 261) will place the pilots between Montreal and Quebec under control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but not so the pilots below Quebec. This Bill that we are discussing will have no effect upon them.

Of course not. If I had succeeded in getting the control of all the pilots on the St. Lawrence route I could have consolidated the two laws. But, as the control by the pilotage authority of Quebec over their own pilots remains, including the control of investigations, I thought we might as well leave the two laws existing, but change the authority vested in the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. If, in a year or two, it is possible to come to an understanding with the pilotage authority of Quebec, we can consolidate the two laws, and have authority which will deal with faults or negligence on the part not only of masters, mates and engineers, but of pilots as well.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I believe the hon. minister is working in the right line. Personally, from all I have been able to gather concerning the state of affairs, I think it is better to have the authority vested in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. But take section 21 of the Act as it is proposed under this Bill :
The certificate of a master, mate, or engineer may be cancelled or suspended by a court bolding a formal investigation, if the court finds that any loss, or damage, or the abandonment or stranding of any ship, or any loss of life has been caused by the wrongful act or default of such master, mate, or engineer

and so on. I would ask the minister if it is not possible and practicable to add the word ' pilot ' either before or after ' master,' mate or engineer,' so as to give the commissioner who is to be appointed under the provisions of this Act. power, after having made an investigation if he finds a pilot

guilty of dereliction of duty, to impose a penalty upon him ? This Bill only gives the commissioner power to impose a penalty upon a master, a mate or an engineer ; why mt include the pilot as well, if he is the officer of the ship who was primarily responsible for the accident ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AN1) FISHERIES. For the reason I have explained. On account of the misunderstanding that exists we have to keep the two statutes separate. I have explained that the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec, and the shipping interests as well as the pilots, who are a corporation, were strongly opposed to any change.
Have we not power in this parliament to make any regulation we please ?

Certainly we have, but it would be a change involving the obliteration to a certain extent of a corporation which has existed for nearly a century. The pilots are jealous of their rights and privileges, and think they can manage their own affairs better under present conditions than the Department of Marine and Fisheries could do it for them. Well, after studying the question, we thought the present was not an opportune time to force them, especially in view of the fact that the sliipping interests were not favourable to a change. If the shipping interests were favourable to the change we might then have concluded that, in the interest of transportation and of the safety of the St. Lawrence route, we would be justified in ignoring the prejudices of the pilots, and passing such a law as we thought proper. But none of the interested parties were willing that we should make the change, in fact they all opposed it; so we concluded that if we could not get a whole loaf, we would take a half loaf. In the city of Montreal the case is different, for there all the interested parties acceded to the wish of the government, and we are proposing a law which will be discussed by this House in a few days that will apply to Montreal. We could have included in the provisions of that Bill the Quebec pilots as well as those of Montreal, and bring them all under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but, as I have explained, the Quebec pilots and the shipping interests there were opposed to it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Then this Bill does not interfere with the pilots, and does not apply to any investigation into their conduct ? I,s the government afraid to tackle the question ?

No, we are not afraid of the pilots, but when we found that all the interested parties, all those who were in-Mr. CLARKE.
terested in making the navigation as safe as possible were opposed to the change, we did not insist upon making the change.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Did the harbour commissioners and the shipping interests oppose this Bill, or did they suggest that the government 'should not make provision in this measure for the appointment of a commissioner to inquire into the conduct of the pilots as well as into that of the masters and mates ?

They did. The harbour commissioners, the shipping interests as well as the corporation of pilots all opposed any change. I sent the same memorandum to the harbour commissioners at Quebec, to the pilots and the shipping interests of Quebec, that I sent to the shipping interests in Montreal, to the board of trade and to the pilots of Montreal. In Montreal everybody consented to the change and approved of it, asked that it should be made ; in Quebec, on the other hand, they all opposed it. .
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If it is in the public interest that a speedy and efficient means should be adopted to ascertain the cause of marine accidents and to impose penalties upon the officer responsible therefor, whether it be a master, a mate or an engineer, why should it not apply as well to the pilot, if he is the person in charge at the time the accident takes place ? Why not make a provision in this Bill to impose a penalty upon him ? I presume the minister is not consulting the interests solely of the pilots in Quebec or Montreal, but of the shipping interests generally, and endeavouring to improve the reputation which the St. Lawrence has. I think this is a very commendable Act, and I cannot understand why the government did not include pilots in the list of officers who may be dealt with by the commissioner.

It appears that I have failed to make myself understood by the hon. gentleman. I said that the pilots of Quebec, the harbour commissioners and the shipping interests of Quebec were all opposed to any change.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Opposed to the government providing a simple means of having an investigation speedily made into the cause of accidents to vessels ?
They have that already in Quebec.
Is this Bill to apply only to the river between Quebec and Montreal '!
With respect to pilots, yes.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I may be allowed to say a word with respect to the conditions existing at Quebec. The pilotage authority for the St. Lawrence is divided into two parts. For that part of the St. Lawrence extending from Quebec eastward to the gulf, it is under the control of the harbour commissioners of Quebec. The harbour commissioners of Quebec have succeeded to what was formerly known as the Trinity Board, and they are now the pilotage authority. They are the authority having absolute control over the pilots' certificates. and they alone can grant a certificate to a pilot, they alone can withdraw the certificate in case of default or misconduct on the part of the pilot. With respect to the pilotage between Quebec and Montreal, heretofore the pilots were under the control of the Montreal harbour commissioners. The Montreal harbour commissioners, as I understand it, granted the pilots' certificates and also had control over the pilots in case of an accident in the river. My hon. friend introduced this Bill for the purpose of dealing with masters, mates or engineers. These are under the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department, their certificates are under the control of that department who can deal with them under the law, and they now have the power of appointing a commissioner, acting under the Department of Marine and Fisheries, for the purpose of dealing with their certificates. They can deal with them in so far as they deal with the certificates of masters, mates or engineers who are under the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department. But, take a certificate of an English captain who comes out here. This certificate can only be dealt with by the board of trade on the other side. In so far as pilots between Montreal and Quebec are concerned, my hon. friend intends by the Bill that he proposes to deal with on Monday next (Bill 261) to place the pilots between Montreal and Quebec under the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department. If that is done, then, it will be optional with him to allow this officer, whoever he may be, to investigate all matters connected with the pilots there because they will be under his control. But, as the pilots below Quebec are left Tinder the control of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, the investigation in the case of an accident is held by the Harbour Commissioners. I may say that the investigation is as speedy as could possibly take place here, because the Quebec Harbour Commissioners are made up of a certain number of gentlemen who are appointed by the government, men representing the city of Quebec, the ship-owners and the merchants and for the purposes of pilotage there is added to the board the president of Ike corporation of pilots, a gentleman possessing expert knowledge. So that, there is a very speedy mode of dealing with the pilot at the time the accident occurs. The captain is obliged by law to report the accident forthwith and the Quebec Harbour Commissioners are obliged to hold this investigation. They have held these investigations and the results have been fairly satisfactory. As my hon. friend pointed out, when it was suggested to make a change all those interested in Quebec opposed any change. Speaking for myself personally I think it would be in the interests of the shipping of the St. Lawrence if all these accidents which occur on the St. Lawrence below) as well as above Quebec were investigated by a court of competent jurisdiction, or by the admiralty court. I would like to place these investigations absolutely beyond the control of such a thing as local influence and I think it would be a step in the right direction if my hon. friend could see: his way clear to make a change so that whenever an accident occurs on the St. Lawrence it would be promptly investigated by the admiralty court, a court which is absolutely qualified to investigate these measures, and the judges of which court have power to appoint assessors for the purpose of assisting them in work of that sort.
Do the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec get power to deal with these matters under the Pilotage Act or under some special legislation applicable to them ?

The Act which is applicable to the harbour commissioners gives them power to deal with these matters independently of the Act respecting pilots.
Mr. BORDEN, (Halifax). It is not under the general Pilolage Act that they proceed ?

No.
Chapter 80 of the Revised Statutes provides for the functions of these commissioners and they get control of the matter under their Act.
Am I correct in saying that the hon. Minister of Justice has just stated that the powers of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners are limited to investigating the conduct of pilots ?

Yes,
they have no jurisdiction to deal with engineers, mates or masters, because they have no control over their certificates.

May I ask the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries if there was

an investigation held into the accident to tlie Carolina wrecked in the Saguenay some time ago ?
Not yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is there going to be an investigation ?
Yes, instructions have been given.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That does not come under the control of the Pilotage Act.

The difficulty about the position, notwithstanding what the hon. Minister of Justice says, is this : I have had some experience in connection with the investigation of accidents under the very Act which is now being amended. Take such a case as that of the French steamship La Burgoyne which collided with the English ship Cromartyshire off the coast of Nova Scotia. We had an investigation under this statute and examined a number of persons who were not ordinarily resident in the province. They were witnesses who were going away in two, three or four days. They could never have been made available for an investigation by the Pilotage Commission, because the commission would not act quickly enough for that. The investigation was held two or three days after the arrival of the damaged ship in the Halifax harbour. If the suggestion of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) could be accepted, the evidence obtained in that way could be made available not only for dealing with tlie masters, officers and engineers, but for dealing with the pilots, whereas under the law as it stands- at the present time, you cannot thus deal with the pilots. Suppose a collision should take place off the harbour of Halifax and the witnesses left in, two. three or four days, or immediately after the investigation under this statute, how are you to get your evidence for the purpose of the investigation into the conduct of the pilots before the Pilotage Commission ? There should be no need of doing the work over again because the evidence which is available for dealing with the masters, engineers aud officers should be available in considering the case of the pilot. You close your investigation and the commissioner reports. You can deal with the masters, engineers and officers, but you cannot deal with the pilots. You may go on and hold your investigation before the Pilotage Commission but you cannot make the same evidence available and that seems to be a strong feature of the suggestion which my hon. friend makes. The pilots stand apart-in a different class altogether.
I admit that the difficulty
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
exists. We are trying to correct these difficulties but it takes some time to convince people that certain things should be done in a certain way. That is the reason why we have been obliged to proceed slowly, but we are moving as quickly as possible towards the point that we desire to attain. In regard to the pilotage of the Montreal district, if the departments had gone into this question without a spirit of conciliation or without a little diplomacy we would have been face to face with very great opposition. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal might have been as jealous of their privileges as the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec have been, and they might have said :	You are taking away part of our
privileges and we object to it. The pilots might have said : We would rather be under the control of the Harbour Commission of Montreal because we know the members of the commission and result would have been that this change might have been delayed for two or three years more. Instead of that we used persuasion, and we tried to convince them that it was in their own interests and in the interest of shipping that this change should be made. They have consented with a good grace and I hope this will be found to be a move in the right direction. I hope that the district of Quebec will come to the same conclusion, especially if this law gives satisfaction to the shipping interests.

I notice in to-day's paper an account of an accident which occurred to the steamer ' Hibernian ' leaving the port of Montreal, within a mile or two of her dock. An accident of a similar nature occurred to another steamer about two months ago right in the harbour of Montreal. Was there an investigation into the circumstances of that accident ?
There was.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Might I ask the result ?

The accident was found not to be the result of any fault of any of the officers ; it was a pure accident that might happen at any time. The accident was due to the fact that at the moment when the steamer was turning around to take the channel, when it was essential that the pilot should be able to see in order to clear his course, a very heavy storm broke over the ship so that the pilot could not see ten feet before him ; the boat sheered aud went aground. There was no fault on the part of the officers. It appears from information I have gathered in the department that the accident this morning occurred under somewhat similar circumstances. I do not wish to pre-judge the case, but it seems from information we have received that possibly those in charge of the steamer allowed the tug to leave her at a point too high in the

channel. An ordinance has been adopted by the harbour commissioners providing that steamship companies are not to allow the tugs to leave their steamers until they come to Maisouneuve, about a mile below the point where the accident occurred this morning, and it may be discovered that the accident was due to the fact that having full confidence that everything was all right, the tug let go and the steamer took a sheer. These accidents are sometimes due to special circumstances, and in this case it is stated that the steering apparatus became entangled in some way just at that moment. Of course, we will know the cause of the accident after the investigation has taken place.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.
Before the motion passes, might I again inquire as to whether the government proposes to bring down any railway subsidies, and if so, when we may expect to have them ?
Yes, railway subsidies will be brought down, I hope on Monday, certainly not later than Tuesday.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee.

We will take up an item in the main estimates that seems to have been overlooked.
New Brunswick-harbours and rivers-Camp-bellton wharf, extension and repairs, $14,400.

I think that this item was passed in a previous sitting but there seems to be a misunderstanding about that. It was allowed to stand at one time. The question arose as to whether the property was being acquired by the department by purchase or whether it was being acquired by expropriation. The information was not furnished to me by the officers of the department at the time, but I find that the property is being acquired by expropriation, and the matter is now in the Justice Department. They were served with notice under the Act and the property was taken over by the government at the time, but we have not yet had a report from the Justice Department regarding the matter.
Might I ask the minister why the item stood ?
Yes, I was not able to inform the House how the department was acquiring this property which belonged, I think, to a Mr. Shives, of Campbellton, New Brunswick.
The government is acquiring it in the regular way ?

The government' is acquiring it by expropriation and the property is now occupied by the Marine Department. It is returning good revenue.
'The MINISTER OF FINANCE. We will take up the supplementary estimates for the Public Works Department at page 9.
Public buildings, Ontario-Ottawa Parliament Buildings-additional accommodation, &c., $7,000.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC W'ORKS. This is intended to cover some further improvements in the attic of this building, which have been asked for by the senators. They complain that their committee room is rather small, and they have made application to the department for a larger one.

In this connection I would like to ask the minister to put the lavatories and bathrooms of the House of Commons into a somewhat more modern condition. There is not a shower bath in the whole establishment.
I will ask the engineer to look into that matter.
I must say that the senators set us a good example. AVhen we go to that end of the building and see what commodious accommodation they have, they put us to the blush.
We are living in hope that we may reach there some day.

In the meantime, it might be well for us to pay a little more attention to the accommodation we have here, though perhaps some of us may not require it very much longer. In this connection I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the atmosphere that permeates some of the rooms. Through the courtesy of the hou. gentleman, several of us have a room up stairs ; but that room, after it has been closed for ten or twelve hours, is positively not habitable for some time after the door is opened. There must be something radically wrong with the ventilation, not only of that room, but of several other rooms and of this Chamber as well. If the hon. minister would look into the subject of the ventilation of all the rooms of this building, he would do the members a substantial service.

The ventilation of this building has been a subject of discussion almost every session. I til ink there has been some improvement in this Chamber from the fans which have been put in. I am inclined to think that while the air is close, we get more fresh

air than formerly, and without a draft. Owing to the construction of the building, it seems impossible to keep the air fresh. I will bring the remarks of my hon. friend to the attention of the chief architect.
.Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). The accommodation around the House of Commons for people who have to do any work is very bad. I have got so tired of calling attention to the kind of accommodation we have in the vicinity of No. 6 and No. 4 that I am almost ashamed to mention it again. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) comforts me with the assurance that No. 6 and No. 4 will not matter much to us after this session, whatever he means by that. If there is to be any additional accommodation for the Senate side, I would be inclined also to put in a claim for the House of Commons side. We have 214 members here, some of whom have to do a good deal of work during the session, and they have their choice of doing it either in the House, when they should 'be listening to what is going on, or doing it under circumstances of very great inconvenience. Members are frequently obliged to hold interviews with people in the hall or in one of the corridors; and when I hold an interview with any gentleman who comes to see me I have to do it to the accompaniment of the click of the typewriter, or else the stenographer in my room has to go out into the hall and wait till the conference is over. While I do not know very much about the disposition of the rooms available at present, I certainly do think that the House of Commons side is in need of additional accommodation. perhaps to a greater extent than the Upper House.

There is no doubt considerable lack of accommodation. The ministers themselves have not the proper accommodation to receive those who want to see them. Parties desiring to interview the ministers have to wait out in the corridors. We are proposing, however, to give from six to eight additional rooms for the accommodation of members by fixing up the upper flat. There are some rooms to be fitted up on the commons side in addition to enlarging the committee room on the Senate side.

The most important change required is the ventilation of this chamber. Although this subject lias been discussed hundreds of times and efforts made from time to time to improve the ventilation, still it is very bad. After the House has been in session a number of hours, and particularly when the gallaries are filled, the air is almost poisonous. I would suggest that the Minister of Public Works should get some of the chemists in the department to test tlie air after the House lias been some hours in session ; and if they demonstrate that it Is dangerous to human life, possibly some-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
thing may then be done to improve it. A good ninny years ago, while the subject of ventilation began to attract attention in London, specimens of the atmosphere were collected in some of the court houses and houses of parliament and other public buildings. at certain hours when the ar was in a vitiated condition, and analysed, and. it was found that it was a source of danger to tlie lives of those who were compelled to breathe it. A good many of our members can obtain relief by remaining away, but those who desire to attend public business steadily, have to sit here almost continually when the House is in session and there can be no doubt that they suffer from tlie bad effects of breathing a vitiated atmosphere. So far as I can judge by my sense of smell, it is certainly not advisable to breathe the air of this chamber any length of time. Still, as one may be deceived by his senses, I would suggest that we should utilize the services of some of the skilful chemists in the government departments and get them to inform us of tlie exact character of that atmosphere in this chamber. Almost every prominent public man in Canada, ever since we have had a parliament has complained from time to time on this subject. I remember reading a speech of Mr. Edward Blake, in which lie complained that he was actually suffering from a species of poisoning when condemned to spend long hours in the House. He was afflicted with liead-aclies, which he had every reason to believe were caused by tlie impure air. It is notorious that a great many members suffer from illness during tlie session. Any one who comes in here from the pure fresh air, after the House has been in session some time, can satisfy himself that it must be the cause of a great deal of tlie ill-health of members of parliament. It is discreditable to us that such a condition should not be remedied. No man. can do his best work intellectually when he is not breathing pure air. A foul atmosphere causes excessive drowsiness which is a species of poisoning. If we are to do our best in this parliament, the atmosphere must be purified.
Especially tlie political atmosphere.

I am not going to introduce anything of a partisan character. I am very much in favour of having something done. For the last thirty-six years this subject has been discussed but nothing satisfactory has ns yet been done. No doubt the officials in charge of the ventilation are doing their best with the facilities at their command, still no reasonable man who has to spend hours in this chamber can fail to feel the ill effects of this vitiated atmosphere. But unless some demonstration be obtained, which can easily be had by making use of skilful scientific men, of the actual con-

dition of affairs, we will go on suffering the same evils.

This question of the ventilation of the chamber has provoked a good de!U of discussion. The problem of securing adequate and proper ventilation is indeed a most difficult one. This chamber in which we are assembled is a box surrounded by passages, with no sunlight except at these upper windows, and they are made as dark as possible. The radical defects in the construction of the building are so great that it is, perhaps, almost impossible to thoroughly remedy the difficulties under which we labour. I imagine that if we had these passages taken out and had this room extended to where we could get sunlight in through the windows and get air when we need it, a great improvement would be affected.
What is this change the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) suggests V

I am about to suggest a slight amelioration of the condition. We have at last, I believe, adopted a plan that 1 advocated for years, of forcing air into the Chamber toy means of fans. Formerly the air was brought in toy subterranean ducts from openings at the side of the hill. Thus, the air came to us practically through sewers, and it was poisonous and deleterious to our health. A good many long discussions had to take place before we could secure the remedy of that evil. I believe the air is (brought in now from where it is pure and forced in by fans. If we would adopt the precaution of allowing the air to escape, and so establish a current through the building, we should have tolerably fresh air. But there is a singular dislike on the part of many individuals to the feeling of a current of air. I have noticed it in crossing the continent on the train. If an attempt is made to ventilate the car, about half the inmates object, the ventilators have to toe closed and the air left vitiated and impure. We used to have windows opened at the top of this Chamber. I am told that, in consequence of putting in the fans, the opening of windows is not advisable, because the fresh air escapes by the windows, while the foul air settles near the floor. If we could have the doors and the outside windows open, and allow the air to pass in and out, the air in the Chamber would be improved. I frequently secure the privilege ,of having that done, and when it is done, I can realize almost instantly the improvement of the atmosphere in the Chamber. But when it is done persons in the Chamber complain of draught ; then the doors must be closed and the current of air stopped. The atmosphere is allowed to stagnate and so to become foul. I advise that the doors be kept open when the weather is moderate enough to allow of this
being done without danger. If the doors are kept closed, the air that is forced in lies dead and grows stagnant, carbonic acid gas is formed and the atmosphere grows more and more deleterious. And the consequence is, as my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) suggests, headaches, lassitude and depression, and all the other results that attend foul and vitiated air. Whether we can ever thoroughly remedy the defects of the ventilation of the Chamber is a question ; but the simple plan I have suggested would give relief. Why it is not permitted, I am unable to understand. Of course, there may be a little current of air in some part of the Chamber that may not be pleasant, but that can be met by putting on additional clothing if a person feels the draught. I secure the opening of doors when Mr. Speaker is in the Chair, and I hear no complaints. If we were simply to allow the air to enter and leave the Chamber that would be a partial remedy of the evils from which we suffer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on this subject of ventilation, as I think the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) who has just taken his seat are directed at me. When tlie windows and doors are open, there is, as you can well understand, a draught passing through the Chamber, and those of us who sit at the Table have our legs bathed in cold air. All three of us, after some hours of such an experience, have had our legs as numb as they can be to the knee. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat is. not very often in the House, nor does he remain very long when he comes. He is free to come in and go out as he pleases. And I have told him, when he has come to me to have the doors open, that it is well enough for one who is free to enter or leave the Chamber, but that I was nailed to my seat for about seven hours a day for months past. The hon. gentleman could go out and get fresh air if he wanted it, without compelling myself and others to sit in a draught that would bring on illness. Regarding the thing simply as a matter of self-preservation, I think the liou. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) is safer in his seat than I in mine, and he should have some compassion and pity on those of us who are forced to remain in the Chamber.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax), Might I ask why Mr. Deputy Speaker does not, under such circumstances, call the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charltonl to the . Chair ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that is what I shall have to do.
I shall be glad to show that it can be done without injury to one's health.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let me tell lion, gentlemen of another thing which nearly destroyed us who sit at the Table. Under the Table is a box that covers a register, through which a fan down below drives cold air. The cold air, striking the under side of the Table, was carried along so that we who sat at the Table had our legs bathed in it constantly. The ' Hansard ' reporters were often forced to raise the lid of the letter-box at the end of the Table so as to keep this cold air from blowing.in their faces. After two or three sessions, I discovered by accident last year that there was such a trap for our health, and, of course, I went to the engineer and had it closed. I believe I have the thanks of the parties who were being destroyed by this system of ventilation for what I did. Unless a better system of ventilation were adopted I certainly would resign my position and go home, rather than stay in the draught between the doors and windows. Then, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) were appointed to my place, he also would go home, not to his own house, but to his long home.
Mr. HUGHES '(Victoria). Eight or nine years ago this matter received a good deal of attention, and I was requested iby some hon. gentlemen then on the government benches to look into it. As a result of suggestions of mine, some improvements were made in various parts of the building. My object was to draw the foul air off. That was the proper principle. The foul air could be drawn out below and the pure air sent in higher up. You will find that the case at the present moment. At times the atmosphere is almost unbearable in this Chamber. The temperature at the present time is nearly 70 ; that is too high for men to sit long in one room. I am satisfied that a very simple principle of ventilation could be evolved. The system at present in vogue appears to be this : The air is forced in over the towers from the underground ducts below. It enters the Chamber from above the galleries. It is bumped over the towers on the sides of the Chamber at both ends. I do not know where it comes in, but it should come in from points high up in this Chamber, and should come in in good volume. If necessary that air could be warmed in cold weather, so that it would not be dangerous to hon. gentlemen who are getting baldheaded. But if taken hold of in a businesslike way, I think a satisfactory system could be evolved, and I trust the Minister of Public Works, before he leaves the office, will secure for us a modern system of ventilation by which the air is drawn out at the bottom and brought in, either cold or warm, at the fop.
1 will bring the remarks of the hon. gentleman to the attention of the chief architect, who I know has given a great deal of atten-
tion to this matter. I am afraid that it is owing to the peculiar construction of the building that we have this difficulty.

I have not heard any very lucid explanation of this $7,000 that is asked for. I have- not heard of any plan being submitted. I think the minister ought to give us some idea of what is to be done with this money. He says in a general way there is some fixing up to be done in the third or fourth stories.
I have not got detailed plans and specifications.
Tell us how you got that $7,000.

We have taken $10,000 in the main estimates, and I then gave all the information of the purposes for which it was required. In addition we are asking for this $7,000 with which the chief architect informs me he can fit up additional rooms in the attic, 1 think three or four. Then a committee of the Senate consisting of the Speaker, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, and the Clerk. I think, waited upon me and asked that some change should be made in the Senate Committee Room. The chief architect thinks that with this $7,000 additional he will be able to make the improvements that were asked for.
Harbours and rivers-Port Arthur and Port William, additional dredging, $75,000.

This is the amount which the chief engineer thinks should be spent at present in these harbours under the plan we have adopted. All the details of the plan have not yet been worked out. The total cost at Port Arthur under the general plan will be about $103,000.
Is that all for dredging ?
Practically. It gives twenty-one feet clear.
Is this work to he done both in the harbour at Tort Arthvfr and on the river ?
Yes.
Does it involve any work on the Mission river ?

Yes. I gathered together all the plans and asked the engineer to make a report. The general plan as outlined here is being carried out. All the appropriations have been spent under a general plan at Port Arthur and Fort William. These improvements will cost in the neighbourhood of $500,000. Those to be done with this money are the most urgent, so that boats may be enabled to get up to the present wharf.
Does tlie present expenditure involve the deepening of tlie Mission river, or is that only part of the larger plan ?

All this work is being carried out under a general plan, and includes the deepening of the Mission river and of the Kaministiquia river, and the dredging for the wharf. I do not think any work will be started on land this season.
How much is to be spent on the Kaministiquia river V
I think, to make all the improvements provided under that plan, it will take about $115,000.
What depth of water will there be in the river ?
Twenty-one feet clear.
Is this work being done by contract or by day labour ?
I think most of the dredging is done by contract, at fifteen cents a yard.

I would like to ask the minister if this sum is in addition to the large amounts of money that have been spent in these harbours during the last five or six years, now amounting to an enormous sum. This is in addition to the very large amount of money that was spent on these harbours during the last eight or ten years. You are going to spend a large amount of money on this harbour. I suppose this is to accommodate' the large vessels going in there and taking cargoes of grain from that port. I did expect that the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) would rise up in his might and say that we are wasting the money of this country, because we are going to be able to carry such enormous quantities of grain by the cheap route that he is advocating that this harbour will become useless. You must accept one horn of the dilemma or the other. We must understand whether we are going to spend this money well in improving our water-ways or whether we are going to spend a large amount of money badly so that as the hon. member for North Norfolk has said grain can be carried so much more cheaply by the all-the-year-ronnd route that he speaks of. I do not know why we should go on and spend so much money on a harbour which is going to be closed up during a portion of the year. Either one plan or the other must be at fault and I would like to know which plan is at fault.

The hon. gentleman should bear in mind, that the blessings to be derived from the transcontinental railway. which will be all that I have depicted, cannot be secured to the country for five
or six years yet. In the meantime, we will need to improve our present methods of transportation from the west, and I apprehend that we shall never entirely dispense with the lake route for reaching the sea. In looking to the future, we have the fact before us that in all probability we shall have a very large market for our food products in the United States. The tendency in the agricultural states is to lessen, year by year, the produtcion of wheat. I remember when the state of Illinois and the state of Iowa were great wheat-producing states, when these two states made a leading business of the production of wheat. To-day neither of these two states grows its own bread.
Does our grain go in there duty free ?

You can travel over both of these states for hours and hours without seeing an acre of wheat. It is said that , the state of Minnesota will cease to produce its own bread within 25 years. Under this condition of things, with the urban population of the United States increasing as rapidly as it is, and there being ten millions or twelve millions of inhabitants in the cities of the central and middle states, we look forward to the time when the United States will be a very large consumer of the food products of our western prairies. Already there is an agitation in the United States for the removal of the duty upon wheat. The removal of the duty upon wheat will be secured in a comparatively short time. When we reach that enormous market we will not reach it to any great extend by the transcontinental railway. The transcontinental railway will serve tlit purpose of carrying our export wheat on its way to Europe, but with the cities that are now' existing, the cities that are growing rapidly, and with the towns of over 4,000 population, having a large number of inhabitants in New England and the middle states, the time is coming when they will depend very largely upon the prairies in the Northwest for their food, and while building the transcontinental railway will improve our facilities for reaching the market of the world and will secure, as far as circumstances will allow, the trade for our own seaports, we will still have in that great country, which has now a population of eighty millions, and likely to be one hundred millions within the life of some men in this House, an ever-increasing market. The shackles placed upon the trade of these two countries will be removed to a large extent, and we shall need the great lakes, wTe shall need the harbour of Port Arthur with 21 or 22 feet of water, we shall need improved facilities for navigation upon the lakes, and this will not interfere with the operation of tlie transcontinental railway or with any other mode of communication that we may adopt for reaching our own sea-

ports for the purpose of exporting our food products to Europe.

We are really grateful for this essay, this delightful word picture, from the hon. memBer for North Norfolk. While it is not very practical, it is certainly very pleasing to listen to. We are going to have the markets of the United States as a result of the deepening of the channel that we are now speaking of. This is going to afford us a market in the United States of one hundred- million people. We have it on authority of the hon. member (Mr. Charlton) that the United States are going to remove the duty on wheat and bread-stuffs and allow the products of this country to go in free, and on that account we are required to deepen the waters of Port Arthur. I do not know what traffic that magnificent railway he has advocated that can draw such an enormous number of trains, each of 2,000 tons of wheat the year round and every day in the year, is going to secure, but he promises to develop the North-west country to a most extraordinary extent. I think that the government should be startled at the extraordinary development that is to be brought about by the hon. gentleman in connection with this railway scheme. I do not think anything could bring home to the minds of the people more clearly the ridiculousness of the project which has been advocated by the hon. gentleman than the statement that we are going to have a market of one hundred millions of people flo the south of us for our breadstuff's.
Why not take it round by way of Quebec, and send it from there ?

I think our friends at Quebec will find that they are going to have a lean time with that road north of the height of land, up in that magnificent clay belt. I say we should call a halt, because we must accept either horn of the dilemma. Either we are doing wrong in building that railway or we are doing wrong in expending a lot of money in improving our navigation. 1 contend that the government are perfectly right, and that the country is perfectly right in going on and improving the navigation of our water-ways and in providing every facility for getting our grain out in that direction. I believe that we should adopt the plan that was suggested not only by the bon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), but by the hon. ex-Minlster of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and spend our money in our own country to bring out our grain to our own ports. I contend that we should spend our money on such projects as are before us, and that we should not go ahead and spend money upon the projects which has been advocated so loyally, so strongly and so learnedly by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). I have no objection to spending money on the harbour of Port Arthur and
upon the harbour of Fort William. This is in the right direction.
Will that $160,000 to be spent at Port Arthur give a depth of 21 feet of water ?
That is the estimate of the chief engineer of the department.
Then, as to Fort William, how much is it proposed to spend there ?
Including the river, and to give a depth of 21 feet all around, it is proposed to expend $300,000, and probably a little over that.
How much has been spent in the past ?
Since confederation there has been $550,000 expended.

I do not object to the expenditure in connection with the deepening of these harbours, but do think that where so much money of the people is expended that it should be expended in a proper way and under proper supervision. A large amount of money is paid out for the dredging of these rivers. Would it not be better to have a proper plan for the whole work, and to let it by contract ? I am satisfied that in that way it could be much more cheaply and satisfactorily done. I do not see why, on an important work of this kind the government of Canada should find it necessary to do part of this work by the day and part of it by the yard, instead of having a proper plan and estimate made, and then letting the work by contract. I am satisfied that a great deal of money would be saved if that were done. I do not object to the expenditure, but I think we should have some better system. I would ask whose dredges are doing this by the day or by the yard. I have been talking with contractors about this work at Port Arthur and they say that we are not getting the best value for our money, and that the work there is costing too much.

I think my hon. friend has been misinformed. I know Mr. Boone, of Toronto, and I think he has the best dredging plant in Canada. From the reports of the auditors of the department, I learn that no contractor has given better satisfaction than he has. I may say that I have heard from parties who have been pressing for this work, absolutely no complaint. Neither the mayor, nor the members of council, nor leading citizens, men interested in the shipping irrespective of political parties who have been here have complained to me of the work that is being done. The hon. member finds fault with everything we are trying to do. I admit as he does that pos-

sibly we may not get the best value for our money owing to the fact that we have not a plan, but I am having a plan and survey made and.then perhaps we may be able to let the work by contract and perhaps get it done at a cheaper rate, but so long as we have no survey and no plan it will be understood that owing to the great variation in the nature of material to be moved you cannot very well make a contract except at various prices, because any person knows that you cannot move hard-pan and rock, &c., for the same price as you can earth, so that we either have to have it done under our own supervision and pay for it according to the material moved or have a plan and survey and let a contract.

I can quite understand that where there is a small contract there can be no objection to the department letting the work by the yard or by the hour, but where nearly half a million dollars is being expended it seems to me to be remarkable that we should have to farm it out by the yard. It is not that the work is not properly done, I suppose you can always get the work done, but at a great cost ; my objection is to the amount the work is costing when let in this manner. I suppose that this gentleman is a competent contractor, and that his plant is a good one, but that is not the qeustion. Sixteen cents a yard seems to be an enormous price, more particularly when there is such a large amount of work to do. The department have under contract the dredging of Owen Sound harbour, and I am satisfied that if the department had done that by the yard it would have cost them twice as much as they are paying by contract. Hence I think it would be better for the government to either cease work or to do as little as possible until they have prepared plans and specifications in order that a contract may be let for this work.
That is exactly what I am trying to do now.

We are approaching, if I understand the minister's estimates, an expenditure of $600,000. First there is the work at Fort William costing half a million dollars and then there is the work at Port Arthur costing $160,000, but the vote asked up to the end of .Tune of next year is altogether only $75,000. It seems to me that such a trifling estimate can only be a drop in the bucket for such a large expenditure and I would ask the minister how lie proposes to apportion this $75,000, what proportion he intends to spend1 at Port Arthur and what at Fort William and whether the work will be done this fall or next spring.
Tlie lion, gentleman has rather exaggerated the figures I gave.
I think $500,000 was the right amount for Fort William ; 1 took it down at the time.

The total estimate of the engineer was $593,000. My hon. friend's error has arisen through his taking the $600,000, or properly $593,000, which is the total estimate for both, Fort William and Port Arthur and adding to it the $163,000 which is the estimate for Port Arthur. It is true that this is a very large expenditure, but my hon. friend will see that we have an amount in the main estimates, I do not remember exactly what amount, and between that and the $75,000 I think we will make very fair progress in that work. This vote is only until the 30th of .Tune of next year. The work is going on now under the estimate.
I agree with my hon. friend, I would like to have been in a position to have plans for this work which will be of great assistance in improving our transportation facilities. When we have completed our improvements there and at Port Colbome I have every confidence that we will reap very material advantage. After we have perfected out plans and completed the surveys we will probably get a great deal more value for our money, but at the same time we could not afford not to go on with this work now because we have had boats standing outside the harbour in the deep water lightering into the wharfs because they were not able to come alongside. Therefore a certain amount of this work had to be proceeded with and I am pleased to know that it has been done on plans that are part of the general plan so that there is no wasting of money in the works that are now going on and they are giving great satisfaction this season because they enable the boats to get up to the wharfs. This is Very important as some of the finest elevators on the continent are now being built there. We are pressing the work. I am unable to say how much is being done at each of these two places because the chief engineer places the dredge wherever the work is most urgent in order to enable the boats to get 1o the wharfs.

Does the hon. gentleman not think that 10 cents a yard is an enormous figure for dredging at Port Arthur ? I am satisfied as I said that Mr. Boone is competent to do the work and that his plant is all right, but the price that is being paid is extremely large. Is work being done at as high prices in any other place ? Tlie ex-Minister Of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) expressed the opinion that it was much cheaper when the work was done by dredges owned and controlled by the government. He said that in that way the work could be done for one-half what contractors charge. I believe that and I think he estimated that dredging could be done by the government dredge for 3 cents

per yard. If that is the case, 16 cents a yard is an enormous price.

I did not say 1G cents ; the average rate estimated by the chief engineer is 15 cents. The price depends altogether on) the materials and the conditions under which the dredging is being done. I do not think that any one who is an authority on these matters would be able to stand up and say whether it can be done better by contract or by government-owned plant ; the cost will be regulated altogether by the conditions. Some material at Port Arthur costs as much as $1.25 to move, some costs 40 cents and the average is 15 cents.

The dredging at Port Arthur is not hard as the material is principally mud, and therefore I think that 16 cents is a very large amount. Have you any similar work being done on the Georgian bay except at Port Arthur where the price is as high as 16 cents a yard ?

The price is fifteen cents not sixteen cents. The chief engineer informs me that that is the average price for the same kind of work all over the Dominion. The prices on the American side are very much higher-so much so that some of the dredges have left Canada, and we had to offer extra inducements to keep some of the plant here.

I am surprised that any one in the department should say that the government are in the habit of paying fifteen cents per yard for dredging on the Georgian bay. Pour or five years ago it was done at half that price. I think it is desirable that all these harbours should be deepened to twenty feet. At the same time, I think we shall get very little for the amount of money we are spending. The contractors will make immense profits. Who is doing this work ?
The Great Lakes Dredging Company.
Is that the only company you have at work at Port Arthur V

No, we have also Mr. Boone, of Toronto. There are four dredges at work. I am anxious to press on the work faster, but it is impossible to procure mare dredges at the present time. I am acting under the advice of the chief engineer, and according to his estimate, these amounts of $85,000 and $75,000 will cover all the work for which we can procure plant.
Will the minister tell us how the prices he pays for contract work will compare with what it costs to do the work with our own dredges ?
I am unable to tell the hon. gentleman, the conditions vary so much.
The officials of the department should be able to keep track of the work, so that the hon. minister could tell.
If we had a systematic set of books we could probably make comparisons. But my hon. friend is asking me to give him the information now.
When may I expect it, if not now V
I can give the hon. gentleman the cost of dredging at any particular place.

1 think the minister will admit that the question is a fair one, and is not at all captious. 1 simply wish to know whether it pays better to do the dredging by contract or with our own dredges and under our own supervision.
I am not able to answer that question.
Can you do it during the session V

I cannot say. It would require considerable experimenting. For instance, the work in the St. Lawrence channel is estimated to cost three cents a yard. That of course does not include interest on the plant, expenses during the winter, payment of officers, and many other things ; nor are the conditions there to be compared with the conditions in small harbours. If a dredge is sent to do dredging for a week at a small port, the expense of its going and coining would form a large part of the cost.

I quite understand the statement made by the hon. minister. I know that he pays more for a small job than he does for a large one. At the same time, we have owned some dredges for a good many years, and it seems to me that the department ought to be able to give some information as to the cost on this point.

I do not consider my hon. friend's question a captious question at all ; but If my hon. friend understood the conditions as I do, he would see the difficulty of making the comparison. I do not know of any work that has been, done for some time which would afford a basis for comparison.

The ex-Minister of Public Works gave a good deal of attention to this matter. He made a statement to the effect that the government with their own dredges could do this work at half the figures the contractors charge. The dredging at Port Arthur is not difficult because it is soft substance and ought to be the cheapest class of work. The hon. gentleman is paying fifteen cents per yard while the exMinister of Public Works said that the gov-

eminent dredges would do the work for three cents a yard. There is an appropriation of $75,000 here. No doubt it is a year or more since the government entered into a contract to pay fifteen cents per yard, and this is for additional dredging. Does the hon. gentleman purpose asking for new tenders in connection with the expenditure of this $75,000, or will he simply hand it over to these people and pay them the same prices they have been charging all along ?

The intention is to' go on with this work at the prices arranged for. I have already explained that some dredges have left Canada already because they get better prices on the other side. That applies to the northern and southern districts.
Are Canadian dredges allowed to work at American ports 7
Yes, in bond, under the same regulations as American dredges are subjected to here.
Are the government satisfied with the work 1 J. Israel Tarte ' is doing this year 7
The dredge or the gentleman ?
The gentleman is turning up more mud than the dredge.

The hon. gentleman quoted the ex-Minister of Public Works, I am not going to assume responsibility for statements made by the ex-minister. Any statements I make with regard to this or other matters will be on information obtained by myself and for which I will be responsible. Sometimes the dredge ' Tarte ' does very good work.

Has the government dredge which was lost on Lake Ontario at Bowmanville been taken up yet 7
' The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. I have already stated several times that no government dredge was lost at Bowmanville. There was a dredge called after the First Minister lost there but it had no connection directly or indirectly with the government.
Is this the only item for dredging in the supplementary estimates 7
No, I am sorry to say it is not. We will come to Nova Scotia by and by.
The minister has not answered the question I have put him. Is it his intention to spend this $75,000 by handing over the work to the companies doing it at their present prices 7

1 do not exactly like the term used by my hon. friend. It is not the intention to hand this money over to anybody, but to have
the work done under the contract made with the department.
When was it made ?
This season. It was a renewal of the prices last season.
It is simply a renewal of the contract at the same prices. Did the hon. gentleman ask anybody else to tender 7
Yes, we have been very active in asking all over tlie country, and I am sorry to say we had to go to the other side of the line to get some of our work done.
Who are the partners in this Great Lake Dredging Company 7
I do not know, but I will get the information and bring it down.
In view of the fact that there is difficulty in getting dredges, is the government considering the propriety of building additional dredges 7
1 think that is a matter of very great importance. I am asking several votes which 1 hope will meet the approval of the House.
Is mot this firm an American one ?	[DOT]
I think that Mr. Bowman, of Southampton, is the principal man. but cannot say positively.
Are they Canadian or American dredges 7
Altogtlier Canadian, so my chief engineer informs me. I shall get the information and bring it down.
The names of the partners -and where the headquarters are 7
Is Mr. Connolly or Captain Sullivan in that company ?
Not that I am aware of. I know nothing directly or indirectly, but they may be.

Does the department know whether or not the deepening of the Mission river will result in lengthening the season during which grain can be carried from Fort William and Port Arthur to the Georgian bay ports 7 Last year 1 went to the mouth of the Mission river in a tug boat, and it was pointed out to me that the opening of the river and the nse of the new -channel created in that way would result in lengthening the season by ten or twelve days.

Representations have been made to the department that that would be the result, but the chief engineer will not take the responsibility of endorsing them. When we have these surveys completed, we will have more definite information to work on.
Mr. THOMSON (Grey), I understand that the hon. minister has promised to bring down the names of those who were in the firm, where their headquarters are and who are connected with this Great Lake Dredging Company.

Yes.
Kingston graving dock-to pay amount of award made in favour of contractors Connolly & Co., by Mr. Justice Burbidge, July 2, 1896, under Orders in Council of January 29, and May 7, 1896, together with price of steam derrick purchased from said firm, interest thereon to be paid at the same rates as that received by the government on their counter claims against Connolly & Co., $46,096.12.

I found that Connolly & Company had several claims against the government and the government also had claims against them, some of them under judgment. This vote really represents some $5,000 or $0,000, being the difference between the amount which Connolly & Company owe the government and the government Connolly & Company. As I understand it, the position the Auditor General took was that the so-called judgment against us that Connolly had was an award of the judge of the Exchequer Court, and not a judgment, and that it was still at the discretion of parliament to pay the amount of that award or not. This matter has been standing for a long time, and I thought it unfair both to Mr. Connolly and the department, that these claims should remain so long. I referred the matter to the officials of the department, and they arranged with the Auditor General and the Finance Department aud all matters between the government and Mr. Connolly were adjusted, the balance being something between $5,000 and $6,000. The reason I cannot give the exact amount is that the Finance Department objected paying the interest that Connolly claimed, the award -or judgment, as he called it-of the Exchequer Court carried with it. I believe it was finally decided that on the judgments that we had against Connolly and the amounts due to him the rate of interest should be t ho same. This item is put in the way the Auditor General and the Finance Department worded it. So, I cannot give, to a few dollars, exactly what the difference would be, but it will not be more than I have stated. Practically we are voting this to ourselves.
Why does not the hon. minister take a vote only for the amount to be paid ?
Because the Auditor General objected to having it that way, and I am anxious to meet his views.
What work is this award for ?

The principal amount due to Connolly is m connection with the Kingston graving dock, and the principal judgment we have against Connolly is in connection with the Quebec harbour works. And' there is another in the hands of the Justice Department, in connection with some security given by Connolly for some person.
Transportation facilities-Port Colborne improvements-South-east breakwater, $25,000.
This item will involve considerable discussion.
There will be another item with relation to this work.
And the subject of this item can be discussed when the other comes up ?

Yes, if hon. gentlemen wish it.
